category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: What is the most common genetic skeletal dysplasia causing disproportionate short stature in children?
back: Achondroplasia.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): "Generalised skeletal abnormalities... Skeletal dysplasia, e.g. achondroplasia"

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: What specific bone growth process is disrupted by the FGFR3 mutation in achondroplasia?
back:
• Gain-in-function mutation in FGFR3 gene.
• Disruption of enchondral bone formation.
• Restricts longitudinal growth of long bones.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): "Achondroplasia is caused by a gain-in-function mutation in the FGFR3 (fibroblast growth factor receptor 3) gene... which affects enchondral bone formation."

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: How does the bone growth defect in achondroplasia affect physical skeletal proportions?
back:
• Disproportionate short stature.
• Limbs are significantly shorter than the trunk.
• Disproportionate limb-to-trunk ratio due to impaired long bone growth.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): "Patients present with disproportionate short stature where the limbs are shorter than the trunk, together with classical clinical and radiographic features"

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: How is achondroplasia classified in terms of prevalence among skeletal dysplasias?
back: It is the most common generalized skeletal dysplasia.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): [Achondroplasia is a generalized skeletal dysplasia... It is the most common skeletal dysplasia.]

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: Describe the effect of achondroplasia on the specific process of bone formation.
back: It primarily affects and impairs enchondral bone formation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): [Achondroplasia is caused by a gain-in-function mutation in the FGFR3... gene... which affects enchondral bone formation.]

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: What type of short stature is characteristic of achondroplasia?
back: Disproportionate short stature, where the limbs are shorter than the trunk.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): [Patients present with disproportionate short stature where the limbs are shorter than the trunk, together with classical clinical and radiographic features.]

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: A patient with achondroplasia reports progressive leg weakness. What anatomical complication is likely?
back: Spinal stenosis or underdevelopment of the foramen magnum causing neurological difficulties.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): [Underdevelopment of the foramen magnum and spinal stenosis can cause neurological difficulties.]

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: Identify the specific gene mutation and chromosome location associated with achondroplasia.
back:
● Gene: Gain-in-function mutation in FGFR3.
● Location: Short arm of chromosome 4.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): [Achondroplasia is caused by a gain-in-function mutation in the FGFR3 (fibroblast growth factor receptor 3) gene, located on the short arm of chromosome (Chr) 4.]

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: List the two classical pelvic radiographic features seen in achondroplasia.
back:
● Horizontal acetabulum.
● Square pelvic wings.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 613 (Book Page): [The acetabulum is horizontal and the pelvic wings seem square: classical features of achondroplasia.]

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: What are the characteristic radiographic findings in the long bones of achondroplasia patients?
back:
● Shortened limbs.
● Widened metaphyses.
● Overlong fibula relative to the tibia.
● Slight bowing.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 613 (Book Page): [radiograph... demonstrating short limbs, widened metaphysis, an overlong fibula and slight bowing.]

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: What is the inheritance pattern of achondroplasia?
back: Autosomal dominant.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): [It is autosomal dominant.]

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: How does the FGFR3 mutation physiologically inhibit growth in achondroplasia?
back: The "gain-in-function" mutation causes overactivity of the receptor, which negatively regulates/inhibits chondrocyte proliferation in the growth plate.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): [Achondroplasia is caused by a gain-in-function mutation in the FGFR3... gene... which affects enchondral bone formation.]

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: Which limb reconstruction techniques are sometimes used to address short stature in achondroplasia?
back: Limb-lengthening techniques and correction of limb alignment.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): [Correction of limb alignment may be necessary and limb-lengthening techniques are used in some countries.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What are the two characteristic radiographic features of chronic osteomyelitis?
back:
- Sequestrum: A piece of dead, devascularized bone.
- Involucrum: New bone formed around the infected area by the periosteum.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): [The infected bone reacts to the infection by separating dead fragments of bone (sequestration) and forming sinuses... New bone is laid down around the infection from the periosteum (involucrum).]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What mechanical conditions define the skeletal environment for direct (primary) bone healing?
back:
- Cortical apposition (zero gap).
- Absolute stability (no movement/strain).
- Compression across the fracture interface.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 445 (Book Page): [Direct bone healing... happens in an environment of cortical apposition and absolute stability with no movement or gap between the fracture fragments... squeeze the two bone ends together (compression).]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Contrast the characteristic skeletal failure in Greenstick versus Torus (Buckle) fractures.
back:
- Greenstick: Failure of the tension cortex with an intact compression cortex.
- Torus: Buckling/impaction of the compression cortex with no tension failure.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 442 (Book Page): [greenstick fractures, where one tension cortex fails. If the compression cortex buckles, they are called torus or buckle fractures.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Which Salter-Harris fracture type uniquely involves the epiphysis, physis, and metaphysis simultaneously?
back: Salter-Harris Type IV. This skeletal feature is associated with a high risk of focal physeal fusion and growth arrest.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 444 (Book Page): [Type IV – fracture line across the epiphysis, across the physis and across the metaphysis. This injury can cause focal fusion of the physis, leading to abnormal growth.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Identify the characteristic pelvic and femoral features of Achondroplasia on radiographs.
back:
- Horizontal acetabulum with square (iliac) pelvic wings.
- Disproportionately short long bones with widened metaphyses.
- Overlong fibula relative to the tibia.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [horizontal acetabulum and the pelvic wings seem square: classical features of achondroplasia... short limbs, widened metaphysis, an overlong fbula.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Categorize pelvic ring fractures according to the Tile classification of skeletal stability.
back:
- Type A: Stable (pelvic ring intact).
- Type B: Partially stable (rotationally unstable, vertically stable).
- Type C: Completely unstable (rotationally and vertically unstable).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 404 (Book Page): [Type A are the most common fractures and are completely stable... Type B... fractures are partially stable... Type C... fracture is completely unstable.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Compare the skeletal reduction goals for intra-articular versus extra-articular fractures.
back:
- Intra-articular: Anatomical reduction (restoring joint surface congruity perfectly).
- Extra-articular: Mechanical alignment (restoring length, alignment, and rotation).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 451 (Book Page): [intra-articular fracture = anatomical reduction. Fractures that do not involve the joint surface generally require restoration of mechanical alignment... extra-articular fracture = mechanical alignment.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: List the pathognomonic skeletal findings in Fibular Hemimelia.
back:
- Absent or hypoplastic fibula.
- Short, bowed tibia with an anteromedial apex.
- Foot anomalies: Absent lateral rays and ball-and-socket ankle joint.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 645 (Book Page): [Table 44.9... Absent lateral rays; tarsal coalition; ball-and-socket ankle joint... Absent or defcient fbula; short, bowed tibia.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What defining features are visible at the metaphysis and physis in active Rickets?
back:
- Widened physes (growth plates).
- Cupped and frayed (irregular) metaphyses.
- General osteopenia and skeletal bowing.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 636 (Book Page): [radiographs in cases of rickets demonstrate widened physes with cupped, fared metaphyses.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Define the skeletal boundaries of the three-column model (Denis) of spinal stability.
back:
- Anterior: ALL and anterior half of vertebral body.
- Middle: Posterior half of vertebral body and PLL.
- Posterior: Posterior elements/neural arch.
- Instability: Injury to ≥2 columns.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 410 (Book Page): [The spine can be divided into three columns: anterior, middle and posterior... If two or more columns of the spine are injured, it is considered unstable.]

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: Define achondroplasia and identify its primary genetic cause.
back:
- Most common skeletal dysplasia
- Caused by a gain-in-function mutation in the FGFR3 gene on chromosome 4
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Achondroplasia is caused by a gain-in-function mutation in the FGFR3 (fbroblast growth factor receptor 3) gene, located on the short arm of chromosome (Chr) 4, which afects enchondral bone formation.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: What is the specific effect of the FGFR3 mutation on bone growth?
back:
- Impairs enchondral bone formation
- Intramembranous ossification (e.g., vault of skull) remains normal
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Achondroplasia is caused by a gain-in-function mutation in the FGFR3... gene... which afects enchondral bone formation.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: Contrast limb and trunk growth proportions in achondroplasia.
back:
- Disproportionate short stature
- Limbs are significantly shorter than the trunk (rhizomelic shortening)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Patients present with disproportionate short stature where the limbs are shorter than the trunk, together with classical clinical and radiographic features

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: A child with achondroplasia presents with sudden limb weakness. What narrowing is likely?
back:
- Spinal stenosis
- Underdevelopment of the foramen magnum
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Underdevelopment of the foramen magnum and spinal stenosis can cause neurological difculties.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: What surgical approach is used to improve limb length in achondroplasia?
back:
- Limb-lengthening techniques (e.g., distraction osteogenesis)
- Correction of mechanical limb alignment
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Correction of limb alignment may be necessary and limb-lengthening techniques are used in some countries.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: What are the pathognomonic radiographic features of the achondroplastic pelvis?
back:
- Horizontal acetabulum
- Square pelvic wings
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 613 (Book Page): The acetabulum is horizontal and the pelvic wings seem square: classical features of achondroplasia.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: Explain the 'gain-in-function' nature of the FGFR3 mutation.
back:
- Mutation overactivates the receptor
- FGFR3 normally inhibits cartilage growth; overactivity causes excessive suppression of long bone growth
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Achondroplasia is caused by a gain-in-function mutation in the FGFR3 (fbroblast growth factor receptor 3) gene... which afects enchondral bone formation.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: How is achondroplasia differentiated from proportionate dwarfism?
back:
- Achondroplasia is disproportionate (limbs < trunk)
- Proportionate dwarfism (e.g., endocrine) involves equal stunting of limbs and trunk
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Patients present with disproportionate short stature where the limbs are shorter than the trunk

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: What is the inheritance pattern of achondroplasia?
back:
- Autosomal dominant
- Most cases result from spontaneous (de novo) mutations
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Achondroplasia is caused by... the FGFR3... gene... It is autosomal dominant.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: Identify the specific chromosome and arm associated with achondroplasia.
back:
- Chromosome 4
- Short arm (4p)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Achondroplasia is caused by a gain-in-function mutation in the FGFR3... gene, located on the short arm of chromosome (Chr) 4

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: Define Achondroplasia and identify its prevalence relative to other skeletal dysplasias.
back: Achondroplasia is the most common generalized skeletal dysplasia. It is a genetic condition characterized by disproportionate short stature.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Achondroplasia is caused by a gain-in-function mutation in the FGFR3 (fibroblast growth factor receptor 3) gene... Patients present with disproportionate short stature.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: Describe the specific pathophysiology and bone growth process affected in achondroplasia.
back: It is caused by a gain-in-function mutation in the FGFR3 gene on Chromosome 4, which inhibits enchondral bone formation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Achondroplasia is caused by a gain-in-function mutation in the FGFR3 (fibroblast growth factor receptor 3) gene, located on the short arm of chromosome (Chr) 4, which affects enchondral bone formation.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: Contrast the physical limb-to-trunk proportions seen in achondroplasia.
back: It causes disproportionate short stature. The limbs are significantly shorter than the trunk (rhizomelic shortening).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Patients present with disproportionate short stature where the limbs are shorter than the trunk, together with classical clinical and radiographic features.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: An achondroplastic infant presents with apnea and limb weakness. Which anatomical risk factor must be evaluated?
back: Underdevelopment of the foramen magnum. This can cause spinal stenosis and serious neurological compromise.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Underdevelopment of the foramen magnum and spinal stenosis can cause neurological difficulties.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: What is the inheritance pattern of the mutation causing achondroplasia?
back: It is an autosomal dominant condition, though many cases result from new spontaneous mutations.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): It is autosomal dominant. Patients present with disproportionate short stature.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: Name the classical radiographic hallmarks of the pelvis in achondroplastic patients.
back:
1. Horizontal acetabulum
2. Square-shaped pelvic wings
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 613 (Book Page): The acetabulum is horizontal and the pelvic wings seem square: classical features of achondroplasia.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: Apply the Hueter-Volkmann principle to explain limb shortening in achondroplasia.
back: The genetic mutation mimics excessive compressive force on the physis, inhibiting longitudinal growth via impaired enchondral ossification.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Achondroplasia... affects enchondral bone formation. [Table 44.1] Hueter-Volkmann principle: Compressive forces inhibit growth.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: Distinguish achondroplasia from rickets based on physeal appearance on X-ray.
back: Achondroplasia shows shortened metaphyses and square pelvis, while Rickets features widened, cupped, and frayed metaphyses.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 614 (Book Page): [Rickets] demonstrate widened physes with cupped, flared metaphyses. Page 613 (Book Page): [Achondroplasia] The acetabulum is horizontal and the pelvic wings seem square.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: How does the gain-in-function FGFR3 mutation disrupt the physiological growth loop?
back: It constitutively activates a signal that over-inhibits chondrocyte proliferation and maturation at the growth plate.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Achondroplasia is caused by a gain-in-function mutation in the FGFR3... gene... which affects enchondral bone formation.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: Identify the specific gene and chromosome arm associated with achondroplasia.
back: FGFR3 gene located on the short arm of Chromosome 4.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Achondroplasia is caused by a gain-in-function mutation in the FGFR3... gene, located on the short arm of chromosome (Chr) 4.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: What is the most common form of generalized skeletal dysplasia?
back: Achondroplasia.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): [Table 44.4] Generalised skeletal abnormalities: Skeletal dysplasia, e.g. achondroplasia

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: Which specific genetic mutation causes achondroplasia?
back: A gain-in-function mutation in the FGFR3 (fibroblast growth factor receptor 3) gene.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Achondroplasia is caused by a gain-in-function mutation in the FGFR3 (fibroblast growth factor receptor 3) gene, located on the short arm of chromosome (Chr) 4

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: How is the physical stature in achondroplasia classified regarding symmetry?
back: Disproportionate short stature (limbs are shorter than the trunk).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Patients present with disproportionate short stature where the limbs are shorter than the trunk

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: A child with achondroplasia presents with neurological deficit. What anatomical sites are likely involved?
back:
● Underdeveloped foramen magnum
● Spinal stenosis
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Underdevelopment of the foramen magnum and spinal stenosis can cause neurological difficulties.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: What surgical procedure is used to address shortened limbs in achondroplastic patients?
back: Limb-lengthening techniques.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Correction of limb alignment may be necessary and limb-lengthening techniques are used in some countries.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: What specific type of bone formation is disrupted in achondroplasia?
back: Enchondral (endochondral) bone formation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Achondroplasia is caused by a gain-in-function mutation in the FGFR3... gene... which affects enchondral bone formation.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: On which chromosome and arm is the FGFR3 gene mutation located?
back: The short arm of chromosome 4.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Achondroplasia is caused by a gain-in-function mutation in the FGFR3... gene, located on the short arm of chromosome (Chr) 4

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: What are the classical radiographic features of the pelvis in achondroplasia?
back:
● Horizontal acetabulum
● Square pelvic wings
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 613 (Book Page): The acetabulum is horizontal and the pelvic wings seem square: classical features of achondroplasia.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: What is the primary inheritance pattern of achondroplasia?
back: Autosomal dominant.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): It is autosomal dominant.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: What anatomical proportion is a hallmark of achondroplasia on clinical summary?
back: Limbs are shorter than the trunk.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 633 (Book Page): Achondroplasia affects enchondral ossification and presents with disproportionate short stature.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: What is the most common form of generalized skeletal dysplasia?
back: Achondroplasia.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): [Generalised skeletal dysplasias] Achondroplasia is caused by a gain-in-function mutation in the FGFR3...

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: What is the pathophysiology of bone growth inhibition in achondroplasia?
back: Gain-in-function mutation in the FGFR3 gene impairs enchondral bone formation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Achondroplasia is caused by a gain-in-function mutation in the FGFR3 (fibroblast growth factor receptor 3) gene... which affects enchondral bone formation.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: Contrast the limb-to-trunk ratio in achondroplasia with proportional short stature.
back: It is disproportionate; the limbs are shorter than the trunk.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Patients present with disproportionate short stature where the limbs are shorter than the trunk...

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: Where on the body do the hands of a child with achondroplasia typically reach?
back: Hands do not reach the midthigh due to short upper limbs.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 613 (Book Page): A child with achondroplasia: his upper limbs are short and his hands do not reach midthigh.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: What is the molecular 'gain-in-function' step that triggers achondroplasia?
back: Mutation in the FGFR3 gene, located on the short arm of chromosome 4.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Achondroplasia is caused by a gain-in-function mutation in the FGFR3 (fibroblast growth factor receptor 3) gene, located on the short arm of chromosome (Chr) 4.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: What are the two pathognomonic pelvic radiographic features of achondroplasia?
back:
• Horizontal acetabulum
• Square pelvic wings
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 613 (Book Page): The acetabulum is horizontal and the pelvic wings seem square: classical features of achondroplasia.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: Which two neurological complications can arise from skeletal underdevelopment in achondroplasia?
back:
• Underdevelopment of foramen magnum
• Spinal stenosis
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Underdevelopment of the foramen magnum and spinal stenosis can cause neurological difficulties.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: Differentiate the primary skeletal site of achondroplasia from typical spondyloepiphyseal dysplasias.
back: Achondroplasia primarily affects the physis/metaphysis (enchondral ossification) causing short limbs.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): ...which affects enchondral bone formation... the limbs are shorter than the trunk.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: What is the inheritance pattern of the common skeletal dysplasia, achondroplasia?
back: Autosomal dominant.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): It is autosomal dominant.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: True/False: Intramembranous ossification is the primary growth mechanism affected in achondroplasia.
back: False. It specifically affects enchondral bone formation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): ...mutation in the FGFR3... gene... which affects enchondral bone formation.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: Define the most common form of skeletal dysplasia and its primary growth defect.
back:
- Achondroplasia.
- It is an autosomal dominant condition that selectively impairs enchondral bone formation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): [Achondroplasia is caused by a gain-in-function mutation in the FGFR3... gene... which affects enchondral bone formation. It is autosomal dominant.]

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: What is the specific genetic and chromosomal cause of achondroplasia?
back:
- Gain-in-function mutation in the FGFR3 gene.
- Located on the short arm of chromosome 4.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): [Achondroplasia is caused by a gain-in-function mutation in the FGFR3 (fibroblast growth factor receptor 3) gene, located on the short arm of chromosome (Chr) 4]

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: Describe the characteristic clinical proportions of a patient with achondroplasia.
back:
- Disproportionate short stature.
- Limbs are significantly shorter than the trunk (rhizomelic shortening).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): [Patients present with disproportionate short stature where the limbs are shorter than the trunk]

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: Which two neurological complications arise from axial skeletal underdevelopment in achondroplasia?
back:
- Underdevelopment of the foramen magnum.
- Spinal stenosis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): [Underdevelopment of the foramen magnum and spinal stenosis can cause neurological difficulties.]

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: How does the mutation in FGFR3 affect the growth of cartilage in the physis?
back: It creates a gain-of-function effect that constitutively inhibits the proliferation of chondrocytes, disrupting enchondral ossification.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): [Achondroplasia is caused by a gain-in-function mutation in the FGFR3... gene... which affects enchondral bone formation.]

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: What are the classical radiographic features of the pelvis in achondroplasia?
back:
- Horizontal acetabulum.
- Square-shaped pelvic wings.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 613 (Book Page): [The acetabulum is horizontal and the pelvic wings seem square: classical features of achondroplasia.]

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: Why is the trunk length less affected than limb length in achondroplasia?
back: The defect specifically targets enchondral ossification (found in long bones) while intramembranous ossification remains relatively intact.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): [Achondroplasia... affects enchondral bone formation.]

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: Identify two common surgical interventions required for limb management in achondroplasia.
back:
- Correction of limb alignment (for bowing).
- Limb-lengthening procedures.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): [Correction of limb alignment may be necessary and limb-lengthening techniques are used in some countries.]

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: What is the inheritance pattern and recurrence risk for achondroplastic parents?
back: Autosomal dominant; though most cases are sporadic mutations, an affected parent has a 50% chance of passing the gene.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): [It is autosomal dominant.]

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: List three extremity features seen on a standing alignment radiograph of an achondroplastic child.
back:
- Shortened long bones.
- Widened metaphyses.
- Overlong fibula relative to the tibia.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 613 (Book Page): [demonstrating short limbs, widened metaphysis, an overlong fibula and slight bowing.]

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: What is the most common generalized skeletal dysplasia affecting humans?
back: Achondroplasia.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): [Achondroplasia] Generalised skeletal abnormalities... [Page 613 (Book Page)] Achondroplasia affects enchondral ossification and presents with disproportionate short stature.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: Which specific process of bone growth is impaired in achondroplasia?
back: Enchondral bone formation (enchondral ossification).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Achondroplasia is caused by a gain-in-function mutation in the FGFR3... gene... which affects enchondral bone formation.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: Describe the characteristic stature and limb-to-trunk ratio in achondroplasia.
back: Disproportionate short stature, where the limbs are significantly shorter than the trunk.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Patients present with disproportionate short stature where the limbs are shorter than the trunk.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: A child with short stature cannot reach their midthigh with their hands. What is the diagnosis?
back: Achondroplasia.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 613 (Book Page): Figure 44.7a: A child with achondroplasia: his upper limbs are short and his hands do not reach midthigh.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: What is the molecular pathophysiology of achondroplasia bone growth inhibition?
back: A gain-in-function mutation in the FGFR3 (fibroblast growth factor receptor 3) gene.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Achondroplasia is caused by a gain-in-function mutation in the FGFR3 (fibroblast growth factor receptor 3) gene.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: On which chromosome is the genetic defect for achondroplasia located?
back: Chromosome 4 (short arm).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): ...located on the short arm of chromosome (Chr) 4.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: What is the inheritance pattern of achondroplasia?
back: Autosomal dominant.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): It is autosomal dominant.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: What are the two characteristic pelvic radiographic features seen in achondroplasia?
back:
1. Horizontal acetabulum
2. Square-looking pelvic wings
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 613 (Book Page): Figure 44.7b: The acetabulum is horizontal and the pelvic wings seem square: classical features of achondroplasia.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: How does achondroplasia affect the metaphyses and fibula length radiographically?
back:
1. Widened metaphyses
2. Overlong fibula (relative to the tibia)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 613 (Book Page): Figure 44.7b: Standing leg length/alignment radiograph... demonstrating... widened metaphysis, an overlong fibula and slight bowing.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: What neurological growth complications arise from underdevelopment in achondroplasia?
back: Underdevelopment of the foramen magnum and spinal stenosis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Underdevelopment of the foramen magnum and spinal stenosis can cause neurological difficulties.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: What is the definition of achondroplasia and its prevalence among skeletal dysplasias?
back:
• Achondroplasia is the most common form of skeletal dysplasia.
• It is characterized by disproportionate short stature.
• Inherited as an autosomal dominant condition.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): [Achondroplasia is a generalized skeletal dysplasia.] ... it is autosomal dominant. Patients present with disproportionate short stature where the limbs are shorter than the trunk.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: What is the underlying genetic mutation and specific chromosomal location responsible for achondroplasia?
back:
• Gene: FGFR3 (Fibroblast Growth Factor Receptor 3).
• Chromosome: Short arm of chromosome 4.
• Mutation Type: Gain-in-function mutation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Achondroplasia is caused by a gain-in-function mutation in the FGFR3 (fibroblast growth factor receptor 3) gene, located on the short arm of chromosome (Chr) 4.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: Contrast the proportional skeletal involvement between the limbs and trunk in achondroplastic patients.
back:
• Stature is disproportionately short.
• Limbs are significantly shorter than the trunk.
• Hands typically do not reach the level of the midthigh.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Patients present with disproportionate short stature where the limbs are shorter than the trunk. ... Page 613 (Book Page): [Fig 44.7] his upper limbs are short and his hands do not reach midthigh.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: Why is physical assessment of hand reach significant in the clinical diagnosis of achondroplasia?
back:
• Shortened limbs (rhizomelia) prevent hands from reaching the midthigh.
• This confirms disproportionate shortening typical of the condition.
• It aids in visual differentiation from proportional short stature.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 613 (Book Page): [Figure 44.7] his upper limbs are short and his hands do not reach midthigh. ... features of achondroplasia.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: Describe the biochemical nature of the FGFR3 mutation associated with achondroplasia.
back:
• It is a gain-in-function mutation.
• This specific mutation results in overactivity of the FGFR3 protein.
• The abnormality primarily disrupts normal endochondral ossification.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Achondroplasia is caused by a gain-in-function mutation in the FGFR3 (fibroblast growth factor receptor 3) gene.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: What specific developmental milestone or physical parameter is diagnostic of achondroplasia on initial inspection?
back:
• Disproportionate short stature (limbs shorter than trunk).
• Characteristic rhizomelic limb shortening.
• Classical facies (often associated with large head/frontal bossing).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Patients present with disproportionate short stature where the limbs are shorter than the trunk ... classical clinical and radiographic features.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: Which specific bone growth process is primarily affected by the gain-in-function FGFR3 mutation?
back:
• Enchondral bone formation (ossification).
• This limits the growth of long bones developed from cartilage templates.
• Intramembranous ossification (flat bones) is largely spared.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): [Achondroplasia] is caused by a gain-in-function mutation ... which affects enchondral bone formation.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: Identify two life-altering neurological complications caused by bony underdevelopment in achondroplasia.
back:
• Underdevelopment of the foramen magnum (risks cord compression).
• Spinal stenosis (causing neurogenic claudication or weakness).
• Both require long-term neurosurgical monitoring.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Underdevelopment of the foramen magnum and spinal stenosis can cause neurological difficulties.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: Describe the radiographic physiological abnormalities found in the pelvis of a patient with achondroplasia.
back:
• Acetabulum is oriented horizontally.
• Pelvic wings (ilia) appear square or box-like.
• Results from inhibited enchondral growth at the pelvic physes.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 613 (Book Page): [Fig 44.7] The acetabulum is horizontal and the pelvic wings seem square: classical features of achondroplasia.

category: Define achondroplasia as the most common skeletal dysplasia and describe its effect on bone growth
front: Q: What is the mode of inheritance for achondroplasia in most familial cases?
back:
• Autosomal dominant.
• Most cases arise from de novo (new) mutations.
• Offspring of an affected individual have a 50% chance of inheritance.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Achondroplasia ... It is autosomal dominant.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What are the two pathognomonic skeletal features of chronic osteomyelitis?
back:
1. Sequestrum: A fragment of dead/necrotic bone separated from living tissue.
2. Involucrum: A sheath of new periosteal bone formed around the sequestrum.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): The infected bone reacts to the infection by separating dead fragments of bone (sequestration) and forming sinuses to drain pus and discharge small bone fragments. New bone is laid down around the infection from the periosteum (involucrum).

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Differentiate between Greenstick and Torus (Buckle) skeletal fractures in pediatric patients.
back:
1. Greenstick Fracture: Failure of the tension cortex (incomplete break).
2. Torus/Buckle Fracture: Failure or buckling of the compression cortex.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 421 (Book Page): These incomplete fractures are called greenstick (Figure 32.8) fractures, where one tension cortex fails. If the compression cortex buckles, they are called torus (Figure 32.9) or buckle fractures.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What are the classic radiographic skeletal hallmarks of active Rickets?
back:
1. Widened physes (growth plates).
2. Cupped and flared metaphyses.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 614 (Book Page): Radiographs in cases of rickets demonstrate widened physes with cupped, fared metaphyses.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
coreConcept: Pathological features of chronic bone infection
front: Q: What are the two defining skeletal features of chronic osteomyelitis?
back:
1. Sequestrum: Fragments of dead bone separated from living bone.
2. Involucrum: A sheath of new bone laid down by the periosteum around the infection.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): [The infected bone reacts to the infection by separating dead fragments of bone (sequestration) and forming sinuses to drain pus and discharge small bone fragments. New bone is laid down around the infection from the periosteum (involucrum)]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: How does the involucrum form in the pathophysiology of osteomyelitis?
back: Pus passing through cortical bone elevates the strong periosteum. This periosteal elevation serves as a potent stimulus for new bone formation, creating the involucrum.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 635 (Book Page): [Pus passes through cortical bone and when it does so it elevates the strong periosteum... As in cases of trauma or tumour, the periosteal elevation is a potent stimulus for new bone formation.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Contrast the radiographic skeletal features of Rickets versus Achondroplasia.
back:
Rickets: Widened physes with cupped, flared metaphyses.
Achondroplasia: Short limbs, horizontal acetabulum, square pelvic wings, and overlong fibula.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [In severe cases the classic radiographic features are seen at all physes with signifcant deformity (widened physes with cupped, flared metaphyses)] and Page 613 (Book Page): [The acetabulum is horizontal and the pelvic wings seem square: classical features of achondroplasia.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Which fracture patterns are pathognomonic or highly specific for non-accidental injury (NAI)?
back:
1. Corner or bucket-handle metaphyseal fractures.
2. Posterior rib fractures.
3. Scapular fractures.
4. Any fracture in a child below walking age.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 637 (Book Page): [Fracture patterns with a high specifcity for non-accidental injury: Posterior rib fractures, Corner or bucket-handle metaphyseal fractures, Scapular fractures, Any fracture in a child below walking age]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
coreConcept: Radiological effects of Bisphosphonates in Osteogenesis Imperfecta
front: Q: What skeletal change appears on radiographs of OI patients treated with bisphosphonates?
back: Multiple dense transverse 'growth lines' (Zebra lines) become visible on the long bones due to cyclical reduction in bone resorption.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Cyclical bisphosphonate treatment... reduces bone pain and the fracture rate... Multiple growth lines are visible in addition to intramedullary devices.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Define the skeletal involvements in a Salter-Harris Type IV injury.
back: The fracture line runs vertically through the epiphysis, crosses the physis, and exits through the metaphysis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [Type IV – fracture line across the epiphysis, across the physis and across the metaphysis.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Identify the four skeletal deformity components of structural Club Foot (CTEV).
back:
1. Hindfoot Equinus
2. Hindfoot Varus
3. Midfoot Adductus
4. Forefoot Cavus (via first ray pronation)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 625 (Book Page): [structural idiopathic club foot has fxed deformity with elements of hindfoot equinus and varus, midfoot adductus and pronation of the frst ray, giving the appearance of forefoot cavus.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Differentiate the specific bones involved in Freiberg’s and Köhler’s osteochondroses.
back:
Freiberg’s: Second metatarsal head.
Köhler’s: Tarsal navicular bone.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 627 (Book Page): [Freiberg’s osteochondrosis presents with forefoot pain and avascular change in the second metatarsal head. Köhler’s disease presents with dorsal forefoot pain and swelling... The navicular becomes avascular.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: State the Hueter–Volkmann principle regarding skeletal growth.
back:
1. Compressive forces inhibit physeal growth.
2. Tensile (stretching) forces stimulate physeal growth.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 609 (Book Page): [Hueter–Volkmann principle: Compressive forces inhibit growth, Tensile forces stimulate growth]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What are the 'four legs' of the zygomatic bone stool relevant in midface trauma?
back:
1. Zygomatic arch
2. Frontozygomatic suture (vertical process)
3. Infraorbital rim
4. Maxillary buttress
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 411 (Book Page): [it is helpful to consider the zygomatic bone as a fourlegged stool... The four legs comprise the zygomatic arch... frontozygomatic (FZ) process... infraorbital rim... and the maxillary buttress.]

category: Identify musculoskeletal complications due to achondroplasia
front: Q: What is the genetic cause of achondroplasia?
back: Gain-in-function mutation in the FGFR3 gene located on the short arm of chromosome 4.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Achondroplasia is caused by a gain-in-function mutation in the FGFR3 (fbroblast growth factor receptor 3) gene, located on the short arm of chromosome (Chr) 4

category: Identify musculoskeletal complications due to achondroplasia
front: Q: Which specific process of bone formation is affected in achondroplasia?
back: Enchondral (endochondral) bone formation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Achondroplasia is caused by a gain-in-function mutation in the FGFR3... gene... which afects enchondral bone formation.

category: Identify musculoskeletal complications due to achondroplasia
front: Q: How is stature proportion categorized in achondroplasia?
back: Disproportionate short stature, where limbs are significantly shorter than the trunk.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Patients present with disproportionate short stature where the limbs are shorter than the trunk

category: Identify musculoskeletal complications due to achondroplasia
front: Q: Name two life-threatening neurological complications arising from skeletal features of achondroplasia.
back:
1. Underdevelopment of the foramen magnum.
2. Spinal stenosis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Underdevelopment of the foramen magnum and spinal stenosis can cause neurological difculties.

category: Identify musculoskeletal complications due to achondroplasia
front: Q: What does the FGFR3 mutation specifically do to inhibit bone growth?
back: It acts as a gain-in-function mutation that constitutively inhibits chondrocyte proliferation and enchondral ossification.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Achondroplasia is caused by a gain-in-function mutation in the FGFR3... which afects enchondral bone formation.

category: Identify musculoskeletal complications due to achondroplasia
front: Q: What are the defining pelvic radiographic features of achondroplasia?
back:
1. Horizontal acetabula.
2. Square pelvic wings.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 613 (Book Page): The acetabulum is horizontal and the pelvic wings seem square: classical features of achondroplasia.

category: Identify musculoskeletal complications due to achondroplasia
front: Q: Which specific fibular abnormality is characteristic of achondroplasia radiographs?
back: The fibula is overlong relative to the tibia, frequently associated with slight bowing.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 613 (Book Page): [Image 44.7b caption] short limbs, widened metaphysis, an overlong fbula and slight bowing.

category: Identify musculoskeletal complications due to achondroplasia
front: Q: What physical sign regarding the hands is a diagnostic clinical feature of achondroplasia?
back: The hands are short and typically do not reach the mid-thigh.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 613 (Book Page): [Image 44.7a caption] his upper limbs are short and his hands do not reach midthigh.

category: Identify musculoskeletal complications due to achondroplasia
front: Q: What is the primary musculoskeletal reason for corrective surgery in achondroplasia?
back: Correction of limb alignment (e.g., bowing) and, occasionally, limb-lengthening.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Correction of limb alignment may be necessary and limb-lengthening techniques are used in some countries.

category: Identify musculoskeletal complications due to achondroplasia
front: Q: What specific change occurs to the metaphyses in achondroplasia?
back: They become widened.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 613 (Book Page): [Image 44.7b caption] short limbs, widened metaphysis, an overlong fbula and slight bowing.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What are the two pathognomonic skeletal features of chronic osteomyelitis?
back: - Sequestrum: A fragment of dead cortical bone. - Involucrum: New bone formed around the infection site by the periosteum.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): The infected bone reacts to the infection by separating dead fragments of bone (sequestration)... New bone is laid down around the infection from the periosteum (involucrum).

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: How does the "Windlass test" identify a flexible vs. fixed flat foot?
back: - Flexible: The medial arch forms and heel corrects to varus when standing on toes. - Fixed: The arch fails to form, indicating structural deformity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 647 (Book Page): Windlass test. Ask the patient to stand on their toes and observe the arch... As soon as the patient stands on their toes, the arch forms. Failure of this indicates a fxed fat foot.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Contrast the characteristic skeletal shapes of extradural vs. subdural hematomas on imaging.
back: - Extradural: Lentiform (biconvex or lens-shaped). - Subdural: Diffuse concave (crescent-shaped), following the brain's surface contour.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page): On CT, extradural haematomas appear as a lentiform (lens-shaped or biconvex) hyperdense lesion... Page 387 (Book Page): subdural blood is free to expand across the brain surface, giving a difuse concave appearance.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: A child presents with an anterolateral tibial bow and a non-healing fracture; what is the diagnosis?
back: Congenital pseudarthrosis of the tibia (associated with neurofibromatosis in 50% of cases).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 646 (Book Page): Congenital pseudarthrosis of the tibia... presents with an anterolateral bow of the tibia with or without a fracture... 50% are associated with neurofbromatosis.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What skeletal feature appears on radiographs following bisphosphonate treatment in Osteogenesis Imperfecta?
back: Multiple visible transverse growth lines occur due to the systemic decrease in bone resorption and turnover.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 636 (Book Page): Cyclical bisphosphonate treatment decreases bone resorption and turnover... Radiograph of a child with osteogenesis imperfecta... Multiple growth lines are visible.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What are the characteristic radiographic features of rickets at the metaphysis?
back: - Widened physes. - Cupped and flared metaphyses. - General skeletal bowing.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 636 (Book Page): In severe cases the classic radiographic features are seen at all physes... widened physes with cupped, fared metaphyses.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: In a normal hip, where should the femoral ossific nucleus lie relative to Perkins’ and Hilgenreiner’s lines?
back: It should lie in the inner lower quadrant; displacement elsewhere suggests developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 639 (Book Page): Perkins’ line (b). The femoral head (ossifc nucleus) of a normal hip lies in the inner lower quadrant.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What specific radiographic feature on an open-mouth view defines an unstable Jefferson fracture?
back: A combined lateral mass deviation exceeding 6.9 mm, which indicates a ruptured transverse ligament.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 418 (Book Page): Rupture of the transverse ligament is present when the combined lateral mass deviation exceeds 6.9 mm.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What does a "Positive J-sign" indicate regarding skeletal patellar tracking?
back: Lateral subluxation of the patella occurring near full extension, signifying a maltracking extensor mechanism.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 515 (Book Page): towards the end of extension, look for lateral subluxation of the patella (‘J’ sign). This indicates maltracking.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What does the Southwick slip angle measure in the skeletal assessment of SCFE?
back: It denotes the degree to which the epiphysis has displaced posteriorly from the metaphysis on a lateral radiograph.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 643 (Book Page): The Southwick slip angle is measured on a lateral radiograph and denotes how far the epiphysis has slipped of the metaphysis.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What are the three classic radiographic components of chronic osteomyelitis?
back:
- Sequestrum: A dead fragment of bone.
- Involucrum: New bone sheath formed around the infection.
- Sinus tracts: Passages for draining pus and bone debris.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): [The infected bone reacts to the infection by separating dead fragments of bone (sequestration) and forming sinuses to drain pus and discharge small bone fragments. New bone is laid down around the infection from the periosteum (involucrum).]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: How do the Hueter-Volkmann principle and Wolff’s law explain bone remodelling in childhood?
back:
- Hueter-Volkmann: Compressive forces inhibit physeal growth; tensile forces stimulate it.
- Wolff’s law: Bone structure alters its deposition and resorption based on applied mechanical stresses.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 631 (Book Page): [Table 44.1: Hueter–Volkmann principle: Compressive forces inhibit growth; Tensile forces stimulate growth. Wolff’s law: Bone deposition and resorption depend on the stresses applied.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Contrast the CT radiographic appearance of extradural vs. acute subdural haematomas.
back:
- Extradural: Lentiform (biconvex/lens-shaped) hyperdense lesion between skull and brain.
- Subdural: Diffuse concave (crescentic) hyperdensity expanding across the brain surface.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page): [On CT, extradural haematomas appear as a lentiform (lens-shaped or biconvex) hyperdense lesion... Page 388 (Book Page): subdural blood is free to expand across the brain surface, giving a diffuse concave appearance.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: An obese adolescent presents with knee pain and external hip rotation. What is the skeletal diagnosis?
back: Slipped Capital (Upper) Femoral Epiphysis (SCFE/SUFE). Symptoms include referred knee pain and a limb held in external rotation and shortening.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 643 (Book Page): [The slipped epiphysis is associated with a ‘cam’ type of femoroacetabular impingement... Page 643 (Book Page): Often presents with knee pain, and a short and externally rotated leg.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What is the skeletal benefit of cyclical bisphosphonate therapy in Osteogenesis Imperfecta (OI)?
back:
- Decreases bone resorption and turnover.
- Reduces fracture frequency and bone pain.
- Increases bone strength to support mobility.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 636 (Book Page): [Cyclical bisphosphonate treatment decreases bone resorption and turnover. This reduces bone pain and the fracture rate, promoting weight-bearing mobility and bone strength.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What is the pathognomonic radiographic skeletal feature of an ACL injury?
back: The Segond fracture, which is a small avulsion fracture located on the anterolateral aspect of the tibia.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 504 (Book Page): [A Segond fracture located on the anterolateral tibia is pathognomonic for an ACL injury.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What does the 'too many toes' sign indicate during clinical examination of the foot?
back: Indicates increased forefoot abduction and a splayed forefoot, which are key features of pes planus (flat foot).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 494 (Book Page): [The ‘too many toes’ sign demonstrates increased forefoot abduction (pes planus [fat foot]) and a splayed forefoot.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Which specific skeletal fracture patterns indicate high specificity for Non-Accidental Injury (NAI)?
back:
- Posterior rib fractures.
- Corner or bucket-handle metaphyseal fractures.
- Scapular fractures.
- Any fracture in a child below walking age.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 637 (Book Page): [Table 44.21: Fracture patterns with a high specificity for non-accidental injury: Multiple fractures at different stages of healing/old fractures; Posterior rib fractures; Corner or bucket-handle metaphyseal fractures; Scapular fractures; Any fracture in a child below walking age.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What are the four structural components of a structural club foot (CTEV) deformity?
back:
- Hindfoot Equinus
- Hindfoot Varus
- Midfoot Adductus
- Forefoot Cavus
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 626 (Book Page): [structural idiopathic club foot has fixed deformity with elements of hindfoot equinus and varus, midfoot adductus and pronation of the first ray, giving the appearance of forefoot cavus.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Identify the three columns defined in the Denis/AO model of spinal stability.
back:
1. Anterior column
2. Middle column
3. Posterior column
Instability occurs if two or more columns are injured.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 389 (Book Page): [The spine can be divided into three columns: anterior, middle and posterior (Figure 30.7). If two or more columns of the spine are injured, it is considered unstable.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What are the characteristic disproportionate skeletal features of achondroplasia?
back:
• Disproportionate short stature (limbs shorter than trunk).
• Horizontal acetabulum and square pelvic wings.
• Relative overgrowth of the fibula.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): [Achondroplasia presents with disproportionate short stature where the limbs are shorter than the trunk... horizontal acetabulum and the pelvic wings seem square.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Define the skeletal defining features of chronic osteomyelitis (sequestrum vs involucrum).
back:
• Sequestrum: A detached fragment of dead cortical bone.
• Involucrum: A sheath of new periosteal bone formed around the infected site.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): [The infected bone reacts to the infection by separating dead fragments of bone (sequestration)... New bone is laid down around the infection from the periosteum (involucrum).]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Contrast the skeletal failure patterns of Greenstick and Torus fractures in children.
back:
• Greenstick: Failure of the tension cortex (one side snaps).
• Torus (Buckle): Buckling failure of the compression cortex without a snap.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 421 (Book Page): [greenstick fractures, where one tension cortex fails. If the compression cortex buckles, they are called torus or buckle fractures.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Which skeletal features identify a Tile Type C pelvic fracture?
back:
• Complete instability of both anterior and posterior complexes.
• Disrupted bones free to displace both horizontally and vertically.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 384 (Book Page): [Type C: This fracture is completely unstable. Both the anterior pelvis and the entire posterior pelvic complexes are disrupted and the disrupted pelvic bones are free to displace horizontally and vertically.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What radiographic features are characteristic of Rickets at the growth plate?
back:
• Widened physes.
• Cupped and flared appearance of the metaphyses.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 614 (Book Page): [In severe cases the classic radiographic features are seen at all physes... demonstrating widened physes with cupped, flared metaphyses.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What are the defining skeletal features of a vertebral Burst fracture?
back:
• Widening of the interpedicular distance.
• Retropulsion of bone fragments into the spinal canal.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 400 (Book Page): [Burst fractures... are characterised by widening of the distance between the pedicles and can be associated with retropulsion of bone fragments into the spinal canal.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Distinguish the tibial bowing patterns of Blount’s disease vs. Congenital Pseudarthrosis.
back:
• Blount’s disease: Posteromedial apex tibial bow.
• Congenital Pseudarthrosis: Anterolateral apex tibial bow.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 624 (Book Page): [Blount’s disease... apex posteromedial tibial bow... Congenital pseudarthrosis of the tibia – the tibial bow has an anterolateral apex.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Describe the skeletal mechanism of the "Miserable Malalignment Syndrome."
back:
• Persistent femoral neck anteversion (excessive internal rotation).
• Compensatory external tibial torsion.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 610 (Book Page): [compensatory external tibial torsion may develop, in which case the foot progression angle will be normal but the child may have symptoms of the miserable malalignment syndrome.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Define Hueter–Volkmann principle vs. Wolff’s law in skeletal growth.
back:
• Hueter–Volkmann: Compression inhibits growth; tension stimulates growth.
• Wolff’s Law: Bone deposition and resorption respond to applied stresses.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 609 (Book Page): [Hueter–Volkmann principle: Compressive forces inhibit growth; Tensile forces stimulate growth. Wolff’s law: Bone deposition and resorption depend on the stresses applied.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What anatomic skeletal feature predisposes the scaphoid proximal pole to avascular necrosis?
back:
• Retrograde blood supply entering at the distal end.
• Waist fractures interrupt supply to the proximal pole.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 433 (Book Page): [The blood supply to the scaphoid enters distally and supplies the scaphoid in a retrograde fashion. As such, a displaced waist of scaphoid fracture interrupts the blood supply to the proximal pole.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What are the two characteristic radiographic components of chronic osteomyelitis?
back:
1. Sequestrum: A fragment of dead, devascularized bone.
2. Involucrum: A sheath of new bone laid down by the periosteum around the infected site.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): [The infected bone reacts to the infection by separating dead fragments of bone (sequestration) and forming sinuses to drain pus and discharge small bone fragments. New bone is laid down around the infection from the periosteum (involucrum).]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What classic skeletal features define Rickets on a radiograph?
back:
1. Widened physes (growth plates).
2. Cupped and flared metaphyses.
3. General skeletal bowing due to failure of bone mineralization.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 614 (Book Page): [In severe cases the classic radiographic features are seen at all physes with signifcant deformity... demonstrate widened physes with cupped, fared metaphyses.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Distinguish the skeletal stability in Tile Type B vs Type C pelvic fractures.
back:
1. Type B: Partially stable; anterior or partial posterior disruption; "open book" rotational instability but no vertical displacement.
2. Type C: Completely unstable; total anterior and posterior complex disruption; both horizontal and vertical displacement.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 405 (Book Page): [Type B... partially stable... can open and close ‘like a book’... no vertical displacement. Type C... completely unstable... both the anterior pelvis and the entire posterior pelvic complexes are disrupted... free to displace horizontally and vertically.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: A 13-year-old obese male presents with knee pain. What skeletal feature identifies SCFE on X-ray?
back:
1. Displacement of the capital femoral epiphysis through the physis.
2. Klein's Line: A line along the superior femoral neck fails to transect the femoral head.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 621 (Book Page): [a ‘stress fracture’ through the physis allows the epiphysis to displace... A line drawn along the upper margin of the femoral neck should transect the femoral head... if it does not do so... a slip is present.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: List the four skeletal components of the "CAVE" deformity corrected during clubfoot manipulation.
back:
1. Cavus: High medial arch.
2. Adductus: Forefoot deviation toward midline.
3. Varus: Heel inversion.
4. Equinus: Plantarflexion at the ankle.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 626 (Book Page): [The standard sequence of manipulations is: C – correction of the apparent forefoot cavus... A – gradual forefoot abduction... V – correction of the hindfoot varus E – correction of hindfoot equinus]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What disproportionate skeletal features characterize Achondroplasia?
back:
1. Rhizomelic shortening (limbs shorter than trunk).
2. Square pelvic wings with horizontal acetabula.
3. Fibula overgrowth relative to the tibia.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 613 (Book Page): [disproportionate short stature where the limbs are shorter than the trunk... short limbs, widened metaphysis, an overlong fbula... the acetabulum is horizontal and the pelvic wings seem square.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: How does the Adams test differentiate structural from functional scoliosis features?
back:
1. Structural: A rib hump increases or persists during forward flexion due to fixed rotation.
2. Functional: The spine straightens and the rib hump disappears during forward flexion.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 477 (Book Page): [structural scoliosis : a rib hump will increase in size... as the patient bends forwards... functional scoliosis : the spine straightens as the patient bends forwards and no rib hump is visible.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What is the defining radiographic skeletal feature of traumatic aortic disruption?
back:
1. A widened mediastinum on chest X-ray.
2. Often associated with fractures of the first and second ribs or the sternum.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 397 (Book Page): [Erect chest radiography can also suggest thoracic aortic disruption, the most common radiological fnding being a widened mediastinum.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Describe the sequential skeletal phases of Legg–Calvé–Perthes disease.
back:
1. Avascular Necrosis: Initial blood supply loss.
2. Collapse/Fragmentation: Resorption of dead bone.
3. Reossification: Regeneration of the femoral head bone.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 619 (Book Page): [The avascular change may afect all or part of the femoral epiphysis. If the avascular bone collapses, this is followed by revascularisation, resorption and fragmentation... and fnally by reossifcation and regeneration.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What skeletal characteristic defines a Greenstick fracture?
back:
1. An incomplete fracture of a long bone.
2. One side (tension cortex) fails/breaks while the other side (compression cortex) remains intact or buckles.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 421 (Book Page): [In children... the fracture line may be incomplete... these incomplete fractures are called greenstick... where one tension cortex fails.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What are the two pathognomonic skeletal features of chronic osteomyelitis?
back:
