• Sequestrum: A fragment of dead bone separated from living tissue.
• Involucrum: A sheath of new bone laid down around the infection by the periosteum.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): [The infected bone reacts to the infection by separating dead fragments of bone (sequestration) and forming sinuses to drain pus and discharge small bone fragments. New bone is laid down around the infection from the periosteum (involucrum)]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Define the Monro-Kellie doctrine in the context of traumatic brain injury.
back:
• The cranium is a 'rigid box' containing incompressible brain, blood, and CSF.
• Expansion of any one content (e.g., haematoma) must be compensated by the exclusion of CSF and venous blood to prevent exponential ICP rise.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 381 (Book Page): [the cranium is a ‘rigid box’ containing a ‘nearly incompressible brain’. Any expansion in the contents, especially haematoma and brain swelling, may be initially accommodated by exclusion of fuid components, venous blood and cerebrospinal fuid (CSF). Further expansion is associated with an exponential rise in ICP]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Contrast the radiographic appearance of Extradural (EDH) vs. Subdural (SDH) haematomas.
back:
• EDH: Lentiform (biconvex/lens-shaped) lesion; does not cross suture lines.
• SDH: Crescentic (concave) lesion; spreads diffusely across the brain surface.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page)-387: [extradural haematomas appear as a lentiform (lens-shaped or biconvex) hyperdense lesion... subdural blood is free to expand across the brain surface, giving a difuse concave appearance.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Which Tile classification of pelvic fracture is considered completely unstable?
back:
• Type C pelvic fractures.
• Characteristics: Complete disruption of anterior and posterior complexes with horizontal and vertical displacement.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 405 (Book Page): [Type C: This fracture is completely unstable. Both the anterior pelvis and the entire posterior pelvic complexes are disrupted and the disrupted pelvic bones are free to displace horizontally and vertically.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What characterizes a Salter-Harris Type II growth plate injury?
back:
• Fracture line through the physis exiting through the metaphysis.
• Results in a triangular metaphyseal fragment.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 423 (Book Page): [Type II – fracture line through the physis exiting through the metaphysis, producing a metaphyseal fragment.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
coreConcept: Clinical Hallmarks of Skull Base Fractures
front: Q: What clinical signs suggest a fracture of the skull base?
back:
• Battle’s sign (mastoid bruising).
• 'Raccoon eyes' (periorbital bruising).
• Haemotympanum (blood in middle ear).
• CSF rhinorrhoea or otorrhoea.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 385 (Book Page): [Clinical evidence of a skull base fracture may include Battle’s sign (Figure 28.3) and ‘racoon’ or ‘panda’ eyes (bilateral periorbital bruising). Haemotympanum... and CSF rhinorrhoea or otorrhoea are also highly suggestive]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: According to the three-column model, what defines spinal instability?
back:
• Injury to two or more columns (Anterior, Middle, or Posterior).
• Indicates the spine cannot withstand physiological loads safely.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 410 (Book Page): [The spine can be divided into three columns: anterior, middle and posterior... If two or more columns of the spine are injured, it is considered unstable.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Differentiate Colles’ from Smith’s fracture by displacement pattern.
back:
• Colles’: Distal radial fragment displaces dorsally (Dinner fork deformity).
• Smith’s: Distal radial fragment displaces volarly/ventrally (Garden spade deformity).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 434 (Book Page): [volar displaced fractures (Smith’s fracture)... Most dorsally displaced fractures (Colles fracture)]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What is the primary mechanical requirement for Direct (Primary) Bone Healing?
back:
• Absolute stability (no movement at fracture site).
• Cortical apposition (compressed bone ends).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 423 (Book Page): [Direct bone healing... happens in an environment of cortical apposition and absolute stability with no movement or gap between the fracture fragments.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
coreConcept: Skeletal Blood Supply and Avascular Necrosis
front: Q: Why is the proximal pole at risk in scaphoid waist fractures?
back:
• Retrograde blood supply: Artery enters distally.
• Waist fractures interrupt proximal flow, leading to Avascular Necrosis (AVN).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 433 (Book Page): [The blood supply to the scaphoid enters distally and supplies the scaphoid in a retrograde fashion. As such, a displaced waist of scaphoid fracture interrupts the blood supply to the proximal pole, leading to avascular necrosis.]

category: Identify musculoskeletal complications due to achondroplasia
front: Q: What is the defining musculoskeletal phenotype of achondroplasia regarding body proportions?
back: Disproportionate short stature, specifically characterized by limbs that are significantly shorter than the trunk.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): [Patients present with disproportionate short stature where the limbs are shorter than the trunk, together with classical clinical and radiographic features.]

category: Identify musculoskeletal complications due to achondroplasia
front: Q: Which specific genetic mutation and inheritance pattern causes achondroplasia?
back:
● Gain-in-function mutation in FGFR3 gene
● Located on chromosome 4p
● Autosomal dominant inheritance
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): [Achondroplasia is caused by a gain-in-function mutation in the FGFR3 (fibroblast growth factor receptor 3) gene, located on the short arm of chromosome (Chr) 4... It is autosomal dominant.]

category: Identify musculoskeletal complications due to achondroplasia
front: Q: How does the skeletal growth failure in achondroplasia differ from proportionate dwarfism?
back: In achondroplasia, enchondral bone formation is specifically affected, causing shortened limbs while the trunk remains relatively normal in size.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): [Achondroplasia is caused by a gain-in-function mutation in the FGFR3... which affects enchondral bone formation. Patients present with disproportionate short stature where the limbs are shorter than the trunk.]

category: Identify musculoskeletal complications due to achondroplasia
front: Q: Which skull base musculoskeletal complication in achondroplasia leads to urgent neurological concerns?
back: Underdevelopment of the foramen magnum, which can cause compression and significant neurological difficulties.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): [Underdevelopment of the foramen magnum and spinal stenosis can cause neurological difficulties.]

category: Identify musculoskeletal complications due to achondroplasia
front: Q: What surgical management steps are used to address limb-length complications in achondroplasia?
back:
● Correction of limb alignment
● Limb-lengthening techniques
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): [Correction of limb alignment may be necessary and limb-lengthening techniques are used in some countries.]

category: Identify musculoskeletal complications due to achondroplasia
front: Q: What are the characteristic radiographic musculoskeletal features of the pelvis in achondroplasia?
back:
● Horizontal acetabulum
● Square-shaped pelvic wings
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 613 (Book Page): [The acetabulum is horizontal and the pelvic wings seem square: classical features of achondroplasia.]

category: Identify musculoskeletal complications due to achondroplasia
front: Q: Which axial skeletal complication in achondroplasia causes narrowed space for the spinal cord?
back: Spinal stenosis, resulting from disordered growth of the vertebrae, causing neurological difficulties.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): [Underdevelopment of the foramen magnum and spinal stenosis can cause neurological difficulties.]

category: Identify musculoskeletal complications due to achondroplasia
front: Q: Contrast the neurological complications of the upper versus lower axial skeleton in achondroplasia.
back:
● Upper: Foramen magnum underdevelopment causing brainstem/cervical cord compression
● Lower: Spinal stenosis affecting the lumbar cord and nerve roots
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): [Underdevelopment of the foramen magnum and spinal stenosis can cause neurological difficulties.]

category: Identify musculoskeletal complications due to achondroplasia
front: Q: Describe the metabolic/physiological loop of FGFR3 in achondroplasia bone growth.
back: Mutation causes overactivation of FGFR3, which inhibits chondrocyte proliferation and maturation, specifically arresting enchondral ossification.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): [Achondroplasia is caused by a gain-in-function mutation in the FGFR3... which affects enchondral bone formation.]

category: Identify musculoskeletal complications due to achondroplasia
front: Q: What characteristic radiographic findings are seen in the long bones of achondroplastic patients?
back:
● Widened metaphyses
● Relative overlength of the fibula compared to the tibia
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 613 (Book Page): [...demonstrating short limbs, widened metaphysis, an overlong fibula and slight bowing.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What are the pathognomonic skeletal features of Rickets visible at the growth plates?
back:
- Widened physes.
- Cupped and flared metaphyses.
- Associated with significant bony deformity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 636 (Book Page): 'In severe cases the classic radiographic features are seen at all physes... demonstrating widened physes with cupped, fared metaphyses.'

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What mechanism leads to the skeletal formation of a sequestrum in chronic osteomyelitis?
back:
- Medullary abscess tracks through cortex.
- Periosteal elevation devascularizes the area.
- Results in cortical bone death and separation of dead fragments.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): 'pus may track through the cortex to form periosteal elevation... This process will devascularise the cortical bone, causing bone death... separating dead fragments of bone (sequestration).'

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Distinguish between the pediatric greenstick and torus (buckle) skeletal fracture patterns.
back:
- Greenstick: One tension cortex fails while the other remains intact.
- Torus: Compression cortex buckles/fails under axial load.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 442 (Book Page): 'greenstick (Figure 32.8) fractures, where one tension cortex fails. If the compression cortex buckles, they are called torus (Figure 32.9) or buckle fractures.'

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: A patient with an acute knee effusion presents with an anterolateral tibial chip fracture. Diagnosis?
back:
- Segond fracture.
- Pathognomonic feature of an Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) rupture.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 526 (Book Page): 'A Segond fracture located on the anterolateral tibia is pathognomonic for an ACL injury.'

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: How does cyclical bisphosphonate therapy clinically alter skeletal features in Osteogenesis Imperfecta?
back:
- Decreases bone resorption and turnover.
- Produces multiple visible growth lines (zebra lines) on radiographs.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 636 (Book Page): 'Cyclical bisphosphonate treatment decreases bone resorption and turnover... Multiple growth lines are visible'

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What skeletal criteria define a Salter-Harris Type IV physeal injury?
back:
- Fracture line crosses the epiphysis.
- Line continues through the physis.
- Line exits through the metaphysis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 444 (Book Page): 'Type IV – fracture line across the epiphysis, across the physis and across the metaphysis.'

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: How is the Southwick angle applied to categorize skeletal displacement in SCFE?
back:
- Denotes how far the epiphysis has slipped off the metaphysis.
- Measured on lateral radiographs of the hip.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 643 (Book Page): 'The Southwick slip angle... denotes how far the epiphysis has slipped off the metaphysis.'

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Distinguish between structural and functional scoliosis using the Forward Bending Test features.
back:
- Structural: Rib hump increases or persists due to rotatory deformity.
- Functional: Spine straightens and rib hump is not visible.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 499 (Book Page): 'structural scoliosis: a rib hump will increase in size... functional scoliosis: the spine straightens as the patient bends forwards and no rib hump is visible.'

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Describe the physiological loop governing skeletal growth according to the Hueter-Volkmann principle.
back:
- Compressive forces inhibit physeal growth.
- Tensile forces stimulate physeal growth.
- Governs bone remodeling and deformity correction.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 631 (Book Page): 'Hueter–Volkmann principle ● Compressive forces inhibit growth ● Tensile forces stimulate growth'

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What skeletal data do the first two symbols in the AO fracture classification provide?
back:
- 1st digit: Specific bone (e.g., 1 for humerus).
- 2nd digit: Bone segment (1-Proximal, 2-Diaphysis, 3-Distal).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page)-444: 'The first number defines the bone and the second number the segment of bone... The letter and number that follows further defines the nature of the injury'

category: Identify musculoskeletal complications due to achondroplasia
front: Q: What is the genetic cause and specific mutation type in achondroplasia?
back:
● Autosomal dominant inheritance
● Gain-in-function mutation in the FGFR3 gene
● Located on the short arm of chromosome 4 (4p)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): [Achondroplasia] is caused by a gain-in-function mutation in the FGFR3 (fibroblast growth factor receptor 3) gene, located on the short arm of chromosome (Chr) 4... It is autosomal dominant.

category: Identify musculoskeletal complications due to achondroplasia
front: Q: Which specific biological process is impaired in achondroplasia, leading to limb shortening?
back:
● Impaired enchondral bone formation
● Primarily affects long bones while the trunk length is relatively preserved
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): [Achondroplasia] affects enchondral bone formation. Patients present with disproportionate short stature where the limbs are shorter than the trunk.

category: Identify musculoskeletal complications due to achondroplasia
front: Q: What defines the hallmark 'disproportionate' stature characteristic of achondroplasia?
back:
● Rhizomelic shortening (limbs shorter than trunk)
● Hands often fail to reach the midthigh level
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Patients present with disproportionate short stature where the limbs are shorter than the trunk... his hands do not reach midthigh.

category: Identify musculoskeletal complications due to achondroplasia
front: Q: An achondroplastic infant presents with apnea and limb weakness. What is the most critical anatomical complication?
back:
● Underdevelopment of the foramen magnum
● Causes compression of the cervicomedullary junction
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Underdevelopment of the foramen magnum and spinal stenosis can cause neurological difficulties.

category: Identify musculoskeletal complications due to achondroplasia
front: Q: What are the two primary spinal complications associated with achondroplasia?
back:
● Underdevelopment of the foramen magnum
● Spinal stenosis (narrowing of the spinal canal)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Underdevelopment of the foramen magnum and spinal stenosis can cause neurological difficulties.

category: Identify musculoskeletal complications due to achondroplasia
front: Q: What are the two defining radiographic features of the pelvis in achondroplasia?
back:
● Horizontal acetabulum
● Square-shaped pelvic wings
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 613 (Book Page): The acetabulum is horizontal and the pelvic wings seem square: classical features of achondroplasia.

category: Identify musculoskeletal complications due to achondroplasia
front: Q: Which specific long bone features are seen on radiographs in achondroplasia?
back:
● Shortened limbs
● Widened metaphyses
● Overlong fibula
● Slight bowing of the legs
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 613 (Book Page): [Radiographs demonstrating] short limbs, widened metaphysis, an overlong fibula and slight bowing.

category: Identify musculoskeletal complications due to achondroplasia
front: Q: What surgical options are used to address limb shortening and alignment in achondroplasia?
back:
● Limb-lengthening techniques
● Corrective osteotomies for limb alignment
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Correction of limb alignment may be necessary and limb-lengthening techniques are used in some countries.

category: Identify musculoskeletal complications due to achondroplasia
front: Q: How is the fibula affected relative to the tibia in achondroplasia?
back:
● The fibula is overlong relative to the tibia
● Often contributes to overall limb bowing
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 613 (Book Page): [Radiographs demonstrating] an overlong fibula and slight bowing.

category: Identify musculoskeletal complications due to achondroplasia
front: Q: Which skeletal region remains relatively normal in length compared to the limbs in achondroplasia?
back:
● The trunk
● Disproportion results from shortened limbs (rhizomelia) attached to a normal-sized trunk
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Patients present with disproportionate short stature where the limbs are shorter than the trunk.

category: Identify musculoskeletal complications due to achondroplasia
front: Q: What is the primary phenotypic hallmark of musculoskeletal development in achondroplasia?
back: Disproportionate short stature characterized by limbs that are significantly shorter than the trunk.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): [Patients present with disproportionate short stature where the limbs are shorter than the trunk...]

category: Identify musculoskeletal complications due to achondroplasia
front: Q: What is the specific genetic and pathophysiological basis of achondroplasia?
back: A gain-in-function mutation in the FGFR3 gene on chromosome 4, which disrupts enchondral bone formation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): [Achondroplasia is caused by a gain-in-function mutation in the FGFR3 (fibroblast growth factor receptor 3) gene, located on the short arm of chromosome (Chr) 4, which affects enchondral bone formation.]

category: Identify musculoskeletal complications due to achondroplasia
front: Q: Contrast the developmental impact of achondroplasia on the limbs versus the trunk.
back: Achondroplasia predominantly affects limb segments, resulting in severe shortening while the trunk length is relatively preserved.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): [Patients present with disproportionate short stature where the limbs are shorter than the trunk...]

category: Identify musculoskeletal complications due to achondroplasia
front: Q: A child with achondroplasia presents with progressive lower limb weakness and hyperreflexia. What anatomical complication is suspected?
back: Spinal stenosis or underdevelopment of the foramen magnum causing neurological compression.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): [Underdevelopment of the foramen magnum and spinal stenosis can cause neurological difficulties.]

category: Identify musculoskeletal complications due to achondroplasia
front: Q: What surgical management step is commonly considered for correcting the limb alignment of patients with achondroplasia?
back: Correction of limb alignment and limb-lengthening techniques.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): [Correction of limb alignment may be necessary and limb-lengthening techniques are used in some countries.]

category: Identify musculoskeletal complications due to achondroplasia
front: Q: What are the characteristic radiographic findings of the pelvis in achondroplasia?
back: The acetabulum is horizontal and the pelvic wings appear square.

category: Identify musculoskeletal complications due to achondroplasia
front: Q: What are the primary musculoskeletal and neurological complications associated with achondroplasia?
back:

- Disproportionate short stature

category: Identify musculoskeletal complications due to achondroplasia

- Specifically impairs enchondral bone formation
- Inherited as autosomal dominant
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Achondroplasia is caused by a gain-in-function mutation in the FGFR3 (fibroblast growth factor receptor 3) gene, located on the short arm of chromosome (Chr) 4, which affects enchondral bone formation.

category: Identify musculoskeletal complications due to achondroplasia

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: What is the classic CT appearance of an acute traumatic extradural haematoma?
back:
- Lentiform (biconvex/lens-shaped) hyperdense lesion.
- Located between the skull and the brain.
- Usually associated with an underlying skull fracture.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page): [On CT, extradural haematomas appear as a lentiform (lens-shaped or biconvex) hyperdense lesion between the skull and the brain, constrained by the adherence of the dura to the skull... A skull fracture will usually be evident.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
coreConcept: Pathological radiographic hallmarks of Chronic Osteomyelitis
front: Q: Which radiographic features characterize the pathological bone reaction in chronic osteomyelitis?
back:
- Sequestrum: Fragments of dead cortical bone.
- Involucrum: New bone formed by the periosteum surrounding the infection.
- Sinuses: Tracks for discharging pus and bone fragments.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): [The infected bone reacts to the infection by separating dead fragments of bone (sequestration) and forming sinuses to drain pus... New bone is laid down around the infection from the periosteum (involucrum).]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
coreConcept: CT differentiation of Subdural Haematoma stages
front: Q: How do acute and chronic subdural haematomas differ in density on CT imaging?
back:
- Acute: Hyperdense (bright white).
- Chronic: Diffuse hypodensity (dark).
- Shape: Typically diffuse and concave (crescentic) along the brain surface.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 387 (Book Page)-388: [subdural blood is free to expand across the brain surface, giving a diffuse concave appearance... acute subdural haematoma (hyperdense)... Imaging reveals diffuse hypodensity overlying the brain surface.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
coreConcept: Radiographic interpretation of Thoracic Aortic Disruption
front: Q: What radiographic findings suggest traumatic thoracic aortic rupture on an erect chest radiograph?
back:
- Widened mediastinum (most common).
- Associated fractures: 1st/2nd ribs, sternum, or scapula.
- Confirmation required via CT mediastinum.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 397 (Book Page): [Erect chest radiography can also suggest thoracic aortic disruption, the most common radiological fnding being a widened mediastinum... The diagnosis is confrmed by a CT scan of the mediastinum.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
coreConcept: Radiographic monitoring of bisphosphonate therapy in OI
front: Q: What radiographic 'Zebra lines' appear in children with Osteogenesis Imperfecta (OI) during medical follow-up?
back:
- Transverse growth lines in the metaphysis.
- Represent the response to cyclical bisphosphonate therapy.
- Visible on follow-up radiographs to monitor treatment.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Cyclical bisphosphonate treatment... Figure 44.12 Radiograph of a child with osteogenesis imperfecta who has been treated with cyclical bisphosphonates. Multiple growth lines are visible.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
coreConcept: Radiographic lines in Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip
front: Q: How is the femoral head position assessed on an AP pelvic radiograph for DDH?
back:
- Draw Hilgenreiner’s (horizontal) and Perkins’ (vertical) lines.
- Normal: Ossific nucleus in the inner lower quadrant.
- DDH: Ossific nucleus in the outer upper quadrant.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): [Figure 44.15 Anteroposterior pelvic radiograph showing Hilgenreiner’s line (a) and Perkins’ line (b). The femoral head (ossifc nucleus) of a normal hip lies in the inner lower quadrant.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
coreConcept: Radiographic parameters of Cervical Spine Instability
front: Q: What specific measurements on a lateral cervical radiograph define clinical spinal instability?
back:
- Sagittal translation >3.5 mm.
- Sagittal angulation >11° compared to the adjacent level.
- Presence of prevertebral soft-tissue swelling.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): [Assess for instability (Figure 30.16): a 3.5 mm of sagittal translation; b sagittal angulation of >11° (compared with the adjacent level).]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
coreConcept: Stages of Legg–Calvé–Perthes disease on radiograph
front: Q: Name the four sequential radiographic stages of Legg–Calvé–Perthes disease.
back:
1. Necrosis (dense ossific nucleus).
2. Fragmentation (resorption of dead bone).
3. Reossification (regeneration of bone).
4. Healing/Remodelling (residual femoral head deformity).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 619 (Book Page): [The avascular bone collapses, this is followed by revascularisation, resorption and fragmentation... and fnally by reossifcation and regeneration (‘healing’) of the bony epiphysis.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: What are the pathognomonic radiographic features of rickets at the growth plate?
back:
- Widened physis (radiolucent growth plate line).
- Cupping and fraying of the metaphysis.
- Generalized bowing of long bone diaphyses.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 614 (Book Page): [Figure 44.11 Radiographs in cases of rickets demonstrate widened physes with cupped, fared metaphyses.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up

back:

Note the right maxillary sinus opacifcation, which is one of the radiological hallmarks of zygomatic fracture due to collection of fnding in the sinus.]

● Extradural: Lentiform (biconvex) hyperdense lesion constrained by dural adherence to the skull.
● Subdural: Diffuse concave (crescent) appearance freely expanding across the brain surface.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page)-388: [On CT, extradural haematomas appear as a lentiform (lens-shaped or biconvex) hyperdense lesion... subdural blood is free to expand across the brain surface, giving a diffuse concave appearance.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: What specific radiographic measurements define mechanical instability on a lateral cervical spine radiograph?
back:
● >3.5 mm of sagittal translation.
● >11° of sagittal angulation compared to the adjacent level.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): [Assess for instability: 3.5 mm of sagittal translation; sagittal angulation of >11° (compared with the adjacent level).]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: Which radiographic finding on an erect chest film suggests a traumatic thoracic aortic disruption?
back:
● Widened mediastinum.
● Diagnosis must be confirmed by a CT scan of the mediastinum showing shear injury distal to the ligamentum arteriosum.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 397 (Book Page): [Erect chest radiography can also suggest thoracic aortic disruption, the most common radiological fnding being a widened mediastinum. The diagnosis is confrmed by a CT scan of the mediastinum.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: What is the significance of the 'Rule of 2s' in extremity trauma radiography?
back:
● 2 views (orthogonal planes).
● 2 joints (above and below injury).
● 2 occasions (repeat in 10–14 days for occult fractures).
● 2 sides (compare with uninjured limb).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 440 (Book Page): [The rule of 2s should be remembered: 2 views... 2 joints... 2 occasions... 2 sides.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: What are the pathognomonic radiographic features of chronic osteomyelitis?
back:
● Sequestrum: A fragment of dead bone separated from living tissue.
● Involucrum: New bone sheath formed by the periosteum around the infected site.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): [The infected bone reacts to the infection by separating dead fragments of bone (sequestration)... New bone is laid down around the infection from the periosteum (involucrum).]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: How is the 'Southwick Angle' utilized in the follow-up of Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis (SCFE)?
back:
● Measured on a lateral radiograph to quantify the degree the epiphysis has slipped off the metaphysis.
● Categorizes slip as mild (<33%), moderate (33–66%), or severe (>66%).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 643 (Book Page)-644: [The Southwick slip angle is measured on a lateral radiograph and denotes how far the epiphysis has slipped off the metaphysis... Mild <33; Moderate 33–66; Severe >66.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: Which radiographic lines define the normal position of the femoral head in infant hip screening?
back:
● Hilgenreiner’s line (horizontal through triradiate cartilages).
● Perkins’ line (vertical through lateral acetabular margin).
● Normal: Ossific nucleus lies in the inner lower quadrant.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 639 (Book Page): [Anteroposterior pelvic radiograph showing Hilgenreiner’s line and Perkins’ line. The femoral head (ossifc nucleus) of a normal hip lies in the inner lower quadrant.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: How does 'Indirect' bone healing differ from 'Direct' bone healing on follow-up radiographs?
back:
● Indirect: Characterized by visible callus formation (secondary healing).
● Direct: No callus visible; occurs through osteoclastic cutting cones and cortical apposition under absolute stability.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 445 (Book Page)-446: [Direct bone healing... heals directly with bone and without callus formation... Indirect bone healing involves a transition from one tissue to another with callus formation.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: Which specific radiographic view is essential to avoid missing a posterior shoulder dislocation?
back:
● Axillary view.
● AP and lateral scapula views may appear falsely normal or only show subtle 'squaring' despite complete posterior displacement.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 441 (Book Page): [AP radiograph... Lateral scapula radiograph... initially reported as normal... True value of the axillary view shown with obvious posterior dislocation of the glenohumeral joint.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: What is the classic radiographic appearance of an extradural haematoma on a CT scan?
back:
• Lentiform (biconvex) shape
• Hyperdense lesion between the skull and brain
• Usually associated with an underlying skull fracture
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page): [On CT, extradural haematomas appear as a lentiform (lens-shaped or biconvex) hyperdense lesion between the skull and the brain, constrained by the adherence of the dura to the skull.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: Why is 'whole-body CT' (WBCT) with IV contrast preferred over selective scanning in polytrauma?
back:
• Rapidly identifies life-threatening pathology (head to pelvis)
• Avoids missing occult internal hemorrhage
• Provides a provisional 'hot report' within minutes
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Computed tomography (CT) from the head to pelvis with IV contrast, the so-called ‘whole-body CT’ (WBCT), is the gold standard investigation in patients with signs or symptoms of multiple injury... There is no role for scanning selective body systems in the severely injured trauma patient.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: How do acute and chronic subdural haematomas differ in density on a CT scan?
back:
• Acute: Hyperdense (bright) and crescent-shaped
• Chronic: Diffuse hypodensity (dark) overlying the brain surface
• Mixed: Indicates acute-on-chronic bleeding
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 388 (Book Page): [Since the dura is not as adherent to the brain as it is to the skull, subdural blood is free to expand across the brain surface, giving a diffuse concave appearance... Imaging reveals diffuse hypodensity overlying the brain surface. Recent bleeding may be isodense or hyperdense, and mixed density can indicate an acute-on-chronic subdural haematoma.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: What does a widened mediastinum on an erect chest radiograph suggest following high-velocity trauma?
back:
• Traumatic thoracic aortic disruption
• Mechanism: Sudden impact shear forces distal to ligamentum arteriosum
• Diagnosis requires CT scan confirmation
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 397 (Book Page): [Erect chest radiography can also suggest thoracic aortic disruption, the most common radiological finding being a widened mediastinum... The diagnosis is confirmed by a CT scan of the mediastinum.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: What is the pharmacological rationale for using IV contrast during trauma CT imaging?
back:
• Visualizes active vascular leakage/hemorrhage
• Enhances solid organ injury visualization (liver, spleen)
• Distinguishes major vessel disruption from non-vascular tissue
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Computed tomography (CT) from the head to pelvis with IV contrast... is the gold standard investigation in patients with signs or symptoms of multiple injury or deranged physiology... A provisional ‘hot report’ can be issued within minutes to identify immediate life-threatening pathology.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: What specific radiographic findings define instability on a lateral cervical spine radiograph?
back:
• >3.5 mm of sagittal translation
• >11° of sagittal angulation compared with the adjacent level
• Prevertebral soft-tissue swelling
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): [Assess for instability: a 3.5 mm of sagittal translation; b sagittal angulation of >11° (compared with the adjacent level).]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: How is the normal position of the femoral head determined on a neonatal pelvic radiograph?
back:
• Ossific nucleus lies in the inner lower quadrant
• Defined by Hilgenreiner’s line and Perkins’ line
• Late ossification is common in DDH
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 618 (Book Page): [The femoral head (ossific nucleus) of a normal hip lies in the inner lower quadrant... defined by Hilgenreiner’s line (a) and Perkins’ line (b).]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: Which CT findings are used to plan surgery for chronic osteomyelitis?
back:
• Sequestrum (dead bone fragments)
• Involucrum (new bone formation around infection)
• Cortical bone erosion and medullary abscesses
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): [The infected bone reacts to the infection by separating dead fragments of bone (sequestration) and forming sinuses... New bone is laid down around the infection from the periosteum (involucrum).]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: In pediatric trauma, how is a Salter-Harris Type II fracture identified radiographically?
back:
• Fracture line passes through the physis
• Exits through the metaphysis
• Leaves a characteristic triangular metaphyseal fragment
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [Type II – fracture line through the physis exiting through the metaphysis, producing a metaphyseal fragment.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: What radiographic finding indicates transverse ligament rupture in a C1 Jefferson fracture?
back:
• Combined lateral mass deviation >6.9 mm
• Observed on the open mouth (odontoid) view
• Indicates instability and potential cord danger
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 418 (Book Page): [Open mouth view of C1/2 demonstrating C1 lateral mass deviation (arrows). Rupture of the transverse ligament is present when the combined lateral mass deviation exceeds 6.9 mm.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: What is the gold standard radiographic investigation for an adult blunt trauma patient with multiple injuries?
back: Whole-body CT (WBCT) with IV contrast from head to pelvis is the gold standard for polytrauma assessment.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Computed tomography (CT) from the head to pelvis with IV contrast, the so-called ‘whole-body CT’ (WBCT), is the gold standard investigation in patients with signs or symptoms of multiple injury or deranged physiology]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: What CT finding is characteristic of an extradural hematoma in a patient with a 'talk and die' history?
back: A lentiform, biconvex, or lens-shaped hyperdense (bright) lesion situated between the skull and the brain dura.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page): [On CT, extradural haematomas appear as a lentiform (lens-shaped or biconvex) hyperdense lesion between the skull and the brain, constrained by the adherence of the dura to the skull.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: Contrast the radiographic appearance of acute versus chronic subdural hematomas on a CT scan.
back: Acute subdural hematomas are hyperdense and crescent-shaped (concave). Chronic cases show diffuse hypodensity (darkness) overlying the brain surface.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 388 (Book Page): [Since the dura is not as adherent to the brain as it is to the skull, subdural blood is free to expand across the brain surface, giving a diffuse concave appearance... Imaging reveals diffuse hypodensity overlying the brain surface.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: Which specific measurements on a lateral cervical spine radiograph indicate mechanical instability in trauma?
back:
Mechanical instability is indicated by: 
- Sagittal translation exceeding 3.5 mm
- Sagittal angulation greater than 11 degrees relative to the adjacent level.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): [Assess for instability (Figure 30.16): a 3.5 mm of sagittal translation; b sagittal angulation of >11° (compared with the adjacent level).]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: What is the most common finding on an erect chest radiograph in a traumatic aortic disruption?
back: A widened mediastinum is the most common radiological finding, often seen following sudden deceleration or vehicle collisions.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 397 (Book Page): [Erect chest radiography can also suggest thoracic aortic disruption, the most common radiological fnding being a widened mediastinum.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: Which classification system describes radiographic growth plate injuries through the epiphysis and physis?
back: The Salter–Harris classification system (Types I to VI) categorizes physis injuries to guide treatment and assess growth arrest risk.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 423 (Book Page): [The severity of injury to the physis is classifed in the Salter–Harris classifcation, which considers whether the fracture line passes through the epiphysis, physis, metaphysis or combinations...]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: How is the normal position of the femoral head determined on an anteroposterior pelvic radiograph in children?
back: The femoral ossific nucleus should lie in the inner lower quadrant defined by Hilgenreiner’s line (horizontal) and Perkins’ line (vertical).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): [The femoral head (ossifc nucleus) of a normal hip lies in the inner lower quadrant. The right hip is normal; the left hip has developmental dysplasia of the hip. (Figure 44.15)]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: Interpret the characteristic 'bone-within-a-bone' radiographic appearance in chronic osteomyelitis.
back: This appearance results from a central sequestrum (dead necrotic bone) being enveloped by a surrounding involucrum (new periosteal bone).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 635 (Book Page): [In cases of untreated or chronic infection this new bone or involucrum may surround the dead bone, the sequestrum, leading to a ‘bone-within-a-bone’ appearance.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: What is the radiographic follow-up for a suspected scaphoid fracture with an initially normal X-ray?
back: If tenderness persists in the anatomical snuffbox, the wrist should be immobilized and radiographs repeated after 10–14 days.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 419 (Book Page): [The rule of 2s... 2 occasions – sometimes the fracture may not be initially visible; a second series of radiographs should be undertaken after 10–14 days if suspicion of bony injury persists. The classic injury here is a scaphoid fracture.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: What radiographic finding identifies an 'open book' pelvic ring fracture?
back: Widening of the pubic symphysis or widening at a pubic ramus fracture site, indicating external rotation of the ilia.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 406 (Book Page): [An ‘open book fracture’ is seen as a widening of the pubic symphysis or widening at the site of a fracture in the pubic ramus.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: What classic shape does an extradural hematoma display on a CT scan?
back:
- Lentiform (lens-shaped)
- Biconvex
- Hyperdense lesion between the skull and the brain
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page): [On CT, extradural haematomas appear as a lentiform (lens-shaped or biconvex) hyperdense lesion between the skull and the brain]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: How does chronic osteomyelitis appear radiographically as a "bone-within-a-bone"?
back:
- Central dead bone (sequestrum)
- Surrounded by new reactive bone (involucrum)
- Separated by an interface of pus or granulation tissue
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 635 (Book Page): [In cases of untreated or chronic infection this new bone or involucrum may surround the dead bone, the sequestrum, leading to a ‘bone-within-a-bone’ appearance]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Contrast the radiographic CT appearance of acute versus chronic subdural hematoma.
back:
- Acute: Hyperdense (bright) crescent/concave appearance
- Chronic: Diffuse hypodensity (dark) overlying the brain surface
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 388 (Book Page): [subdural blood is free to expand across the brain surface, giving a diffuse concave appearance. ... Imaging reveals diffuse hypodensity overlying the brain surface.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Why is a "frog" lateral pelvic radiograph essential for interpreting suspected childhood hip pathology?
back:
- Displacement in SCFE is often only obvious on lateral views
- Essential for diagnosing subtle Perthes’ disease or slipped epiphysis
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 621 (Book Page): [Displacement is often more obvious on a lateral view and the diagnosis can be missed if only the anteroposterior radiograph is checked.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: What radiographic feature identifies past cyclical bisphosphonate use in a child with Osteogenesis Imperfecta?
back:
- Multiple transverse radiodense "growth lines"
- Located in the metaphyses of long bones
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Figure 44.12 Radiograph of a child with osteogenesis imperfecta who has been treated with cyclical bisphosphonates. Multiple growth lines are visible]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
coreConcept: Radiological diagnosis of developmental dysplasia of the hip
front: Which specific pelvic radiographic lines are used to diagnose infant hip dysplasia?
back:
- Hilgenreiner’s line (horizontal)
- Perkins’ line (vertical)
- Normal femoral nucleus lies in the inner lower quadrant
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): [Figure 44.15 Anteroposterior pelvic radiograph showing Hilgenreiner’s line (a) and Perkins’ line (b). The femoral head (ossific nucleus) of a normal hip lies in the inner lower quadrant.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
coreConcept: Grading of Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis
front: How is the severity of Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis interpreted on lateral radiographs?
back:
- Based on metaphyseal uncovering percentage:
- Mild: <33%
- Moderate: 33–66%
- Severe: >66%
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 622 (Book Page): [Table 44.8 Grading of the severity of slip of the capital femoral epiphysis. ... Severe >66%]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Contrast the radiographic findings of Blount’s disease with physiological bowlegs.
back:
- Blount's: Sharp proximal medial tibial physeal abnormality; progressive vara
- Physiological: Symmetrical, smooth bowing that corrects spontaneously by age 2
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 624 (Book Page): [Blount’s disease ... progressive and often severe tibia vara ... The radiographic features are diagnostic (Figure 44.27).]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: What are the characteristic radiographic findings in the metaphyses of a child with active rickets?
back:
- Widened physes (growth plates)
- Cupped and flared metaphyses
- Due to inadequate mineralization of growing bone
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 614 (Book Page): [Figure 44.11 Radiographs in cases of rickets demonstrate widened physes with cupped, flared metaphyses.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
coreConcept: Pathognomonic imaging signs in knee trauma
front: Which radiographic finding is considered pathognomonic for an Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) injury?
back:
- Segond fracture
- Small avulsion fracture of the anterolateral tibia
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 504 (Book Page): [A Segond fracture located on the anterolateral tibia is pathognomonic for an ACL injury.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: What is the classic shape and density of an extradural haematoma on a CT scan?
back:
- Shape: Lentiform (biconvex/lens-shaped)
- Density: Hyperdense
- Feature: Limited by cranial sutures due to dural adherence.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page): [On CT, extradural haematomas appear as a lentiform (lens-shaped or biconvex) hyperdense lesion between the skull and the brain, constrained by the adherence of the dura to the skull.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: Contrast the radiographic shape of an acute subdural haematoma with an extradural haematoma.
back:
- Subdural: Diffuse concave (crescentic) appearance
- Extradural: Convex/Lentiform appearance
- Mechanism: Subdural blood spreads across the brain surface as the dura is less adherent.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 388 (Book Page): [Since the dura is not as adherent to the brain as it is to the skull, subdural blood is free to expand across the brain surface, giving a diffuse concave appearance.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
coreConcept: Radiographic Assessment of Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip
front: Q: How is the normal position of the femoral head defined using Hilgenreiner's and Perkins' lines?
back:
- Hilgenreiner’s: Horizontal line through triradiate cartilages
- Perkins’: Vertical line from lateral acetabular roof
- Normal Finding: Ossific nucleus lies in the inner lower quadrant.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): [Anteroposterior pelvic radiograph showing Hilgenreiner’s line (a) and Perkins’ line (b). The femoral head (ossifc nucleus) of a normal hip lies in the inner lower quadrant.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: Which specific fracture patterns on a paediatric radiograph are pathognomonic for non-accidental injury (NAI)?
back:
- Metaphyseal corner (bucket-handle) fractures
- Posterior rib fractures
- Scapular fractures
- Fractures at different stages of healing.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 637 (Book Page): [Table 44.21 Fracture patterns with a high specifcity for non-accidental injury. Multiple fractures at different stages of healing/old fractures; Posterior rib fractures; Corner or bucket-handle metaphyseal fractures; Scapular fractures.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: What is the cardinal sign of traumatic thoracic aortic disruption on an erect chest radiograph?
back:
- Widened mediastinum
- Often associated with 1st/2nd rib, clavicle, or sternal fractures.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 397 (Book Page): [Erect chest radiography can also suggest thoracic aortic disruption, the most common radiological fnding being a widened mediastinum.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
coreConcept: Radiographic Markers of Chronic Bone Infection
front: Q: Define 'sequestrum' and 'involucrum' as seen in radiographs of chronic osteomyelitis.
back:
- Sequestrum: Detached fragment of dead bone
- Involucrum: New sheath of bone formed around the sequestrum by the periosteum.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 628 (Book Page): [In cases of untreated or chronic infection this new bone or involucrum may surround the dead bone, the sequestrum, leading to a ‘bone-within-a-bone’ appearance.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
coreConcept: Radiographic Criteria for Cervical Spine Instability
front: Q: What lateral cervical radiograph measurements indicate potential spinal instability?
back:
- Sagittal translation: >3.5 mm
- Sagittal angulation: >11° (compared to adjacent levels)
- Significant prevertebral soft-tissue swelling.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): [Assess for instability (Figure 30.16): a 3.5 mm of sagittal translation; b sagittal angulation of >11° (compared with the adjacent level).]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: Describe the radiographic finding that confirms a Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis (SCFE) on AP view.
back: - Trethowan’s sign: A line drawn along the superior femoral neck (Klein's line) fails to transect the femoral head.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 621 (Book Page): [A line drawn along the upper margin of the femoral neck should transect the femoral head (right side); if it does not do so (left side) a slip is present.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: Describe the fracture line involvement in a Salter-Harris Type IV injury.
back:
- Fracture line passes vertically through:
1. Epiphysis
2. Physis (growth plate)
3. Metaphysis
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 423 (Book Page): [Type IV – fracture line across the epiphysis, across the physis and across the metaphysis. This injury can cause focal fusion of the physis, leading to abnormal growth.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: What are the characteristic metaphyseal radiographic signs of rickets?
back:
- Widened physes
- Cupped metaphyses
- Frayed (flared) metaphyseal margins.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 614 (Book Page): [Radiographs in cases of rickets demonstrate widened physes with cupped, fared metaphyses.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: What constitutes the "Rule of 2s" in the initial radiographic evaluation of extremity trauma?
back:
- 2 views: Orthogonal planes
- 2 joints: Joint above and below
- 2 occasions: Repeat after 10–14 days for occult fractures
- 2 sides: Comparison with uninjured side.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 419 (Book Page): [The rule of 2s should be remembered: 2 views... 2 joints... 2 occasions... 2 sides]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: Radiographically, how is clinical union distinguished from consolidation during the fracture healing process?
back:
- Union: Callus is seen bridging the fracture site.
- Consolidation: The return of a normal cortical bone pattern is visible across the previous fracture line.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 424 (Book Page): [Radiologically a fracture has united when the callus bridges the fracture site... Consolidation... demonstrated by the return of the normal cortical pattern.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: Contrast the characteristic radiographic findings of Salter-Harris Type II and Type III growth plate injuries.
back:
- Type II: Fracture line through the physis exiting through the metaphysis (metaphyseal fragment).
- Type III: Fracture line through the physis exiting through the epiphysis (intra-articular).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 423 (Book Page): [Type II – fracture line through the physis exiting through the metaphysis... Type III – fracture line through the physis exiting through the epiphysis (intra-articular).]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: Which specific radiographic alignment check on a lateral wrist view identifies a perilunate dislocation?
back:
- Ensure the lunate resides correctly in the radiocarpal fossa.
- Ensure the capitate is seated within the concavity ("cup") of the lunate.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 433 (Book Page): [Review of the radiographs should particularly ensure the anatomical location of the lunate in the radiocarpal fossa and that the capitate in the ‘cup’ of the lunate is maintained.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
coreConcept: Follow-up of Metabolic Bone Disease Treatment
front: Q: What radiographic finding identifies a positive response to bisphosphonate therapy in a child with Osteogenesis Imperfecta?
back: - Appearance of multiple horizontal radiodense growth lines (zebra lines) in the metaphyses of long bones.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Radiograph of a child with osteogenesis imperfecta who has been treated with cyclical bisphosphonates. Multiple growth lines are visible...]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
coreConcept: Radiographic Evaluation of Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip
front: Q: In pediatric hip radiographs, what intersection defines the normal quadrant for the femoral ossific nucleus?
back:
- The intersection of Hilgenreiner’s line (horizontal) and Perkins’ line (vertical).
- The nucleus should lie in the lower inner quadrant.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): [The femoral head (ossific nucleus) of a normal hip lies in the inner lower quadrant.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: Why is an axillary view essential when an AP shoulder radiograph appears normal after injury?
back:
- It is the only view that reliably identifies a posterior shoulder dislocation.
- Shows the humeral head displaced posterior to the glenoid fossa.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 420 (Book Page): [Axillary view – true value of the axillary view shown with obvious posterior dislocation of the glenohumeral joint.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: Distinguish the radiographic features of a sequestrum and an involucrum in chronic osteomyelitis.
back:
- Sequestrum: A dense fragment of dead bone detached from the living bone.
- Involucrum: A sheath of new periosteal bone surrounding the sequestrum.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 618 (Book Page): [In cases of untreated or chronic infection this new bone or involucrum may surround the dead bone, the sequestrum, leading to a ‘bone-within-a-bone’ appearance.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: What are the pathognomonic radiographic growth plate features seen in active nutritional rickets?
back:
- Widened physes.
- Cupped and flared metaphyses due to inadequate mineralization of the bone matrix.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 636 (Book Page): [Radiographs in cases of rickets demonstrate widened physes with cupped, flared metaphyses.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: Which specific radiographic sign on an AP pelvic view indicates Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis (SCFE)?
back: - Trethowan's sign (Klein's line): A line drawn along the superior margin of the femoral neck fails to transect the femoral head.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 621 (Book Page): [A line drawn along the upper margin of the femoral neck should transect the femoral head... if it does not do so... a slip is present.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: What is the characteristic CT appearance of an acute extradural haematoma?
back:
- Lentiform (lens-shaped) or biconvex morphology
- Hyperdense (bright) appearance between skull and brain
- Typically does not cross suture lines
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page): [On CT, extradural haematomas appear as a lentiform (lens-shaped or biconvex) hyperdense lesion between the skull and the brain, constrained by the adherence of the dura to the skull.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
coreConcept: Radiographic evidence of necrotic bone and reactive repair
front: Q: How do sequestrum and involucrum appear radiographically in chronic osteomyelitis?
back:
- Sequestrum: Dense, radio-opaque fragments of dead bone separated from living tissue.
- Involucrum: A sheath of reactive new periosteal bone surrounding the infection site.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): [The infected bone reacts to the infection by separating dead fragments of bone (sequestration)... New bone is laid down around the infection from the periosteum (involucrum).]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
coreConcept: Diagnostic imaging criteria for Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis
front: Q: Contrast the radiographic interpretation of Klein’s line in a normal hip versus SCFE.
back:
- Normal: A line along the superior femoral neck margin intersects the femoral head.
- SCFE: The line fails to intersect the epiphysis (Trethowan’s sign) due to displacement.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 621 (Book Page): [A line drawn along the upper margin of the femoral neck should transect the femoral head (right side); if it does not do so (left side) a slip is present.]

category: Outline management principles
front: Q: What is the primary functional advantage of a dedicated trauma team in severe injury management?
back: It allows Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) principles to be applied simultaneously (concurrently) rather than sequentially to identify life-threatening injuries.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 375 (Book Page): [The principal advantage of a trauma team is that this activity can occur concurrently instead of sequentially; while the anaesthetist is assessing and managing the patient’s airway, another team member can be assessing and managing the patient’s breathing, etc.]

category: Outline management principles
front: Q: What are the specific systolic blood pressure targets for permissive hypotension in trauma resuscitation?
back:
• 70–90 mmHg for most trauma patients
• >90 mmHg if a head injury is suspected.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [For a short time, this can be achieved with a target systolic blood pressure of 70–90 mmHg, although a higher pressure of >90 mmHg should be the target if a head injury is suspected.]

category: Outline management principles
front: Q: What defines the clinical choice between Early Total Care (ETC) and Damage Control Surgery (DCS)?
back:
• ETC: Definitive injury management within 36 hours for stable patients.
• DCS: Life/limb saving procedures only; definitive repair is deferred until physiology is optimized.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [ETC describes the definitive management of a patient’s injuries within 36 hours of injury after a period of initial resuscitation. DCS describes simultaneous resuscitation with early rapid life- and limb-saving surgery. Time-consuming definitive surgery is deferred until the patient’s physiological status allows.]

category: Outline management principles
front: Q: What specific drainage volumes indicate the need for urgent thoracotomy in a massive haemothorax?
back:
• Initial drainage >1500 mL
• Ongoing hemorrhage >200 mL/h over 3–4 hours.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): [Initial drainage of more than 1500 mL of blood or ongoing haemorrhage of more than 200 mL/h over 3–4 hours is generally considered an indication for urgent thoracotomy.]

category: Outline management principles
front: Q: What is the recommended dosing regimen for Tranexamic Acid in bleeding trauma patients?
back:
• 1 gram intravenously over 10 minutes
• Followed by 1 gram over 8 hours
• Must be given within 3 hours of injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [One gram is given intravenously over 10 minutes, followed by a further 1-g dose over 8 hours... the first dose should not be administered more than 3 hours from injury.]

category: Outline management principles
front: Q: What investigation is considered the gold standard for adult blunt trauma with deranged physiology?
back: Whole-body CT (WBCT) from head to pelvis with intravenous contrast.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Computed tomography (CT) from the head to pelvis with IV contrast, the so-called ‘whole-body CT’ (WBCT), is the gold standard investigation in patients with signs or symptoms of multiple injury or deranged physiology.]

category: Outline management principles
front: Q: Outline the 'Four Ps' management strategy for operative control of liver injuries.
back:
1. Pressure (direct bimanual compression)
2. Pringle manoeuvre (portal triad compression)
3. Plug (silicone or Sengstaken tube)
4. Pack (definitive packing).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 401 (Book Page): [The operative management of liver injuries can be summarised as ‘the four Ps’: Pressure; Pringle; Plug; Pack.]

category: Outline management principles
front: Q: Why is pericardiocentesis contraindicated in the management of penetrating traumatic cardiac tamponade?
back: Penetrating injury results in substantial clotted blood in the pericardium, preventing aspiration; definitive management requires surgical sternotomy or thoracotomy for repair.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): [Pericardiocentesis has no role in the management of cardiac tamponade secondary to penetrating myocardial injury. The correct immediate treatment of tamponade is operative, either via a subxiphoid window or by open surgery (sternotomy or left anterolateral thoracotomy).]

category: Outline management principles
front: Q: Which physiological marker is utilized to determine resuscitation adequacy and readiness for ETC?
back:
Venous lactate:
• <2 mmol/L: Suitable for ETC
• >5 mmol/L: Indicates DCS is required.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 380 (Book Page): [A normal lactate (<2 mmol/L) is a sign that the patient is probably resuscitated and suitable for ETC. >5 mmol/L – DCS.]

category: Outline management principles
front: Q: What three components constitute the 'Triad of Death' in severely traumatized patients?
back:
1. Acidosis
2. Coagulopathy
3. Hypothermia.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [the ‘triad of death’ – a cycle of acidosis, coagulopathy and hypothermia – may develop and result in multiorgan failure and death.]

category: Outline management principles
front: What is the priority sequence for the primary survey in severe trauma management?
back:
cABCDE:
- c: Exsanguinating external haemorrhage control.
- A: Airway with cervical spine control.
- B: Breathing and ventilation.
- C: Circulation and haemorrhage control (pelvic binder if blunt trauma).
- D: Disability (GCS/pupils).
- E: Exposure and environment (keep warm).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [The primary survey aims to identify and manage the most immediately life-threatening pathologies first and follows cABCDE.]

category: Outline management principles
front: Explain the management principle of permissive hypotension in acute trauma resuscitation.
back: Maintaining blood supply to vital organs using time-limited target systolic pressures of 70–90 mmHg. Higher targets (>90 mmHg) are required for suspected head injuries. Excessive crystalloids are avoided to prevent haemodilution, coagulopathy, and ARDS.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [The initial aim of resuscitation is to maintain the blood supply to the vital organs... this can be achieved with a target systolic blood pressure of 70–90 mmHg, although a higher pressure of >90 mmHg should be the target if a head injury is suspected.]

category: Outline management principles
front: Distinguish between Damage Control Surgery (DCS) and Early Total Care (ETC) principles.
back:
ETC: Definitive management of all injuries (long bone/spinal/pelvic) within 36 hours for stable patients.
DCS: Priority for life-saving procedures (haemorrhage control, cavity decompression) in unstable patients, deferring definitive reconstruction until physiological optimization.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [ETC allows definitive fixation of all unstable long bone, spinal and pelvic fractures within 36 hours of injury... DCS describes simultaneous resuscitation with early rapid life- and limb-saving surgery.]

category: Outline management principles
front: Outline the management principles for severe hypovolaemia and massive transfusion protocols.
back: Resuscitate using warmed blood and blood products in a 1:1:1 ratio (Packed Red Cells: Fresh-Frozen Plasma : Platelets). Crystalloids are limited to small boluses (e.g., 250mL) only until blood products become available.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Severely injured hypovolaemic patients should be resuscitated with blood and blood products, not crystalloid/colloid fluids... protocol that aims to provide blood and blood products in a ratio of 1 packed red cells : 1 fresh-frozen plasma : 1 platelets.]

category: Outline management principles
front: State the administration principles for Tranexamic Acid (TXA) in trauma haemorrhage.
back: Give 1g IV over 10 minutes, followed by 1g infusion over 8 hours. Ideally administered within the first hour; must not be started more than 3 hours from injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [One gram is given intravenously over 10 minutes, followed by a further 1-g dose over 8 hours... ideally within the first hour from injury; the first dose should not be administered more than 3 hours from injury.]

category: Outline management principles
front: Outline management decisions based on venous lactate levels during resuscitation.
back:
- <2 mmol/L: Resuscitated; suitable for ETC.
- 2–3 mmol/L: Monitor trend and other markers.
- >3 mmol/L: Under-resuscitated; require further resuscitation or DCS.
- >5 mmol/L: DCS indicated.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 380 (Book Page): [<2 mmol/L – ETC; 2–3 mmol/L – look at the trend; >3 mmol/L – may be under-resuscitated; >5 mmol/L – DCS]

category: Outline management principles
front: Outline the management principles for controlling raised intracranial pressure (ICP).
back:
1. Optimize sedation, analgesia, and ventilation (PaCO2 4.5–5.0 kPa).
2. Head elevation and loosening neck collars.
3. Active control of seizures and pyrexia.
4. Fluid management (avoid hypotonic solutions).
5. Mannitol or hypertonic saline for sweling.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 389 (Book Page): [Management of the intubated patient... is guided by ICP monitoring... maintained elevated ICP exceeding 20–25 mmHg is associated with a poor outcome... ICP can be controlled by simple measures, including raising the head of the bed.]

category: Outline management principles
front: Outline the immediate management principles for open fractures in the ED.
back:
1. Photograph injury; document neurovascular status.
2. Gross reduction/splinting of displacement.
3. Moist saline dressing (no primary closure).
4. Early broad-spectrum IV antibiotics.
5. Tetanus prophylaxis.
6. Urgent surgical debridement and stabilization.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 444 (Book Page): [Take a photograph... Assess neurovascular status... Splint the affected limb... Apply a moist saline dressing... Administer intravenous antibiotics according to local protocols.]

category: Outline management principles
front: Describe the diagnostic and emergency management principles for compartment syndrome.
back:
Diagnosis: Pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch, and paraesthesia.
Management: Split all casts/dressings to skin, keep limb at heart level (not elevated), and perform emergency surgical fasciotomy.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 444 (Book Page): [Compartment syndrome is a clinical diagnosis characterised by pain out of proportion... Emergency treatment involves splitting casts and/or dressings to the skin and elevating the extremity... perform definitive treatment with fasciotomies.]

category: Outline management principles
front: What are the immediate management principles for native joint septic arthritis?
back:
1. Joint aspiration for microscopy/culture.
2. Urgent surgical joint washout (irrigation) to prevent cartilage destruction.
3. Analgesia and splintage.
4. Systemic IV antibiotics for 3–6 weeks, tailored to sensitivities.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 600 (Book Page): [The treatment of a presumed septic arthritis therefore requires the prompt removal of pus from the joint and appropriate adequate antibiotic therapy. Pain relief and rest are also important.]

category: Outline management principles
front: What are the four fundamental stages in the general management of a musculoskeletal fracture?
back:
- Reduce: Restore alignment.
- Hold: Stabilize the fracture.
- Heal: Monitor bone union.
- Rehabilitate: Restore function.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 424 (Book Page): [Treatment can be considered under the following headings... reduce; hold; heal; rehabilitate.]

category: Outline management principles
front: Why is excessive intravenous crystalloid or colloid use discouraged in severe trauma resuscitation?
back:
- Causes hemodilution.
- Increases coagulopathy.
