category: Discuss the role of surgical and non-surgical interventions in improving function and quality of life
front: Q: How does Early Total Care (ETC) improve functional outcomes compared to delayed fixation?
back: It facilitates nursing care, allows early mobilisation, and reduces pulmonary complications and intensive care length of stay.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [For musculoskeletal injuries, ETC allows defnitive fxation of all unstable long bone, spinal and pelvic fractures within 36 hours of injury. This facilitates nursing care, allows early mobilisation of the patient and reduces pulmonary complications and length of stay on intensive care.]

category: Discuss the role of surgical and non-surgical interventions in improving function and quality of life
front: Q: What are the primary non-surgical interventions for improving function in flail chest?
back: Oxygen administration, adequate analgesia (including opiates/local blocks), and physiotherapy to prevent hypoxia and respiratory failure.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): [Currently, treatment consists of oxygen administration, adequate analgesia (including opiates) and physiotherapy. If a chest tube is in place, topical intrapleural local analgesia introduced via the tube can also be used.]

category: Discuss the role of surgical and non-surgical interventions in improving function and quality of life
front: Q: What is the specific role of the Debridement, Antibiotics, and Implant Retention (DAIR) strategy in PJI?
back: To salvage well-fixed implants by excising infected tissue and modular components while using long-term antibiotics to suppress infection.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 602 (Book Page): [Debridement, antibiotics and implant retention - ‘DAIR’. This can only be undertaken if the prosthesis is well fxed. ... all infected soft tissue and necrotic bone must be fully excised and modular components exchanged.]

category: Discuss the role of surgical and non-surgical interventions in improving function and quality of life
front: Q: How is the Ponseti method used non-surgically to improve function in clubfoot?
back: Serial manipulation and above-knee casting correct the deformity, followed by a percutaneous Achilles tenotomy and long-term bracing.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 648 (Book Page): [The Ponseti method corrects foot deformity in 95% of idiopathic cases without the need for a formal surgical release... A specifc set of manoeuvres, followed by a series of well-moulded above-knee plaster casts, results in gradual correction.]

category: Discuss the role of surgical and non-surgical interventions in improving function and quality of life
front: Q: What is the functional aim of the 'Reduce, Hold, Heal, Rehabilitate' principle?
back: To optimise the healing environment while providing enough stability to allow early joint movement and prevent 'plaster disease' (stiffness).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 425 (Book Page): [The aim is to: minimise the period of disability by speeding up the healing process or providing enough stability to return to normal function while the fracture heals.]

category: Discuss the role of surgical and non-surgical interventions in improving function and quality of life
front: Q: When is surgical excision indicated to improve function in tarsal coalition?
back: In rigid, symptomatic cases to relieve pain and restore hindfoot motion before secondary degenerative changes develop.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 649 (Book Page): [Treatment is initially conservative, but if the coalition requires surgical excision this should be performed before degenerative changes develop.]

category: Discuss the role of surgical and non-surgical interventions in improving function and quality of life
front: Q: How do simple non-surgical nursing measures improve outcomes in TBI patients?
back: Raising the head of the bed and loosening cervical collars improve venous drainage, which lowers ICP and prevents secondary brain injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 390 (Book Page): [ICP can be controlled by simple measures, including raising the head of the bed and loosening the collar to improve venous drainage.]

category: Discuss the role of surgical and non-surgical interventions in improving function and quality of life
front: Q: What is the primary conservative approach to managing neuromuscular contractures in children?
back: Multidisciplinary use of physiotherapy, orthotics (splinting), and positioning systems to maintain muscle length and joint excursion.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 631 (Book Page): [In general, it is important to maintain good joint movement, muscle length and tendon excursion. ... The use of splints, positioning techniques and seating and sleeping systems is common with the aim of preventing fxed contractures.]

category: Discuss the role of surgical and non-surgical interventions in improving function and quality of life
front: Q: What is the primary functional objective of the non-surgical Ponseti method in treating idiopathic clubfoot?
back: Corrects multiplanar foot deformity through serial manipulation and casting. It successfully avoids formal surgical release and resultant joint stiffness in 95% of idiopathic cases.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 626 (Book Page): [The Ponseti method corrects foot deformity in 95% of idiopathic cases without the need for a formal surgical release and is the treatment of choice for all feet.]

category: Discuss the role of surgical and non-surgical interventions in improving function and quality of life
front: Q: How does the Early Total Care (ETC) surgical approach improve recovery in stable polytrauma patients?
back: Definitive fixation of long bone/spinal fractures within 36 hours. This facilitates easier nursing, promotes early mobilization, and reduces pulmonary complications or prolonged intensive care stays.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [For musculoskeletal injuries, ETC allows defnitive fxation of all unstable long bone, spinal and pelvic fractures within 36 hours of injury. This facilitates nursing care, allows early mobilisation of the patient and reduces pulmonary complications and length of stay on intensive care.]

category: Discuss the role of surgical and non-surgical interventions in improving function and quality of life
front: Q: Contrast the mechanical requirements and functional goals for intra-articular versus extra-articular fracture reduction.
back: Intra-articular requires absolute stability/anatomical reduction to prevent secondary arthritis. Extra-articular focuses on mechanical alignment (length, rotation, angulation) and relative stability to facilitate early functional mobilization.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 424 (Book Page): [Intra-articular fractures require an anatomical reduction and absolute stability. ... Fractures that do not involve the joint surface generally require restoration of mechanical alignment of the joints above and below.]

category: Discuss the role of surgical and non-surgical interventions in improving function and quality of life
front: Q: How does computerized gait analysis guide surgical intervention in children with spastic diplegia?
back: Provides objective evidence of multiplanar joint mechanics. This allows planning of Single-Event Multilevel Surgery (SEMLS) to correct bone/soft-tissue procedures, improving overall posture and walking efficiency.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 632 (Book Page): [Computerised analysis provides objective evidence of joint movement and mechanics in multiple planes... Appropriate bone and soft-tissue procedures can then be planned.]

category: Discuss the role of surgical and non-surgical interventions in improving function and quality of life
front: Q: What is the functional role of cyclical bisphosphonate therapy in managing Osteogenesis Imperfecta (OI)?
back: Decreases bone resorption and turnover. Clinically, it reduces bone pain, lowers fracture rates, and improves the patient’s capacity for weight-bearing mobility and bone strength.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Cyclical bisphosphonate treatment decreases bone resorption and turnover. This reduces bone pain and the fracture rate, promoting weight-bearing mobility and bone strength.]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: Define scoliosis and its primary planes of deformity.
back: Scoliosis is a spinal deformity in three planes. The most characteristic features are lateral curvature and a rotational component.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The term ‘scoliosis’ describes spinal deformity in three planes: lateral curvature is the most obvious deformity while the rotational component is most apparent in forward fexion when the rib asymmetry creates a ‘rib hump’.]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: Distinguish between structural and functional scoliosis during the Adams forward bend test.
back: Structural: Rib hump increases due to rotational deformity. Functional: Spine straightens on flexion and no rib hump is visible (often due to leg length discrepancy).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 477 (Book Page): [structural scoliosis: a rib hump will increase in size (bulge posteriorly on the thoracic convex side) as the patient bends forwards; this is diagnostic of idiopathic thoracic scoliosis (rotatory deformity); functional scoliosis: the spine straightens as the patient bends forwards and no rib hump is visible]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: List the four primary aetiological categories of scoliosis.
back:
1. Idiopathic (most common)
2. Neuromuscular
3. Syndromic
4. Congenital
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The cause may be idiopathic, neuromuscular, related to a syndrome or congenital.]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: How is idiopathic scoliosis classified based on the age of onset?
back:
1. Early onset: <10 years
2. Adolescent: 11–18 years
3. Adult: Onset at skeletal maturity
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Table 44.12 Classification of idiopathic scoliosis. Early onset <10 years; Adolescent 11–18 years; Adult Onset at maturity]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: Identify the gold standard radiological measurement for scoliosis severity.
back: The Cobb angle. It is a radiological measurement used to define the severity of the curve and guide management.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The Cobb angle is a radiological measurement that defnes severity and guides treatment (Figure 44.36).]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
coreConcept: Clinical significance of the Rib Hump
front: Q: What does the 'rib hump' clinically signify in a child with spinal deformity?
back: It signifies the rotational component of a structural scoliosis, where vertebrae rotate and push the ribs posteriorly on the convex side.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [the rotational component is most apparent in forward fexion when the rib asymmetry creates a ‘rib hump’... this is diagnostic of idiopathic thoracic scoliosis (rotatory deformity)]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: A 13-year-old girl presents with a painless lateral spinal curve and a rib hump. Diagnosis?
back: Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis (AIS). It is the most common structural curve type and is typically painless.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The adolescent idiopathic curve is the most common, afecting girls more than boys. Idiopathic scoliosis is generally not painful]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: What specific 'red flag' finding suggests scoliosis is not idiopathic?
back: Significant back pain. Idiopathic scoliosis is usually painless; pain suggests infection or underlying tumour.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Idiopathic scoliosis is generally not painful and, therefore, in the presence of signifcant pain tumour and infection must be excluded.]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: Define the two primary bone defects causing congenital scoliosis.
back:
1. Failure of formation: e.g., a hemivertebra.
2. Failure of segmentation: e.g., unilateral/bilateral fusions or bars.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Congenital vertebral deformities are failures either of formation (a hemivertebra) or of segmentation (unilateral or bilateral fusions or bars).]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: Identify the most common anatomical region for idiopathic scoliosis development.
back: The thoracic spine. It often presents with a right-sided convexity (rib hump).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The adolescent idiopathic curve is the most common... lateral curvature is the most obvious deformity while the rotational component is most apparent in forward fexion when the rib asymmetry creates a ‘rib hump’] (referenced with Figure 44.36 showing thoracic curve)

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: Define scoliosis and the specific planes of deformity involved.
back:
1. Spinal deformity in three planes.
2. Lateral curvature (most visible).
3. Rotational component (visible in forward flexion).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The term ‘scoliosis’ describes spinal deformity in three planes: lateral curvature is the most obvious deformity while the rotational component is most apparent in forward fexion when the rib asymmetry creates a ‘rib hump’ (Figure 44.35).]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: Distinguish between structural and functional scoliosis using the forward bending test.
back:
1. Structural: Rib hump increases/persists (rotatory deformity).
2. Functional: Spine straightens and rib hump disappears (flexible deformity).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 477 (Book Page): [structural scoliosis : a rib hump will increase in size (bulge posteriorly on the thoracic convex side) as the patient bends forwards... functional scoliosis : the spine straightens as the patient bends forwards and no rib hump is visible]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: List the four primary etiological categories of scoliosis.
back:
1. Idiopathic (most common).
2. Neuromuscular.
3. Syndromic.
4. Congenital.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The cause may be idiopathic, neuromuscular, related to a syndrome or congenital.]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: How is idiopathic scoliosis classified based on the age of onset?
back:
1. Early onset: <10 years.
2. Adolescent: 11–18 years.
3. Adult: Onset at maturity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [TABLE 44.12 Classifcation of idiopathic scoliosis. Type Age at onset Early onset <10 years Adolescent 11–18 years Adult Onset at maturity]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: What is the gold standard radiological measurement for scoliosis severity?
back: The Cobb angle.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The Cobb angle is a radiological measurement that defnes severity and guides treatment.]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: Identify two secondary causes of functional (non-structural) scoliosis.
back:
1. Abnormal leg lengths (leg length discrepancy).
2. Muscle spasm (often in the lumbar region).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 477 (Book Page): [this fexible deformity is secondary to other abnormalities such as abnormal leg lengths and muscle spasm in the lumbar region.]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: Define the two categories of congenital vertebral deformities leading to scoliosis.
back:
1. Failure of formation: e.g., Hemivertebra.
2. Failure of segmentation: e.g., Unilateral/bilateral fusions or bars.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Congenital vertebral deformities are failures either of formation (a hemivertebra) or of segmentation (unilateral or bilateral fusions or bars).]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: In a child with scoliosis, what is the clinical significance of significant back pain?
back: Red flag for tumor or infection (idiopathic scoliosis is typically painless).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Idiopathic scoliosis is generally not painful and, therefore, in the presence of signifcant pain tumour and infection must be excluded.]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: Outline the treatment thresholds for scoliosis based on Cobb angle measurements.
back:
1. <20°: Observation.
2. 25–40°: Bracing (if progressive).
3. >40°: Surgery (instrumentation and fusion).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Curves <20° do not need treatment, progressive curves of 25–40° may be braced and those >40° are considered for surgery...]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: Why are 'growing rods' used specifically in early-onset scoliosis?
back: To preserve spinal growth and lung development (most occurs in early childhood) while controlling curvature.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [As most lung development occurs in early childhood, the management of early-onset scoliosis must preserve growth: casting techniques or the use of ‘growing rods’ may be appropriate.]

category: Discuss the role of surgical and non-surgical interventions in improving function and quality of life
front: Q: What surgical intervention is used to address short stature in achondroplasia?
back: Limb-lengthening/reconstruction techniques. These procedures aim to improve functional hand reach and overall height to enhance quality of life.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): [Correction of limb alignment may be necessary and limb-lengthening techniques are used in some countries.]

category: Discuss the role of surgical and non-surgical interventions in improving function and quality of life
front: Q: Describe the primary non-surgical intervention for correcting idiopathic clubfoot.
back: The Ponseti Method. It involves serial manipulation and above-knee casting, correcting foot deformity in 95% of cases without major surgery.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 626 (Book Page): [The Ponseti method corrects foot deformity in 95% of idiopathic cases without the need for a formal surgical release and is the treatment of choice for all feet.]

category: Discuss the role of surgical and non-surgical interventions in improving function and quality of life
front: Q: Which non-surgical device is the standard treatment for DDH in neonates up to 6 months?
back: The Pavlik harness. It maintains the hip in flexion and abduction to encourage joint stability and acetabular remodelling.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): [Hips that remain unstable or that are dislocated at rest are treated with harnesses or splints that obtain and maintain reduction with the hip abducted and fexed.]

category: Discuss the role of surgical and non-surgical interventions in improving function and quality of life
front: Q: What is the goal of Single-Event Multilevel Surgery (SEMLS) in children with Cerebral Palsy?
back: To improve gait by correcting multiple bone and soft-tissue deformities simultaneously, enhancing overall ambulatory function.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 632 (Book Page): [Single-event multilevel surgery (SEMLS) is popular... Appropriate bone and soft-tissue procedures can then be planned.]

category: Discuss the role of surgical and non-surgical interventions in improving function and quality of life
front: Q: Why is intramedullary stabilization preferred over plates for fractures in Osteogenesis Imperfecta?
back: Plates create stress risers in brittle bone. Intramedullary devices stabilize the whole bone and permit growth while maintaining alignment.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Intramedullary techniques for stabilisation of fractures or osteotomies are preferred to plate fxation.]

category: Discuss the role of surgical and non-surgical interventions in improving function and quality of life
front: Q: What is the primary role of the Ilizarov method in complex chronic osteomyelitis?
back: Distraction osteogenesis. It fills bone defects after radical resection and stabilizes the limb while allowing early functional rehabilitation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 606 (Book Page): [The Ilizarov method, which uses distraction osteogenesis to fll bone defects, is a powerful and successful technique in these cases.]

category: Discuss the role of surgical and non-surgical interventions in improving function and quality of life
front: Q: Under what specific clinical condition is the "DAIR" strategy indicated for PJI?
back: Indicated for early or well-fixed infections where the prosthesis is stable and soft tissues allow thorough debridement.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 602 (Book Page): [Debridement, antibiotics and implant retention - ‘DAIR’... can only be undertaken if the prosthesis is well fxed.]

category: Discuss the role of surgical and non-surgical interventions in improving function and quality of life
front: Q: At what Cobb angle threshold is spinal fusion surgery generally considered for scoliosis?
back: Curves exceeding 40°. Surgery involves instrumenting and fusing the spine to prevent progressive pulmonary and mechanical dysfunction.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Curves <20° do not need treatment, progressive curves of 25–40° may be braced and those >40° are considered for surgery, which involves instrumenting and fusing the spine.]

category: Discuss the role of surgical and non-surgical interventions in improving function and quality of life
front: Q: What is the role of surgical excision in managing a tarsal coalition?
back: Indicated for symptomatic, rigid flat feet to relieve pain and improve hindfoot mobility before degenerative joint changes occur.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 627 (Book Page): [If the coalition requires surgical excision this should be performed before degenerative changes develop.]

category: Discuss the role of surgical and non-surgical interventions in improving function and quality of life
front: Q: What non-surgical intervention is used for early-onset scoliosis to preserve lung growth?
back: Casting techniques or the use of "growing rods." These manage deformity while allowing for vital thoracic cage and lung development.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [As most lung development occurs in early childhood, the management of early-onset scoliosis must preserve growth: casting techniques or the use of ‘growing rods’ may be appropriate.]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: Define scoliosis as presented in paediatric orthopaedics.
back:
A spinal deformity in three planes: 
- Lateral curvature
- Rotational component (fixed rib hump)
- Anteroposterior deformity
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The term ‘scoliosis’ describes spinal deformity in three planes: lateral curvature is the most obvious deformity while the rotational component is most apparent in forward fexion when the rib asymmetry creates a ‘rib hump’]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: What are the four primary aetiological categories of scoliosis?
back:
- Idiopathic (most common)
- Neuromuscular
- Syndromic
- Congenital
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The cause may be idiopathic, neuromuscular, related to a syndrome or congenital.]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: Differentiate between structural and functional scoliosis using the forward bending test.
back:
- Structural: Rib hump increases/bulges posteriorly on forward flexion.
- Functional: Spine straightens; deformity is due to external factors (e.g., leg length discrepancy).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 477 (Book Page): [structural scoliosis: a rib hump will increase in size... functional scoliosis: the spine straightens as the patient bends forwards and no rib hump is visible]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: A 14-year-old girl presents with a painless thoracic curve. What is the most likely diagnosis?
back: Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis (AIS).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The adolescent idiopathic curve is the most common, afecting girls more than boys. Idiopathic scoliosis is generally not painful]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: What are the two types of congenital vertebral malformations causing scoliosis?
back:
- Failure of formation (e.g., hemivertebra)
- Failure of segmentation (e.g., unilateral/bilateral bars or fusions)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Congenital vertebral deformities are failures either of formation (a hemivertebra) or of segmentation (unilateral or bilateral fusions or bars).]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: Classify idiopathic scoliosis based on age at onset.
back:
- Early onset: <10 years
- Adolescent: 11–18 years
- Adult: At maturity
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Table 44.12 Classification of idiopathic scoliosis: Early onset <10 years, Adolescent 11–18 years, Adult Onset at maturity]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: Why is preservation of growth the priority in treating early-onset scoliosis?
back: Most lung development occurs in early childhood; early fusion or restrictive deformity can impair pulmonary function.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [As most lung development occurs in early childhood, the management of early-onset scoliosis must preserve growth]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: A child presents with scoliosis and severe night pain. What must be excluded?
back: Tumour and Infection.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Idiopathic scoliosis is generally not painful and, therefore, in the presence of signifcant pain tumour and infection must be excluded.]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: List the Cobb angle treatment thresholds for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis.
back:
- <20°: Observation
- 25°–40°: Bracing (if progressive)
- >40°: Surgery (Instrumentation and Fusion)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Curves <20° do not need treatment, progressive curves of 25–40° may be braced and those >40° are considered for surgery, which involves instrumenting and fusing the spine]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: What radiological measurement defines the severity of scoliosis?
back: The Cobb angle.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The Cobb angle is a radiological measurement that defnes severity and guides treatment]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: Define scoliosis based on its planes of deformity.
back: A spinal deformity occurring in three planes, characterized by lateral curvature and a rotational component.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The term ‘scoliosis’ describes spinal deformity in three planes: lateral curvature is the most obvious deformity while the rotational component is most apparent in forward fexion]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: What are the four primary etiological categories of scoliosis?
back:
• Idiopathic (most common)
• Neuromuscular
• Syndromic
• Congenital
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The cause may be idiopathic, neuromuscular, related to a syndrome or congenital.]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: Contrast structural scoliosis and functional scoliosis during clinical examination.
back:
• Structural: Rotatory deformity (rib hump) persists or increases during forward flexion.
• Functional: Spine straightens and rib hump disappears on bending (e.g., from leg length discrepancy).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 498 (Book Page): [structural scoliosis : a rib hump will increase in size... as the patient bends forwards... functional scoliosis : the spine straightens as the patient bends forwards and no rib hump is visible]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: A 14-year-old girl presents with a painless lateral spinal curve. What is the most likely diagnosis?
back: Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis (AIS).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The adolescent idiopathic curve is the most common, afecting girls more than boys. Idiopathic scoliosis is generally not painful]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: Classify idiopathic scoliosis based on the age of onset.
back:
• Early onset: <10 years
• Adolescent: 11–18 years
• Adult: At skeletal maturity
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Table 44.12 Classifcation of idiopathic scoliosis. Type: Early onset (<10 years); Adolescent (11–18 years); Adult (Onset at maturity)]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: Which radiological measurement is used to define scoliosis severity and guide treatment?
back: The Cobb angle.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The Cobb angle is a radiological measurement that defnes severity and guides treatment]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: What are the Cobb angle thresholds for bracing and surgery in adolescent scoliosis?
back:
• 25–40°: Bracing (if progressive)
• >40°: Surgery (instrumentation and fusion)
• <20°: Observation only
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Curves <20° do not need treatment, progressive curves of 25–40° may be braced and those >40° are considered for surgery]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: Why is persistent back pain considered a 'red flag' in a child with scoliosis?
back: Idiopathic scoliosis is typically painless; pain suggests underlying infection or tumor.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Idiopathic scoliosis is generally not painful and, therefore, in the presence of signifcant pain tumour and infection must be excluded.]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: Why does early-onset scoliosis (<10 years) require growth-preserving management?
back: Most lung development occurs in early childhood; early fusion or severe curves can permanently impair pulmonary function.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [As most lung development occurs in early childhood, the management of early-onset scoliosis must preserve growth]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: Define the two types of congenital vertebral deformities causing scoliosis.
back:
• Failures of formation: e.g., hemivertebra
• Failures of segmentation: e.g., unilateral bar or bilateral fusion
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Congenital vertebral deformities are failures either of formation (a hemivertebra) or of segmentation (unilateral or bilateral fusions or bars).]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: Define scoliosis.
back: A multiplanar spinal deformity involving lateral curvature and a rotational component, which is clinically visible as a rib hump during forward flexion.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The term ‘scoliosis’ describes spinal deformity in three planes: lateral curvature is the most obvious deformity while the rotational component is most apparent in forward fexion when the rib asymmetry creates a ‘rib hump’]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: Contrast the physical findings of structural versus functional scoliosis in the forward bending test.
back: Structural: The rib hump increases in size or persists due to rotatory deformity. Functional: The spine straightens and no rib hump is visible; caused by non-spinal factors like leg length discrepancy.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 477 (Book Page): [structural scoliosis: a rib hump will increase in size (bulge posteriorly on the thoracic convex side) as the patient bends forwards... functional scoliosis: the spine straightens as the patient bends forwards and no rib hump is visible]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: Categorize idiopathic scoliosis based on the age of onset.
back:
1. Early onset: Under 10 years.
2. Adolescent: 11–18 years.
3. Adult: Onset occurs after skeletal maturity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Table 44.12 Classifcation of idiopathic scoliosis. Type Age at onset Early onset <10 years Adolescent 11–18 years Adult Onset at maturity]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: A child presents with scoliosis accompanied by significant pain. What serious underlying pathologies must be excluded?
back: Tumor and infection; idiopathic scoliosis is typically painless, so significant pain serves as a clinical 'red flag' for secondary causes.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Idiopathic scoliosis is generally not painful and, therefore, in the presence of signifcant pain tumour and infection must be excluded.]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: Which pharmacological agents are used to manage muscle tone in neuromuscular scoliosis (e.g., Cerebral Palsy)?
back:
1. Diazepam.
2. Baclofen.
3. Botulinum toxin (neuromuscular blocker for focal reduction).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 632 (Book Page): [Tone can be reduced with drugs (e.g. diazepam and baclofen). Alternatively, neuromuscular blockers such as botulinum toxin allow a focal reduction in tone]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: What is the gold standard radiological measurement used to define scoliosis severity?
back: The Cobb angle.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The Cobb angle is a radiological measurement that defnes severity and guides treatment]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: Define congenital scoliosis and its two primary vertebral causes.
back: Scoliosis caused by underlying bony malformations present at birth, specifically failure of formation (e.g., hemivertebra) or failure of segmentation (e.g., unilateral bars).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Congenital vertebral deformities are failures either of formation (a hemivertebra) or of segmentation (unilateral or bilateral fusions or bars). The clinical result is usually a scoliosis]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: How is scoliosis caused by leg length discrepancy (LLD) differentiated from adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS)?
back: LLD causes a postural (functional) scoliosis that straightens on forward bending, whereas AIS is a structural rotatory deformity that persists.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 477 (Book Page): [functional scoliosis: the spine straightens as the patient bends forwards... secondary to other abnormalities such as abnormal leg lengths]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: Explain the relationship between the age of scoliosis onset and the likelihood of progression.
back: Inversely related; generally, the earlier the age of onset, the more likely the spinal deformity is to be progressive.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [In general, the earlier the onset, the more likely the deformity is to be progressive.]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: List the Cobb angle thresholds for observation, bracing, and surgery in adolescent scoliosis.
back:
1. <20°: Observation.
2. 25–40°: Bracing (if progressive).
3. >40°: Surgical instrumentation and fusion.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Curves <20° do not need treatment, progressive curves of 25–40° may be braced and those >40° are considered for surgery, which involves instrumenting and fushing the spine]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: Define scoliosis and its primary clinical components.
back:
A three-plane spinal deformity involving:
- Lateral curvature.
- Rotational component (visible as a rib hump).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The term ‘scoliosis’ describes spinal deformity in three planes: lateral curvature is the most obvious deformity while the rotational component is most apparent in forward fexion when the rib asymmetry creates a ‘rib hump’.]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: Contrast the underlying cause of structural versus functional scoliosis.
back:
- Structural: Rotatory deformity (e.g., idiopathic).
- Functional: Flexible deformity secondary to non-spinal causes like leg length discrepancy or muscle spasm.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 477 (Book Page): [structural scoliosis: a rib hump will increase in size (bulge posteriorly on the thoracic convex side) as the patient bends forwards; this is diagnostic of idiopathic thoracic scoliosis (rotatory deformity); functional scoliosis: the spine straightens as the patient bends forwards and no rib hump is visible; this fexible deformity is secondary to other abnormalities such as abnormal leg lengths and muscle spasm in the lumbar region.]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: List the four primary etiologic types of scoliosis.
back:
1. Idiopathic (most common).
2. Neuromuscular.
3. Syndromic.
4. Congenital.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The cause may be idiopathic, neuromuscular, related to a syndrome or congenital.]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
coreConcept: Clinical Presentation of Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis
front: Q: A 13-year-old girl presents with painless spinal curvature and a rib hump. Most likely diagnosis?
back: Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis (AIS).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The adolescent idiopathic curve is the most common, afecting girls more than boys. Idiopathic scoliosis is generally not painful]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: Distinguish between the two mechanical causes of congenital scoliosis.
back:
1. Failure of formation: Resulting in a hemivertebra.
2. Failure of segmentation: Resulting in unilateral or bilateral bars (fusions).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Congenital vertebral deformities are failures either of formation (a hemivertebra) or of segmentation (unilateral or bilateral fusions or bars).]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: What are the diagnostic criteria for idiopathic scoliosis based on age?
back:
- Early onset: <10 years.
- Adolescent: 11–18 years.
- Adult: Onset after skeletal maturity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Table 44.12 Classifcation of idiopathic scoliosis. Early onset <10 years; Adolescent 11–18 years; Adult Onset at maturity]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: How is the physical severity of a scoliotic curve clinically assessed in forward flexion?
back: Using the Adam’s forward bend test to identify a "rib hump," which indicates the degree of vertebral rotation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The term ‘scoliosis’ describes spinal deformity in three planes... the rotational component is most apparent in forward fexion when the rib asymmetry creates a ‘rib hump’.]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: In a child with scoliosis, what does significant back pain suggest?
back: Red flag for non-idiopathic pathology, specifically infection or tumor.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Idiopathic scoliosis is generally not painful and, therefore, in the presence of signifcant pain tumour and infection must be excluded.]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: How does the age of onset correlate with scoliosis progression risk?
back: The earlier the onset of the deformity, the more likely it is to be progressive.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [In general, the earlier the onset, the more likely the deformity is to be progressive.]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: What radiographic feature distinguishes a hemivertebra in congenital scoliosis?
back: It represents a failure of formation of a vertebral part.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Congenital vertebral deformities are failures either of formation (a hemivertebra) or of segmentation]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: Define scoliosis.
back:
A multiplanar spinal deformity characterized by:
* Lateral curvature in the coronal plane.
* Axial rotation (causing a rib hump).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The term ‘scoliosis’ describes spinal deformity in three planes: lateral curvature is the most obvious deformity while the rotational component is most apparent in forward fexion when the rib asymmetry creates a ‘rib hump’. ]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: Classify idiopathic scoliosis by age of onset.
back:
1. Early onset: <10 years.
2. Adolescent: 11–18 years.
3. Adult: Onset at skeletal maturity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Table 44.12 Classifcation of idiopathic scoliosis. Type Age at onset Early onset <10 years Adolescent 11–18 years Adult Onset at maturity]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: Define the four primary etiological categories of structural scoliosis.
back:
1. Idiopathic (most common).
2. Neuromuscular.
3. Syndromic.
4. Congenital (bony malformation).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The cause may be idiopathic, neuromuscular, related to a syndrome or congenital.]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: Differentiate functional from structural scoliosis using the Adams test.
back:
* Functional: Spine straightens and rib hump disappears on forward flexion.
* Structural: Rib hump persists or increases on forward flexion.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 499 (Book Page): [structural scoliosis : a rib hump will increase in size... functional scoliosis : the spine straightens as the patient bends forwards and no rib hump is visible]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: What is the significance of significant back pain in a child with scoliosis?
back: Idiopathic scoliosis is generally painless; significant pain is a "red flag" necessitating exclusion of infection or tumor.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Idiopathic scoliosis is generally not painful and, therefore, in the presence of signifcant pain tumour and infection must be excluded.]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: Define the Cobb angle thresholds for scoliosis treatment.
back:
* <20°: Observation.
* 25–40° (Progressive): Bracing.
* >40°: Surgical consideration (instrumentation and fusion).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Curves <20° do not need treatment, progressive curves of 25–40° may be braced and those >40° are considered for surgery, which involves instrumenting and fusing the spine]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: How does the age of onset predict the natural history of scoliosis?
back: Earlier onset increases the likelihood of the deformity being progressive.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [In general, the earlier the onset, the more likely the deformity is to be progressive.]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: Define congenital scoliosis by its underlying bony mechanisms.
back:
1. Failure of formation (e.g., hemivertebra).
2. Failure of segmentation (e.g., unilateral bars or fusions).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Congenital vertebral deformities are failures either of formation (a hemivertebra) or of segmentation (unilateral or bilateral fusions or bars).]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: What type of scoliosis is caused by leg length discrepancy (LLD)?
back: Functional (Postural) scoliosis; the spine straightens on forward bending.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [A leg length discrepancy causes a postural scoliosis... functional scoliosis : the spine straightens as the patient bends forwards]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: Which specific physical feature is diagnostic of the axial rotation in structural scoliosis?
back: The rib hump, appearing as posterior rib asymmetry during forward flexion.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [the rotational component is most apparent in forward fexion when the rib asymmetry creates a ‘rib hump’. ]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: How is scoliosis clinically defined in terms of its three-dimensional planes of deformity?
back:
Scoliosis involves:
• Lateral curvature (coronal plane).
• Rotational component (axial plane), causing a posterior "rib hump."
• Deformity most apparent during forward flexion.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The term ‘scoliosis’ describes spinal deformity in three planes: lateral curvature is the most obvious deformity while the rotational component is most apparent in forward fexion when the rib asymmetry creates a ‘rib hump’. ]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: Which four primary etiological categories are used to classify scoliosis cases?
back:
The four main types are:
• Idiopathic (most common).
• Neuromuscular (e.g., cerebral palsy).
• Congenital (vertebral malformations).
• Syndromic related.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The cause may be idiopathic, neuromuscular, related to a syndrome or congenital.]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: Differentiate between structural and functional scoliosis using the Adams forward bend test findings.
back:
• Structural: Rib hump increases or persists due to fixed vertebral rotation.
• Functional: Spine straightens during forward bending; no rib hump is visible.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 477 (Book Page): [structural scoliosis: a rib hump will increase in size (bulge posteriorly on the thoracic convex side) as the patient bends forwards... functional scoliosis: the spine straightens as the patient bends forwards and no rib hump is visible]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: An 11-year-old presents with painless spinal curvature. How is idiopathic scoliosis classified by age?
back:
• Early onset: <10 years.
• Adolescent: 11–18 years.
• Adult: Onset after skeletal maturity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Table 44.12 Classifcation of idiopathic scoliosis. Early onset <10 years, Adolescent 11–18 years, Adult Onset at maturity]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: What management thresholds are recommended based on the radiological Cobb angle measurement?
back:
• <20°: Observation/No treatment.
• 25–40°: Bracing (if the curve is progressive).
• >40°: Surgery (spinal instrumentation and fusion).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The Cobb angle is a radiological measurement that defnes severity and guides treatment. Curves <20° do not need treatment, progressive curves of 25–40° may be braced and those >40° are considered for surgery]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: What underlying vertebral failures characterize congenital scoliosis and why is bracing ineffective?
back:
Failures of:
• Formation (e.g., hemivertebra).
• Segmentation (unilateral bars or fusions).
• Bracing is ineffective because the primary cause is a rigid bony malformation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Congenital vertebral deformities are failures either of formation (a hemivertebra) or of segmentation (unilateral or bilateral fusions or bars)... Bracing is inefective for congenital vertebral deformities.]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: Why must idiopathic scoliosis with significant pain trigger investigation for tumors or infection?
back: True idiopathic scoliosis is generally painless. Significant back pain in a child is a "red flag" for serious underlying spinal pathology.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Idiopathic scoliosis is generally not painful and, therefore, in the presence of signifcant pain tumour and infection must be excluded.]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: Contrast the clinical presentation of early-onset vs. adolescent idiopathic scoliosis management priorities.
back:
• Early-onset (<10y): Management must preserve spinal/thoracic growth (e.g., "growing rods") to allow lung development.
• Adolescent (11-18y): Priorities shift to definitive curve correction and fusion.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [In general, the earlier the onset, the more likely the deformity is to be progressive. As most lung development occurs in early childhood, the management of early-onset scoliosis must preserve growth: casting techniques or the use of ‘growing rods’ may be appropriate.]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: What specific clinical finding differentiates postural scoliosis caused by leg length discrepancy?
back: A postural scoliosis develops because the pelvis tilts to compensate for unequal leg lengths; the curve typically resolves when the patient sits.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [A leg length discrepancy causes a postural scoliosis.]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: Which two imaging planes are essential for calculating the Cobb angle in scoliosis?
back: A posteroanterior (PA) radiograph of the whole spine is primarily used to measure the lateral curvature degree.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 630 (Book Page): [Figure 44.36 Posteroanterior radiograph of a spine with a scoliosis (right thoracic), with a Cobb angle of 40°.]

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: Define scoliosis in the context of paediatric spinal deformity.
back: A multiplanar spinal deformity involving lateral curvature and a rotational component.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): The term ‘scoliosis’ describes spinal deformity in three planes: lateral curvature is the most obvious deformity while the rotational component is most apparent in forward flexion...

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: List the four primary etiological categories of scoliosis.
back:
1. Idiopathic
2. Neuromuscular
3. Syndromic
4. Congenital
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): The cause may be idiopathic, neuromuscular, related to a syndrome or congenital.

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: How is the rotational component of structural scoliosis clinically identified?
back: Adams forward bend test; reveals a posterior rib hump on the thoracic convex side.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): the rotational component is most apparent in forward flexion when the rib asymmetry creates a ‘rib hump’ (Figure 44.35).

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: A child presents with spinal asymmetry that resolves during forward bending. Diagnosis?
back: Functional scoliosis; a flexible deformity typically secondary to leg length discrepancy or muscle spasm.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): functional scoliosis: the spine straightens as the patient bends forwards and no rib hump is visible; this flexible deformity is secondary to other abnormalities such as abnormal leg lengths and muscle spasm...

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: What is the primary management goal for early-onset scoliosis (<10 years)?
back: Growth preservation to facilitate normal lung development using casting or growing rods.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): As most lung development occurs in early childhood, the management of early-onset scoliosis must preserve growth: casting techniques or the use of ‘growing rods’ may be appropriate.

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: What radiographic measurement defines scoliosis severity and guides treatment?
back: The Cobb angle.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): The Cobb angle is a radiological measurement that defines severity and guides treatment (Figure 44.36).

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: State the Cobb angle thresholds for bracing and surgery in adolescent scoliosis.
back: Bracing: 25–40°; Surgery: >40°.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): progressive curves of 25–40° may be braced and those >40° are considered for surgery, which involves instrumenting and fusing the spine...

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: Why is significant back pain a 'red flag' in scoliosis cases?
back: Idiopathic scoliosis is generally painless; pain suggests underlying tumor or infection.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): Idiopathic scoliosis is generally not painful and, therefore, in the presence of significant pain tumour and infection must be excluded.

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: Name the two developmental failures that result in congenital scoliosis.
back:
1. Failure of formation (e.g., hemivertebra)
2. Failure of segmentation (e.g., unilateral bars).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): Congenital vertebral deformities are failures either of formation (a hemivertebra) or of segmentation (unilateral or bilateral fusions or bars).

category: Define scoliosis and its types
front: Q: How is idiopathic scoliosis classified by age of onset?
back: Early onset (<10 years), Adolescent (11–18 years), Adult (at maturity).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page), Table 44.12: Early onset <10 years; Adolescent 11–18 years; Adult Onset at maturity.

category: Identify clinical features and screening methods for scoliosis
front: Q: In how many planes is the spinal deformity of scoliosis described?
back:
Three planes:
- Lateral curvature
- Rotational deformity
- Sagittal deformity
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The term ‘scoliosis’ describes spinal deformity in three planes: lateral curvature is the most obvious deformity while the rotational component is most apparent in forward fexion]

category: Identify clinical features and screening methods for scoliosis
front: Q: What anatomical mechanism produces the 'rib hump' seen in scoliosis screening?
back: The rotational component of the vertebral deformity, which is most prominent during forward flexion.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [the rotational component is most apparent in forward fexion when the rib asymmetry creates a ‘rib hump’]

category: Identify clinical features and screening methods for scoliosis
front: Q: How do structural and functional scoliosis differ during the forward bending test?
back:
- Structural: Rib hump persists or increases.
- Functional: Spine straightens; rib hump disappears.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 498 (Book Page): [structural scoliosis: a rib hump will increase in size... as the patient bends forwards... functional scoliosis: the spine straightens as the patient bends forwards and no rib hump is visible]

category: Identify clinical features and screening methods for scoliosis
front: Q: A 14-year-old female presents with shoulder asymmetry but no pain. What is the most likely diagnosis?
back: Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis (the most common structural scoliosis, typically painless).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The adolescent idiopathic curve is the most common... Idiopathic scoliosis is generally not painful]

category: Identify clinical features and screening methods for scoliosis
front: Q: What is the management protocol for a scoliosis patient with a Cobb angle of 25°–40°?
back: Bracing is indicated for progressive curves in this range.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [progressive curves of 25–40° may be braced and those >40° are considered for surgery]

category: Identify clinical features and screening methods for scoliosis
front: Q: What is the definitive radiological measurement used to quantify scoliosis severity?
back: The Cobb Angle.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The Cobb angle is a radiological measurement that defnes severity and guides treatment]

category: Identify clinical features and screening methods for scoliosis
front: Q: Which non-spinal physical exam finding can cause a postural (functional) scoliosis?
back: Leg Length Discrepancy (LLD).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [A leg length discrepancy causes a postural scoliosis]

category: Identify clinical features and screening methods for scoliosis
front: Q: What are the two primary differential concerns if a scoliotic curve is associated with significant pain?
back:
1. Infection
2. Tumour
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Idiopathic scoliosis is generally not painful and, therefore, in the presence of signifcant pain tumour and infection must be excluded.]

category: Identify clinical features and screening methods for scoliosis
front: Q: Define the age boundaries for 'Early Onset' versus 'Adolescent' idiopathic scoliosis.
back:
- Early Onset: <10 years
- Adolescent: 11–18 years
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Table 44.12: Early onset <10 years; Adolescent 11–18 years]

category: Identify clinical features and screening methods for scoliosis
front: Q: Name two bony malformations responsible for congenital scoliosis.
back:
1. Hemivertebra (failure of formation)
2. Failure of segmentation (unilateral/bilateral bars)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Congenital vertebral deformities are failures either of formation (a hemivertebra) or of segmentation (unilateral or bilateral fusions or bars).]

category: Identify clinical features and screening methods for scoliosis
front: Q: What are the three components that defne the deformity seen in scoliosis?
back:
● Lateral curvature of the spine
● Rotational component (producing a rib hump)
● Deformity in three planes
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The term ‘scoliosis’ describes spinal deformity in three planes: lateral curvature is the most obvious deformity while the rotational component is most apparent in forward fexion when the rib asymmetry creates a ‘rib hump’.]

category: Identify clinical features and screening methods for scoliosis
front: Q: What is the mechanism distinguishing a rib hump in structural versus functional scoliosis?
back:
● Structural: Rib hump increases/persists in forward fexion due to rotation.
● Functional: Rib hump/curve disappears in forward fexion.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [structural scoliosis : a rib hump will increase in size (bulge posteriorly on the thoracic convex side) as the patient bends forwards... functional scoliosis : the spine straightens as the patient bends forwards and no rib hump is visible]

category: Identify clinical features and screening methods for scoliosis
front: Q: How is idiopathic scoliosis clinically differentiated from scoliosis caused by infection or tumour?
back:
● Presence of pain: Idiopathic scoliosis is generally painless.
● Pain in scoliosis demands exclusion of infection or malignancy.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Idiopathic scoliosis is generally not painful and, therefore, in the presence of signifcant pain tumour and infection must be excluded.]

category: Identify clinical features and screening methods for scoliosis
front: Q: A 13-year-old girl presents with shoulder asymmetry and a 45° Cobb angle. Diagnosis and next step?
back:
● Diagnosis: Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis (AIS).
● Next step: Consideration for surgical instrumentation and fusion.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Adolescent 11–18 years... curves <20° do not need treatment, progressive curves of 25–40° may be braced and those >40° are considered for surgery, which involves instrumenting and fusing the spine.]

category: Identify clinical features and screening methods for scoliosis
front: Q: What are the management thresholds for scoliosis based on Cobb angle severity?
back:
● <20°: Observation only.
● 25°–40°: Bracing (for progressive curves).
● >40°: Surgical instrumentation and fusion.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Curves <20° do not need treatment, progressive curves of 25–40° may be braced and those >40° are considered for surgery, which involves instrumenting and fusing the spine.]

category: Identify clinical features and screening methods for scoliosis
front: Q: What is the defnitive physical examination screening method for scoliosis rotation?
back:
● Adams forward bend test.
● Positive result: Asymmetry/bulge (rib hump) on the thoracic convex side.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [the rotational component is most apparent in forward fexion when the rib asymmetry creates a ‘rib hump’... structural scoliosis : a rib hump will increase in size (bulge posteriorly on the thoracic convex side) as the patient bends forwards]

category: Identify clinical features and screening methods for scoliosis
front: Q: Which extra-spinal clinical finding causes a ‘postural scoliosis’ requiring differentiation from AIS?
back:
● Leg length discrepancy (LLD).
● Correcting LLD typically resolves the postural curvature.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [A leg length discrepancy causes a postural scoliosis... functional scoliosis : the spine straightens as the patient bends forwards and no rib hump is visible; this fexible deformity is secondary to other abnormalities such as abnormal leg lengths]

category: Identify clinical features and screening methods for scoliosis
front: Q: Contrast the treatment efficacy of bracing in congenital versus idiopathic scoliosis.
back:
● Idiopathic: Bracing can slow progression in 25°–40° curves.
● Congenital: Bracing is ineffective for bony malformations (hemivertebra/bars).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Congenital vertebral deformities are failures either of formation (a hemivertebra) or of segmentation (unilateral or bilateral fusions or bars)... Bracing is inefective for congenital vertebral deformities.]

category: Identify clinical features and screening methods for scoliosis
front: Q: Why is spinal growth preservation prioritized over early fusion in early-onset scoliosis?
back:
● Lung development occurs primarily in early childhood.
● Early fusion restricts thoracic expansion and pulmonary capacity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [As most lung development occurs in early childhood, the management of early-onset scoliosis must preserve growth: casting techniques or the use of ‘growing rods’ may be appropriate.]

category: Identify clinical features and screening methods for scoliosis
front: Q: Which radiological measurement is the standard for assessing scoliosis curve severity?
back:
● Cobb angle.
● Measured from AP/PA radiographs to guide observation, bracing, or surgery.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The Cobb angle is a radiological measurement that defnes severity and guides treatment ( Figure 44.36 ).]

category: Identify clinical features and screening methods for scoliosis
front: Q: Define scoliosis in terms of the anatomical planes of deformity.
back:
● Multiplanar deformity consisting of:
● Lateral curvature (coronal plane).
● Vertebral rotation (axial plane).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): The term ‘scoliosis’ describes spinal deformity in three planes: lateral curvature is the most obvious deformity while the rotational component is most apparent in forward fexion when the rib asymmetry creates a ‘rib hump’.

category: Identify clinical features and screening methods for scoliosis
front: Q: Contrast the findings of structural versus functional scoliosis during the forward bending test.
back:
● Structural: Rib hump persists/increases on the convex side (rotatory deformity).
● Functional: Spine straightens and rib hump disappears (secondary to leg length difference or muscle spasm).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 477 (Book Page): structural scoliosis: a rib hump will increase in size (bulge posteriorly on the thoracic convex side) as the patient bends forwards; this is diagnostic of idiopathic thoracic scoliosis (rotatory deformity); functional scoliosis: the spine straightens as the patient bends forwards and no rib hump is visible.

category: Identify clinical features and screening methods for scoliosis
front: Q: How is the Adams forward bend test performed for scoliosis screening?
back:
● Patient bends forward to touch toes.
● Examiner inspects from behind for rib asymmetry (rib hump).
● Primarily identifies the rotational component of the deformity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): lateral curvature is the most obvious deformity while the rotational component is most apparent in forward fexion when the rib asymmetry creates a ‘rib hump’ (Figure 44.35).

category: Identify clinical features and screening methods for scoliosis
front: Q: A child with scoliosis presents with significant back pain. What does this clinical feature suggest?
back:
● Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis is usually painless.
● Significant pain is a "red flag" for:
  1. Spinal tumor.
  2. Infection.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): Idiopathic scoliosis is generally not painful and, therefore, in the presence of signifcant pain tumour and infection must be excluded.

category: Identify clinical features and screening methods for scoliosis
front: Q: What are the treatment thresholds for scoliosis based on the Cobb angle measurement?
back:
● <20°: Observation/no treatment.
● 25–40°: Bracing (if the curve is progressive).
● >40°: Surgical consideration (instrumentation and spinal fusion).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): Curves <20° do not need treatment, progressive curves of 25–40° may be braced and those >40° are considered for surgery, which involves instrumenting and fusing the spine.

category: Identify clinical features and screening methods for scoliosis
front: Q: What is the gold-standard radiological measurement for quantifying scoliosis severity?
back:
● Cobb angle.
● Measured on a posteroanterior (PA) radiograph.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): The Cobb angle is a radiological measurement that defnes severity and guides treatment (Figure 44.36).

category: Identify clinical features and screening methods for scoliosis
front: Q: List the clinical features of scoliosis during a static standing inspection.
back:
● Shoulder height asymmetry.
● Ribcage/scapular asymmetry.
● Pelvic tilt (asymmetrical iliac crest height).
● Midline deviation (plumb line not falling through gluteal crease).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 477 (Book Page): Check for asymmetry of the shoulder and ribcage suggesting scoliosis... Look for a diference in the height of the iliac crests (pelvic tilt). Assess for coronal plane deformity, such as scoliosis.

category: Identify clinical features and screening methods for scoliosis
front: Q: Distinguish the clinical significance of early-onset vs. adolescent idiopathic scoliosis.
back:
● Early-onset (<10 years): High risk of progression; requires growth-preserving treatments.
● Adolescent (11–18 years): Most common; management determined by Cobb angle and skeletal maturity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): In general, the earlier the onset, the more likely the deformity is to be progressive. As most lung development occurs in early childhood, the management of early-onset scoliosis must preserve growth.

category: Identify clinical features and screening methods for scoliosis
front: Q: Which demographic is most frequently affected by adolescent idiopathic scoliosis?
back: ● Adolescent girls are affected significantly more than boys.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): The adolescent idiopathic curve is the most common, afecting girls more than boys.

category: Identify clinical features and screening methods for scoliosis
front: Q: Identify the specific clinical sign used to describe forefoot abduction in a patient with a postural scoliosis secondary to leg length discrepancy.
back:
● "Too many toes" sign.
● Indicates compensatory foot changes (e.g., pes planus) that can exacerbate pelvic tilt and postural scoliosis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 494 (Book Page): Look from behind and count the number of toes that can be seen. The ‘too many toes’ sign demonstrates increased forefoot abduction (pes planus [fat foot]) and a splayed forefoot.

category: Identify clinical features and screening methods for scoliosis
front: Q: Define the structural components of scoliosis as identified on clinical examination.
back:
• Multiplanar spinal deformity
• Lateral curvature
• Rotational component (visible as a rib hump)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The term ‘scoliosis’ describes spinal deformity in three planes: lateral curvature is the most obvious deformity while the rotational component is most apparent in forward fexion when the rib asymmetry creates a ‘rib hump’.]

category: Identify clinical features and screening methods for scoliosis
front: Q: What anatomical mechanism creates the 'rib hump' characteristic of structural scoliosis?
back:
• Vertebral rotation toward the convex side of the curve
• Posterior displacement of the ribs on the same side
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 498 (Book Page): [structural scoliosis: a rib hump will increase in size (bulge posteriorly on the thoracic convex side) as the patient bends forwards; this is diagnostic of idiopathic thoracic scoliosis (rotatory deformity)]

category: Identify clinical features and screening methods for scoliosis
front: Q: Distinguish between structural and functional scoliosis using the Adams Forward Bending Test.
back:
• Structural: Rib hump persists or increases
• Functional: Spine straightens and rib hump disappears
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 498 (Book Page): [structural scoliosis: a rib hump will increase in size... as the patient bends forwards... functional scoliosis: the spine straightens as the patient bends forwards and no rib hump is visible]

category: Identify clinical features and screening methods for scoliosis
front: Q: An adolescent with scoliosis presents with localized night pain. What serious pathologies must be excluded?
back:
• Spinal infection
• Spinal tumor
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Idiopathic scoliosis is generally not painful and, therefore, in the presence of signifcant pain tumour and infection must be excluded.]

category: Identify clinical features and screening methods for scoliosis
front: Q: Identify the radiographic measurement used to define scoliosis severity and guide treatment.
back:
• Cobb angle
• Measured on posteroanterior radiographs
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The Cobb angle is a radiological measurement that defnes severity and guides treatment (Figure 44.36).]

category: Identify clinical features and screening methods for scoliosis
front: Q: What are the primary thresholds for Cobb angle management in idiopathic scoliosis?
back:
• <20°: Observation only
• 25°–40°: Bracing (if progressive)
• >40°: Surgical consideration (instrumentation and fusion)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Curves <20° do not need treatment, progressive curves of 25–40° may be braced and those >40° are considered for surgery, which involves instrumenting and fusing the spine]

category: Identify clinical features and screening methods for scoliosis
front: Q: Describe the clinical assessment for coronal plane spinal balance in a standing patient.
back:
• Plumb line dropped from C7 spinous process
• Should fall through the center of the gluteal crease
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 476 (Book Page): [A ‘plumb line’ dropped from the spinous process of C7 should fall through the gluteal crease (Figure 35.2). If it falls to either side of the cleft, lateral tilt of the spine is present.]

category: Identify clinical features and screening methods for scoliosis
front: Q: A toddler with a leg length discrepancy appears to have scoliosis. What is the diagnosis?
back:
• Postural (Functional) scoliosis
• Secondary to pelvic tilt
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [A leg length discrepancy causes a postural scoliosis... functional scoliosis... is secondary to other abnormalities such as abnormal leg lengths]

category: Identify clinical features and screening methods for scoliosis
front: Q: Why is early detection critical in early-onset scoliosis (onset <10 years)?
back:
• To preserve lung development
• Most lung growth occurs in early childhood
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [As most lung development occurs in early childhood, the management of early-onset scoliosis must preserve growth: casting techniques or the use of ‘growing rods’ may be appropriate.]

category: Identify clinical features and screening methods for scoliosis
front: Q: Identify three key findings on visual inspection of the standing patient with scoliosis.
back:
• Shoulder level asymmetry
• Ribcage/waist asymmetry
• Pelvic tilt
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 477 (Book Page): [Front. Check for asymmetry of the shoulder and ribcage suggesting scoliosis. Back. Look for a diference in the height of the iliac crests (pelvic tilt).]

category: Identify clinical features and screening methods for scoliosis
front: Q: What three-dimensional planes of deformity characterize the clinical definition of scoliosis?
back:
- Lateral curvature
- Rotational component (vertebral rotation)
- Sagittal plane deformity
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The term ‘scoliosis’ describes spinal deformity in three planes: lateral curvature is the most obvious deformity while the rotational component is most apparent in forward fexion when the rib asymmetry creates a ‘rib hump’. The cause may be idiopathic, neuromuscular, related to a syndrome or congenital.]

category: Identify clinical features and screening methods for scoliosis
front: Q: What mechanism is responsible for the 'rib hump' observed in structural scoliosis during forward flexion?
back: - Vertebral rotation causes the ribs to bulge posteriorly on the convex side of the curve.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The rotational component is most apparent in forward fexion when the rib asymmetry creates a ‘rib hump’. ... structural scoliosis: a rib hump will increase in size (bulge posteriorly on the thoracic convex side) as the patient bends forwards; this is diagnostic of idiopathic thoracic scoliosis (rotatory deformity)]

category: Identify clinical features and screening methods for scoliosis
