category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: What must be excluded if a child presents with painful scoliosis?
back:
- Spinal tumour.
- Spinal infection.
- Note: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis is typically painless.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Idiopathic scoliosis is generally not painful and, therefore, in the presence of signifcant pain tumour and infection must be excluded.]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: What is the multidisciplinary management for an adolescent with a 35° progressive curve?
back:
- Spinal bracing (orthotic management).
- Standard for progressive curves between 25° and 40°.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Curves <20° do not need treatment, progressive curves of 25–40° may be braced and those >40° are considered for surgery...]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: What surgical threshold and techniques are used for severe structural scoliosis?
back:
- Threshold: Cobb angle >40°.
- Techniques: Spinal instrumentation and fusion.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The Cobb angle is a radiological measurement that defnes severity and guides treatment. Curves <20° do not need treatment, progressive curves of 25–40° may be braced and those >40° are considered for surgery, which involves instrumenting and fusing the spine.]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: Which test differentiates structural from functional scoliosis in a multidisciplinary screening?
back:
- Adams forward bend test.
- Structural: Rib hump increases/persists.
- Functional: Spine straightens (often due to leg length discrepancy).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [structural scoliosis : a rib hump will increase in size (bulge posteriorly on the thoracic convex side) as the patient bends forwards... functional scoliosis : the spine straightens as the patient bends forwards and no rib hump is visible; this fexible deformity is secondary to other abnormalities such as abnormal leg lengths...]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: What conservative components are essential in a multidisciplinary neuromuscular scoliosis team?
back:
- Physiotherapy: Maintains joint range and muscle length.
- Orthotists: Seating systems and spinal bracing.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 631 (Book Page): [A multidisciplinary approach to management is essential. Physiotherapy and orthotic management may reduce the need for surgical intervention and postoperatively they ensure that the surgical benefts are maximised. ... The use of splints, positioning techniques and seating and sleeping sys - tems is common...]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
coreConcept: Total Body Involvement (TBI) vs Ambulant management
front: Q: Contrast management focus in ambulant vs. non-ambulant (TBI) neuromuscular scoliosis.
back:
- Ambulant: Gait analysis to plan bone/soft tissue surgery (SEMLS).
- Non-ambulant: Focuses on seating position, pelvic symmetry, and preventing total body involvement.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 632 (Book Page): [In the child with total body involvement (TBI) and high muscle tone, hip subluxation leading to dislocation is common... Aggressive management of a spinal deformity initially concentrates on seating position and subsequently emphasises spinal bracing or surgery.]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: How do physiological growth laws influence multidisciplinary scoliosis planning?
back:
- Hueter-Volkmann Principle: Symmetrical growth depends on improving mechanical pressure.
- Multidisciplinary goal: Orthotics and casting reverse abnormal growth by altering bone stresses.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 609 (Book Page): [The conservative treatment of common conditions... considers remodelling ability with an understanding of the Hueter–Volkmann principle and Wolf’s law... Page 629 (Book Page): ...management of early-onset scoliosis must preserve growth: casting techniques... may be appropriate.]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: What is the most common structural scoliosis encountered by multidisciplinary teams?
back:
- Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis (AIS).
- Affects girls more frequently than boys.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The adolescent idiopathic curve is the most common, afecting girls more than boys.]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: What physical examination maneuver is used to identify the rotational component of scoliosis?
back:
- Adams forward bend test.
- Diagnostic of rotatory deformity if a "rib hump" appears or increases during the maneuver.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [lateral curvature is the most obvious deformity while the rotational component is most apparent in forward fexion when the rib asymmetry creates a ‘rib hump’]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: Why is preserving spinal growth critical in the multidisciplinary management of early-onset scoliosis?
back:
- Prevents thoracic constriction.
- Most lung development occurs in early childhood; restrictive spinal deformity can impair pulmonary capacity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [As most lung development occurs in early childhood, the management of early-onset scoliosis must preserve growth: casting techniques or the use of ‘growing rods’ may be appropriate.]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: Differentiate the findings of structural versus functional scoliosis during forward bending.
back:
- Structural: Rib hump persists/increases (rotatory deformity).
- Functional: Spine straightens and rib hump disappears (often secondary to leg length discrepancy).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 477 (Book Page): [structural scoliosis: a rib hump will increase in size... as the patient bends forwards... functional scoliosis: the spine straightens as the patient bends forwards and no rib hump is visible]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: What is the indicated management for a progressive adolescent idiopathic scoliosis curve of 30°?
back:
- Bracing (orthotic management).
- Indicated for progressive curves measuring between 25° and 40°.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [progressive curves of 25–40° may be braced and those >40° are considered for surgery, which involves instrumenting and fusing the spine]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: At what Cobb angle threshold is surgical intervention typically recommended for scoliosis?
back:
- Greater than 40°.
- Involves spinal instrumentation and fusion.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [progressive curves of 25–40° may be braced and those >40° are considered for surgery, which involves instrumenting and fusing the spine]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: What radiological measurement is the gold standard for defining scoliosis severity?
back:
- Cobb angle.
- Used to categorize the curve and determine the management protocol (observation, bracing, or surgery).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The Cobb angle is a radiological measurement that defnes severity and guides treatment]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: What multidisciplinary approach is appropriate for an idiopathic scoliosis curve less than 20°?
back:
- Observation only.
- Regular monitoring to check for progression without active intervention.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Curves <20° do not need treatment, progressive curves of 25–40° may be braced and those >40° are considered for surgery]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: If a child with scoliosis presents with significant pain, what serious pathologies must be excluded?
back:
- Infection.
- Spinal tumor.
- Note: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis is generally painless.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Idiopathic scoliosis is generally not painful and, therefore, in the presence of signifcant pain tumour and infection must be excluded.]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: How does the age of onset relate to the likelihood of scoliosis curve progression?
back:
- The earlier the onset, the higher the risk of progression.
- Early-onset curves (<10 years) are more likely to require growth-preserving surgery.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [In general, the earlier the onset, the more likely the deformity is to be progressive.]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: Define the three planes of deformity involved in a scoliosis curve.
back:
- Coronal: Lateral curvature.
- Axial: Vertebral rotation (rib hump).
- Sagittal: Changes in kyphosis/lordosis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The term ‘scoliosis’ describes spinal deformity in three planes: lateral curvature is the most obvious deformity while the rotational component is most apparent in forward fexion]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: What are the three primary management levels for structural scoliosis based on the Cobb angle?
back:
* Observation: Curves <20°.
* Bracing: Progressive curves 25–40°.
* Surgery: Curves >40° (instrumentation and fusion).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): Curves <20° do not need treatment, progressive curves of 25–40° may be braced and those >40° are considered for surgery, which involves instrumenting and fusing the spine.

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: What is the specific goal of multidisciplinary management in early-onset scoliosis (<10 years)?
back: Growth preservation. Management utilizes serial casting or ‘growing rods’ to allow trunk and lung development while controlling the curve.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): The management of early-onset scoliosis must preserve growth: casting techniques or the use of ‘growing rods’ may be appropriate.

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: Which physical examination finding identifies the rotational component of a structural scoliosis?
back: A persistent rib hump. This is best visualized during the Adams forward bend test as the child flexes the spine.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): the rotational component is most apparent in forward fexion when the rib asymmetry creates a ‘rib hump’ (Figure 44.35).

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: In multidisciplinary neuromuscular care, what is the initial management focus for spinal deformity?
back: Optimizing seating position. This precedes and supports subsequent interventions like spinal bracing or surgery.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 632 (Book Page): Aggressive management of a spinal deformity initially concentrates on seating position and subsequently emphasises spinal bracing or surgery.

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: What multidisciplinary red flag mandates investigation for tumor or infection in a scoliosis patient?
back: Significant pain. Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis is typically painless; unrelenting or night pain mandates imaging to exclude serious pathology.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): Idiopathic scoliosis is generally not painful and, therefore, in the presence of signifcant pain tumour and infection must be excluded.

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: What radiographic standard is used to monitor scoliosis progression and determine treatment pathways?
back: The Cobb angle. It is measured on posteroanterior radiographs to define severity and guide decisions between bracing and surgery.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): The Cobb angle is a radiological measurement that defnes severity and guides treatment (Figure 44.36).

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: What is the role of physiotherapy and splinting in the management of neuromuscular scoliosis?
back:
* Maintain joint range and muscle length.
* Prevent fixed contractures.
* Optimize posture and seating to improve quality of life.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 631 (Book Page): In general, it is important to maintain good joint movement, muscle length and tendon excursion... The use of splints, positioning techniques and seating and sleeping systems is common with the aim of preventing fxed contractures.

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: How does a leg length discrepancy (LLD) affect the multidisciplinary diagnosis of scoliosis?
back: It causes functional (postural) scoliosis. The spinal curve resolves when the LLD is corrected or during forward bending, unlike structural scoliosis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): A leg length discrepancy causes a postural scoliosis (Summary Box 44.16).

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: What is the primary indication for surgical spinal instrumentation and fusion in scoliosis?
back: Cobb angle >40°. Surgery aims to correct multiplanar deformity and prevent progressive respiratory or visceral compromise.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): progressive curves of 25–40° may be braced and those >40° are considered for surgery, which involves instrumenting and fusing the spine.

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: What defines the age-based classification of adolescent idiopathic scoliosis?
back: Onset between the ages of 11 and 18 years. It is the most common form of structural scoliosis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): Table 44.12: Adolescent [idiopathic scoliosis]: 11–18 years.

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: What clinical finding during the Adams forward bend test identifies a structural scoliosis?
back: The presence of a rib hump. This identifies the rotational component of the spinal deformity, which is most apparent in forward flexion.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The term ‘scoliosis’ describes spinal deformity in three planes: lateral curvature is the most obvious deformity while the rotational component is most apparent in forward fexion when the rib asymmetry creates a ‘rib hump’.]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: Why does the multidisciplinary management of early-onset scoliosis prioritize growth preservation over spinal fusion?
back: To avoid compromising lung development. Most lung growth occurs in early childhood; early fusion restricts thoracic volume and can lead to pulmonary complications.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [As most lung development occurs in early childhood, the management of early-onset scoliosis must preserve growth: casting techniques or the use of ‘growing rods’ may be appropriate.]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: How is a structural scoliosis distinguished from a functional scoliosis during clinical examination?
back: Functional scoliosis straightens during forward bending and lacks a rib hump. It is usually secondary to non-spinal factors like leg length discrepancy.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 611 (Book Page): [functional scoliosis: the spine straightens as the patient bends forwards and no rib hump is visible; this fexible deformity is secondary to other abnormalities such as abnormal leg lengths and muscle spasm in the lumbar region.]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: A 13-year-old girl is diagnosed with a progressive idiopathic scoliosis curve of 35°. What multidisciplinary treatment is indicated?
back: Orthotic bracing. Progressive curves between 25° and 40° are managed with braces to prevent further progression before skeletal maturity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Curves <20° do not need treatment, progressive curves of 25–40° may be braced and those >40° are considered for surgery]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: Which medications are used in the multidisciplinary management of neuromuscular scoliosis to reduce deforming spasticity?
back:
1. Oral diazepam.
2. Baclofen (oral or intrathecal).
3. Botulinum toxin (for focal reduction of high muscle tone).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 632 (Book Page): [Tone can be reduced with drugs (e.g. diazepam and baclofen). Alternatively, neuromuscular blockers such as botulinum toxin allow a focal reduction in tone by preventing acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction.]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: What Cobb angle threshold typically indicates the need for surgical instrumentation and fusion in scoliosis?
back: A Cobb angle exceeding 40°. This angle is the primary radiological guide for deciding when to transition from bracing to surgery.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [those >40° are considered for surgery, which involves instrumenting and fushing the spine. The Cobb angle is a radiological measurement that defnes severity and guides treatment]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: What is the primary functional objective of using "growing rods" in pediatric scoliosis management?
back: To control the lateral curvature while allowing for continued vertical spinal growth and thoracic expansion for pulmonary health.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [In general, the earlier the onset, the more likely the deformity is to be progressive. As most lung development occurs in early childhood, the management of early-onset scoliosis must preserve growth: casting techniques or the use of ‘growing rods’ may be appropriate.]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
coreConcept: Red Flags in Paediatric Back Pain
front: Q: Why is persistent spinal pain considered a "red flag" in a child presenting with scoliosis?
back: Idiopathic scoliosis is generally painless. Significant pain associated with a curve necessitates investigation for underlying tumor or infection.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Idiopathic scoliosis is generally not painful and, therefore, in the presence of signifcant pain tumour and infection must be excluded.]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: According to the Hueter–Volkmann principle, how do mechanical forces contribute to vertebral wedge formation in scoliosis?
back: Compressive forces (on the curve concavity) inhibit growth, while tensile forces (on the convexity) stimulate it, resulting in progressive asymmetrical vertebral development.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 609 (Book Page): [Hueter–Volkmann principle: Compressive forces inhibit growth; Tensile forces stimulate growth. Bone deposition and resorption depend on the stresses applied (Wolff’s law).]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: What are the three age-related classifications of idiopathic scoliosis used by orthopaedic teams?
back:
1. Early onset: <10 years.
2. Adolescent: 11–18 years.
3. Adult: Onset at maturity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [TABLE 44.12 Classifcation of idiopathic scoliosis. Early onset <10 years, Adolescent 11–18 years, Adult Onset at maturity.]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: At what Cobb angle threshold is surgery typically considered for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis?
back: Surgery is considered for curves greater than 40 degrees to address multiplanar deformity and potential progression.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): 'Curves <20 degrees do not need treatment, progressive curves of 25–40 degrees may be braced and those >40 degrees are considered for surgery, which involves instrumenting and fusing the spine.'

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: In the multidisciplinary management of scoliosis, how does muscle imbalance impact bone growth?
back: Abnormal muscle pull, combined with gravity, alters bone growth through asymmetrical forces, leading to progressive deformity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 631 (Book Page): 'Abnormal muscle pull, particularly in combination with the effects of gravity, alters bone growth, leading to deformity and joint contracture.'

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: How is structural scoliosis distinguished from functional scoliosis using the forward bending test?
back: Structural scoliosis: A rib hump increases or bulges posteriorly due to rotation. Functional scoliosis: The spine straightens without a visible hump.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 627 (Book Page): 'structural scoliosis: a rib hump will increase in size (bulge posteriorly on the thoracic convex side) as the patient bends forwards... functional scoliosis: the spine straightens as the patient bends forwards and no rib hump is visible.'

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: A 9-year-old presents with early-onset scoliosis. What multidisciplinary goal is unique to this age group?
back: Preservation of spinal growth is critical to allow for lung development, which occurs primarily in early childhood.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): 'As most lung development occurs in early childhood, the management of early-onset scoliosis must preserve growth: casting techniques or the use of growing rods may be appropriate.'

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: Which pharmacological agents are utilized in multidisciplinary management to reduce tone in neuromuscular scoliosis?
back: * Diazepam and baclofen (systemic reduction). * Botulinum toxin (focal reduction).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 632 (Book Page): 'Tone can be reduced with drugs (e.g. diazepam and baclofen). Alternatively, neuromuscular blockers such as botulinum toxin allow a focal reduction in tone.'

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: What defines the radiological Cobb angle in scoliosis assessment?
back: It is a radiological measurement used to define the severity of the lateral spinal curvature and guide treatment decisions.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): 'The Cobb angle is a radiological measurement that defines severity and guides treatment.'

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: How do multidisciplinary team members coordinate non-surgical scoliosis management?
back: * Physiotherapy: Focuses on core strength and stability. * Orthotics: Utilizes bracing for progressive curves (25-40 degrees).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 631 (Book Page): 'A multidisciplinary approach to management is essential. Physiotherapy and orthotic management may reduce the need for surgical intervention.'

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: In a child presenting with scoliosis and significant back pain, what must be excluded?
back: Tumors and infection must be excluded, as idiopathic scoliosis is typically painless.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): 'Idiopathic scoliosis is generally not painful and, therefore, in the presence of significant pain tumour and infection must be excluded.'

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: Describe the physiological feedback loop that exacerbates neuromuscular spinal deformity.
back: High tone/imbalance leads to deformity; this places muscles at a mechanical disadvantage, causing further loss of control and worsening deformity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 631 (Book Page): 'Muscles are relatively weak and... they are no longer strong enough to control a heavier limb, particularly when deformity means they are working at a mechanical disadvantage.'

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: Which specific idiopathic scoliosis type is most prevalent and which gender is primarily affected?
back: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis; it affects girls more frequently than boys.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): 'The adolescent idiopathic curve is the most common, affecting girls more than boys.'

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: What radiological measurement defines scoliosis severity and guides treatment decisions?
back:
The Cobb angle.

* <20°: Observation
* 25°–40°: Bracing (if progressive)
* >40°: Surgery (instrumentation/fusion)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The Cobb angle is a radiological measurement that defines severity and guides treatment... Curves <20° do not need treatment, progressive curves of 25–40° may be braced and those >40° are considered for surgery.]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: How is the rotational component of scoliosis clinically assessed during physical examination?
back: Via the Adams forward bend test. The examiner looks for rib asymmetry or a "rib hump" caused by vertebral rotation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The rotational component is most apparent in forward flexion when the rib asymmetry creates a ‘rib hump’.]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: Contrast structural idiopathic scoliosis with functional scoliosis during the forward bend test.
back:
Structural: Rib hump increases/persists during forward flexion.
Functional: The spine straightens and no rib hump is visible (often secondary to leg length discrepancy).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [structural scoliosis: a rib hump will increase in size (bulge posteriorly on the thoracic convex side) as the patient bends forwards... functional scoliosis: the spine straightens as the patient bends forwards and no rib hump is visible.]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: What is the primary management goal for early-onset scoliosis (onset <10 years)?
back: Preservation of spinal and lung growth. Management techniques include serial casting or the use of "growing rods."
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [As most lung development occurs in early childhood, the management of early-onset scoliosis must preserve growth: casting techniques or the use of ‘growing rods’ may be appropriate.]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: Which intervention is indicated for progressive adolescent idiopathic curves between 25° and 40°?
back: Spinal bracing (Orthotic management).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [progressive curves of 25–40° may be braced.]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: What clinical symptom is a "red flag" for infection or tumor rather than idiopathic scoliosis?
back: Significant back pain. Idiopathic scoliosis is generally painless.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Idiopathic scoliosis is generally not painful and, therefore, in the presence of significant pain tumor and infection must be excluded.]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: In a multidisciplinary approach, what are the three tiers of idiopathic scoliosis management?
back:
1. Observation (for mild curves <20°)
2. Bracing/Orthotics (for moderate/progressive curves 25–40°)
3. Surgery/Fusion (for severe curves >40°)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Treatment depends on the severity and likelihood of curve progression – it varies from observation, through bracing to surgery.]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: What is the significance of the age of onset in the natural history of scoliosis?
back: The earlier the onset of scoliosis, the higher the likelihood that the deformity will be progressive.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [In general, the earlier the onset, the more likely the deformity is to be progressive.]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: What is the most common cause of non-structural postural scoliosis?
back: Leg length discrepancy (LLD).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [A leg length discrepancy causes a postural scoliosis.]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: Which anatomical plane deformities are included in the definition of scoliosis?
back: Deformity in all three planes: coronal (lateral curvature), sagittal, and axial (rotational).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The term ‘scoliosis’ describes spinal deformity in three planes: lateral curvature is the most obvious deformity while the rotational component is most apparent in forward flexion.]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: What is the primary radiological measurement used to define scoliosis severity and guide treatment decisions?
back: The Cobb angle. Curves <20° generally require no treatment; progressive curves of 25–40° may require bracing; curves >40° are considered for surgical intervention.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The Cobb angle is a radiological measurement that defnes severity and guides treatment (Figure 44.36). Curves <20° do not need treatment, progressive curves of 25–40° may be braced and those >40° are considered for surgery.]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: Beyond lateral curvature, which physiological component defines the three-dimensional deformity in structural scoliosis?
back: Spinal rotation. This rotational component is clinically most apparent in forward flexion, where it creates a visible "rib hump" or posterior bulge.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The term ‘scoliosis’ describes spinal deformity in three planes: lateral curvature is the most obvious deformity while the rotational component is most apparent in forward fexion when the rib asymmetry creates a ‘rib hump’.]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: How is structural scoliosis differentiated from functional scoliosis during clinical examination?
back: Using the Adams forward bend test. Functional curves straighten during forward flexion without a rib hump; structural curves maintain deformity and present a visible rib hump.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [In structural scoliosis: a rib hump will increase in size... as the patient bends forwards; this is diagnostic of idiopathic thoracic scoliosis... functional scoliosis: the spine straightens as the patient bends forwards and no rib hump is visible.]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
coreConcept: Surgical Indications for Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis
front: Q: A 14-year-old female presents with an idiopathic thoracic curve measuring 45 degrees. What is the standard management?
back: Surgical instrumentation and fusion. Curves exceeding 40° are generally treated operatively to correct the multiplanar deformity and prevent long-term progression.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [those >40° are considered for surgery, which involves instrumenting and fusing the spine.]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: What non-operative management is indicated for progressive idiopathic scoliosis curves measuring between 25 and 40 degrees?
back: Spinal bracing. This is utilized in adolescents with remaining growth potential to arrest curve progression before skeletal maturity is reached.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [progressive curves of 25–40° may be braced]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: What clinical hallmark indicates the rotational deformity of scoliosis during the Adams forward bend test?
back: The rib hump. It is characterized by rib asymmetry where ribs bulge posteriorly on the convex side of the spinal curve.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [the rotational component is most apparent in forward fexion when the rib asymmetry creates a ‘rib hump’... a rib hump will increase in size (bulge posteriorly on the thoracic convex side).]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: Why must management of early-onset scoliosis prioritize growth preservation over immediate spinal fusion?
back: To allow for pulmonary development. Most lung development occurs in early childhood; procedures like casting or "growing rods" are used to preserve growth.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [As most lung development occurs in early childhood, the management of early-onset scoliosis must preserve growth: casting techniques or the use of ‘growing rods’ may be appropriate.]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: In a pediatric patient with scoliosis, which clinical symptom should prompt urgent investigation for infection or tumor?
back: Significant back pain. Idiopathic scoliosis is generally painless; unrelenting or night pain is a "red flag" necessitating MRI to exclude serious underlying pathology.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Idiopathic scoliosis is generally not painful and, therefore, in the presence of signifcant pain tumour and infection must be excluded.]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: How does the age of onset impact the natural history and management of idiopathic scoliosis?
back: Earlier onset increases the likelihood of progression. Curves appearing in younger children carry a higher risk of becoming severe before skeletal maturity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [In general, the earlier the onset, the more likely the deformity is to be progressive.]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: Contrast the efficacy of bracing in idiopathic scoliosis versus congenital vertebral deformities.
back: Bracing is effective for progressive idiopathic curves but ineffective for congenital deformities. Congenital cases result from structural malformations (e.g., hemivertebrae) requiring different management.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Bracing is inefective for congenital vertebral deformities.]

category: Define osteogenesis imperfecta and describe its genetic basis and abnormal collagen formation
front: Q: What is the clinical definition of Osteogenesis Imperfecta (OI)?
back: A spectrum of conditions characterized by a qualitative and/or quantitative abnormality in collagen production, leading to increased bone fragility.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) represents a spectrum of conditions linked by a qualitative and/or quantitative abnormality of collagen production.]

category: Define osteogenesis imperfecta and describe its genetic basis and abnormal collagen formation
front: Q: Describe the pathophysiological basis of abnormal collagen formation in OI.
back: Mutations in collagen genes result in either a reduced volume (quantitative) or structurally defective (qualitative) Type I collagen matrix.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) represents a spectrum of conditions linked by a qualitative and/or quantitative abnormality of collagen production.]

category: Define osteogenesis imperfecta and describe its genetic basis and abnormal collagen formation
front: Q: Contrast qualitative versus quantitative collagen defects in OI phenotypes.
back: Qualitative defects involve structurally abnormal collagen, whereas quantitative defects involve a reduction in the total amount of normal collagen produced.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) represents a spectrum of conditions linked by a qualitative and/or quantitative abnormality of collagen production.]

category: Define osteogenesis imperfecta and describe its genetic basis and abnormal collagen formation
front: Q: A child presents with multiple fractures, blue sclerae, and ligamentous laxity. Explain the underlying systemic defect.
back: Defective Type I collagen production affects all collagen-containing structures, including the bone matrix, ocular sclerae, and connective ligaments.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [All structures containing collagen may be affected, accounting for the ligamentous laxity, blue sclerae and poor teeth in some phenotypes.]

category: Define osteogenesis imperfecta and describe its genetic basis and abnormal collagen formation
front: Q: What is the specific genetic basis for the majority of Osteogenesis Imperfecta cases?
back: Most identified genetic mutations occur within the genes responsible for the coding and synthesis of collagen proteins.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Most identified mutations affect the collagen genes.]

category: Define osteogenesis imperfecta and describe its genetic basis and abnormal collagen formation
front: Q: Which specific type of collagen is primarily defective in Osteogenesis Imperfecta?
back: Type I collagen.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 636 (Book Page): [In OI: There is defective type I collagen production.]

category: Define osteogenesis imperfecta and describe its genetic basis and abnormal collagen formation
front: Q: Explain the clinical significance of the bone healing process in patients with OI.
back: Despite extreme fragility and frequent breakage, bone tissue in OI characteristically heals promptly and effectively following a fracture.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [The bone may break easily but it heals promptly and well.]

category: Define osteogenesis imperfecta and describe its genetic basis and abnormal collagen formation
front: Q: Why does OI present with dental abnormalities (dentinogenesis imperfecta)?
back: Dental structures utilize Type I collagen; genetic mutations leading to defective collagen production result in weak, poorly formed teeth.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [All structures containing collagen may be affected, accounting for the... poor teeth in some phenotypes.]

category: Define osteogenesis imperfecta and describe its genetic basis and abnormal collagen formation
front: Q: Describe the physiological effect of cyclical bisphosphonates on OI bone tissue.
back: Bisphosphonates decrease bone resorption and turnover, which reduces bone pain and fracture rates while increasing weight-bearing stability.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Cyclical bisphosphonate treatment decreases bone resorption and turnover. This reduces bone pain and the fracture rate, promoting weight-bearing mobility.]

category: Define osteogenesis imperfecta and describe its genetic basis and abnormal collagen formation
front: Q: What is the primary clinical hallmark of the bone matrix in Osteogenesis Imperfecta?
back: Pathological fragility (brittleness) resulting in frequent fractures and progressive skeletal deformity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 636 (Book Page): [In severe forms frequent fractures lead to progressive deformity, which in turn increases fracture risk.]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: Define the three-dimensional deformity known as scoliosis.
back: Scoliosis consists of lateral spinal curvature and a rotational component, most apparent as a 'rib hump' during forward flexion.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The term ‘scoliosis’ describes spinal deformity in three planes: lateral curvature is the most obvious deformity while the rotational component is most apparent in forward fexion when the rib asymmetry creates a ‘rib hump’.]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: Explain the physiological rationale for preserving growth in early-onset scoliosis management.
back: Most lung development occurs in early childhood; management must preserve spinal growth via casting or 'growing rods' to avoid compromising respiratory function.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [As most lung development occurs in early childhood, the management of early-onset scoliosis must preserve growth: casting techniques or the use of ‘growing rods’ may be appropriate.]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: Contrast the forward bend test findings in structural versus functional scoliosis.
back: Structural: The rib hump increases/bulges on the convex side. Functional: The spine straightens and no rib hump is visible (e.g., due to leg length discrepancy).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 477 (Book Page): [structural scoliosis: a rib hump will increase in size... functional scoliosis: the spine straightens as the patient bends forwards and no rib hump is visible.]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: A child with GMFCS V Cerebral Palsy presents with scoliosis; outline the multidisciplinary management steps.
back: 1. Optimize seating position and posture symmetry. 2. Utilize spinal bracing. 3. Consider surgery if the hip is at risk or the curve compromises sitting function.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 632 (Book Page): [In the child with total body involvement (TBI) and high muscle tone, hip subluxation leading to dislocation is common... Aggressive management of a spinal deformity initially concentrates on seating position and subsequently emphasises spinal bracing or surgery.]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: Outline the surgical management thresholds based on the Cobb angle in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis.
back: * <20°: Observation. * 25–40° (if progressive): Bracing. * >40°: Surgical instrumentation and spinal fusion.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Curves <20° do not need treatment, progressive curves of 25–40° may be braced and those >40° are considered for surgery, which involves instrumenting and fusing the spine.]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: List the 'red flag' findings in a pediatric patient presenting with scoliosis and back pain.
back: 1. Systemic illness/fever. 2. Night pain. 3. Progressive neurological deficit. 4. Presence of an unrelenting pain (suggests infection or tumor).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 630 (Book Page): [Back pain in a child is a ‘red fag’ for serious spinal pathology... Systemic illness, fever or weight loss; Progressive neurological defcit; Unrelenting or night pain; Spinal deformity.]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: How is the Cobb angle measured in the multidisciplinary assessment of spinal deformity?
back: It is a radiological measurement used to define severity, guide treatment decisions, and monitor for curve progression.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The Cobb angle is a radiological measurement that defnes severity and guides treatment.]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: Contrast the management of a postural scoliosis due to LLD versus an adolescent idiopathic scoliosis.
back: Postural: Resolves by correcting the leg length discrepancy (LLD). Idiopathic: Requires monitoring, bracing, or surgery based on Cobb angle and progression.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The cause may be idiopathic, neuromuscular, related to a syndrome or congenital... A leg length discrepancy causes a postural scoliosis.]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: Explain the application of Wolf’s Law and the Hueter-Volkmann principle in conservative scoliosis treatment.
back: Bracing alters compressive/tensile forces on the vertebrae to improve the biomechanical environment, theoretically reversing abnormal growth patterns via remodeling.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 609 (Book Page): [The conservative treatment of common conditions... considers remodelling ability with an understanding of the Hueter–Volkmann principle and Wolf’s law: improving the biomechanical environment may reverse abnormal growth.]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: Identify the most common age of onset and gender for idiopathic scoliosis requiring intervention.
back: Adolescent onset (11–18 years), affecting girls significantly more often than boys.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The adolescent idiopathic curve is the most common, afecting girls more than boys. Adolescent (11–18 years).]

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: How is the spinal deformity of scoliosis categorized in terms of anatomical planes?
back:
* Lateral curvature in the coronal plane.
* Rotational component in the axial plane (rib hump).
* Associated sagittal plane changes.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): The term ‘scoliosis’ describes spinal deformity in three planes: lateral curvature is the most obvious deformity while the rotational component is most apparent in forward fexion when the rib asymmetry creates a ‘rib hump’.

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: What are the primary objectives of the multidisciplinary team in neuromuscular scoliosis?
back:
* Maintenance of joint range of movement.
* Prevention of fixed contractures.
* Management of muscle tone and spinal positioning (seating systems).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 631 (Book Page): A multidisciplinary approach to management is essential. Primary therapy aims to maintain range of movement and prevent fxed contractures with an emphasis on managing tone and position. The use of splints, positioning techniques and seating and sleeping systems is common.

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: How does the Adams forward bend test assist the multidisciplinary team in scoliosis classification?
back:
* Structural: Rib hump persists or increases due to rotation.
* Functional: Spine straightens and rib hump disappears (e.g., postural/leg length discrepancy).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 477 (Book Page): Forward bending test... structural scoliosis: a rib hump will increase in size... diagnostic of idiopathic thoracic scoliosis (rotatory deformity); functional scoliosis: the spine straightens as the patient bends forwards and no rib hump is visible.

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: List the multidisciplinary management thresholds based on the Cobb angle.
back:
* <20°: Observation.
* 25°–40°: Bracing (Orthotics).
* >40°: Surgical consideration (Instrumentation and fusion).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): The Cobb angle is a radiological measurement that defnes severity and guides treatment... Curves <20° do not need treatment, progressive curves of 25–40° may be braced and those >40° are considered for surgery, which involves instrumenting and fusing the spine.

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: What is the multidisciplinary rationale for avoiding early spinal fusion in early-onset scoliosis?
back:
* Most lung development occurs in early childhood.
* Strategy: Utilize serial casting or "growing rods" to preserve spinal growth and lung volume.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): As most lung development occurs in early childhood, the management of early-onset scoliosis must preserve growth: casting techniques or the use of ‘growing rods’ may be appropriate.

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: List the age-based classification of idiopathic scoliosis used to guide management.
back:
* Early onset: <10 years.
* Adolescent: 11–18 years.
* Adult: Onset at maturity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): Table 44.12 Classifcation of idiopathic scoliosis. Early onset <10 years; Adolescent 11–18 years; Adult Onset at maturity.

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: What are the non-surgical multidisciplinary interventions used for scoliosis?
back:
* Orthotics (spinal bracing).
* Physiotherapy (core stabilization and muscle balancing).
* Specialized seating and sleeping systems.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 631 (Book Page): Physiotherapy and orthotic management may reduce the need for surgical intervention... the use of splints, positioning techniques and seating and sleeping systems is common.

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
coreConcept: Red Flags in Paediatric Spinal Pain
front: Q: Which 'red flag' clinical findings in scoliosis necessitate urgent investigation for tumor or infection?
back:
* Systemic illness, fever, or weight loss.
* Unrelenting or night pain.
* Progressive neurological deficit.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 630 (Book Page): Red fag symptoms and signs for spinal pathology: Systemic illness, fever or weight loss; Progressive neurological defcit; Unrelenting or night pain; Spinal deformity.

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
coreConcept: Spinal Management in TBI Cerebral Palsy
front: Q: How is spinal deformity managed in children with total body involvement (TBI) Cerebral Palsy?
back:
* Focus initially on seating position optimization.
* Subsequent intervention includes spinal bracing or surgery to maintain symmetry and pelvic position.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 632 (Book Page): In the child with total body involvement (TBI)... Aggressive management of a spinal deformity initially concentrates on seating position and subsequently emphasises spinal bracing or surgery.

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
front: Q: What is the postoperative role of physiotherapy in the multidisciplinary management of scoliosis?
back:
* Ensuring surgical benefits are maximized.
* Facilitating functional rehabilitation and mobility post-fusion.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 631 (Book Page): Physiotherapy and orthotic management may reduce the need for surgical intervention and postoperatively they ensure that the surgical benefts are maximised.

category: Define osteogenesis imperfecta and describe its genetic basis and abnormal collagen formation
front: Q: Define Osteogenesis Imperfecta (OI) and its primary clinical characteristic.
back: OI is a spectrum of disorders caused by qualitative or quantitative abnormalities in collagen production, leading to 'brittle bones' that fracture easily.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) represents a spectrum of conditions linked by a qualitative and/or quantitative abnormality of collagen production. The bone may break easily but it heals promptly and well.]

category: Define osteogenesis imperfecta and describe its genetic basis and abnormal collagen formation
front: Q: Describe the underlying pathophysiological mechanism of bone fragility in Osteogenesis Imperfecta.
back: Genetic mutations result in defective Type I collagen synthesis, which impairs the structural integrity of the bone matrix and other connective tissues.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) represents a spectrum of conditions linked by a qualitative and/or quantitative abnormality of collagen production. Most identifed mutations afect the collagen genes.]

category: Define osteogenesis imperfecta and describe its genetic basis and abnormal collagen formation
front: Q: Distinguish between qualitative and quantitative collagen defects in Osteogenesis Imperfecta.
back: Qualitative defects involve structural abnormalities in the collagen produced, while quantitative defects involve a reduced volume of normally structured collagen.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) represents a spectrum of conditions linked by a qualitative and/or quantitative abnormality of collagen production.]

category: Define osteogenesis imperfecta and describe its genetic basis and abnormal collagen formation
front: Q: A child presents with frequent fractures from low-energy trauma, blue sclerae, and joint hyperlaxity. What is the diagnosis?
back: Osteogenesis Imperfecta (Brittle Bone Disease), likely caused by a mutation in Type I collagen genes.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [The bone may break easily but it heals promptly and well. All structures containing collagen may be afected, accounting for the ligamentous laxity, blue sclerae and poor teeth in some phenotypes.]

category: Define osteogenesis imperfecta and describe its genetic basis and abnormal collagen formation
front: Q: What is the primary pharmacological management goal when using cyclical bisphosphonates in OI?
back: To decrease bone resorption and turnover, thereby reducing bone pain, decreasing fracture rates, and promoting bone strength.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Cyclical bisphosphonate treatment decreases bone resorption and turnover. This reduces bone pain and the fracture rate, promoting weight-bearing mobility and bone strength]

category: Define osteogenesis imperfecta and describe its genetic basis and abnormal collagen formation
front: Q: List the common non-skeletal clinical features seen in patients with Osteogenesis Imperfecta.
back:
● Translucent blue sclerae
● Dentinogenesis imperfecta (poor teeth)
● Ligamentous hyperlaxity
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [All structures containing collagen may be afected, accounting for the ligamentous laxity, blue sclerae and poor teeth in some phenotypes.]

category: Define osteogenesis imperfecta and describe its genetic basis and abnormal collagen formation
coreConcept: Surgical Stabilization in Brittle Bone Disease
front: Q: Why are intramedullary techniques preferred over plate fixation for surgical stabilization in OI?
back: They provide better axial support for brittle bones and allow for skeletal growth while maintaining alignment more effectively than plates.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Intramedullary techniques for stabilisation of fractures or osteotomies are preferred to plate fxation.]

category: Define osteogenesis imperfecta and describe its genetic basis and abnormal collagen formation
front: Q: A toddler with multiple fractures is evaluated for NAI. Which finding specifically suggests OI over abuse?
back: Presence of blue sclerae, ligamentous laxity, dentinogenesis imperfecta, and radiographic evidence of generalized osteopenia.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [All structures containing collagen may be afected, accounting for the ligamentous laxity, blue sclerae and poor teeth in some phenotypes.]

category: Define osteogenesis imperfecta and describe its genetic basis and abnormal collagen formation
front: Q: Explain the paradoxical relationship between bone breakage and healing in Osteogenesis Imperfecta.
back: While the bone is highly susceptible to fracture due to abnormal collagen, the biological healing process remains intact, allowing fractures to heal promptly.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [The bone may break easily but it heals promptly and well.]

category: Define osteogenesis imperfecta and describe its genetic basis and abnormal collagen formation
front: Q: Mutations in which specific protein family are responsible for Osteogenesis Imperfecta?
back: Collagen genes (specifically those encoding for Type I Collagen).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Most identifed mutations afect the collagen genes.]

category: Define osteogenesis imperfecta and describe its genetic basis and abnormal collagen formation
front: Q: Define Osteogenesis Imperfecta (OI) according to its underlying pathology.
back: A: A spectrum of conditions linked by a qualitative or quantitative abnormality of collagen production, leading to fragile bones.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) represents a spectrum of conditions linked by a qualitative and/or quantitative abnormality of collagen production.]

category: Define osteogenesis imperfecta and describe its genetic basis and abnormal collagen formation
front: Q: What is the primary genetic basis for most identified cases of Osteogenesis Imperfecta?
back: A: Most cases result from identified genetic mutations that specifically affect the collagen genes.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Most identified mutations affect the collagen genes.]

category: Define osteogenesis imperfecta and describe its genetic basis and abnormal collagen formation
front: Q: Which specific protein type is defective in Brittle Bone Disease?
back: A: Type I Collagen.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) represents a spectrum of conditions linked by a qualitative and/or quantitative abnormality of collagen production. . . All structures containing collagen may be affected... account for ligamentous laxity... the defect lies in the organic matrix (collagen)]

category: Define osteogenesis imperfecta and describe its genetic basis and abnormal collagen formation
front: Q: A child with blue sclerae presents with a femur fracture from minor trauma. Describe the collagen defect.
back: A: The mutation causes a qualitative or quantitative abnormality in Type I collagen synthesis, affecting bones, teeth, and ligaments.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [All structures containing collagen may be affected, accounting for the ligamentous laxity, blue sclerae and poor teeth in some phenotypes.]

category: Define osteogenesis imperfecta and describe its genetic basis and abnormal collagen formation
front: Q: Contrast the bone breaking and bone healing characteristics in Osteogenesis Imperfecta.
back: A: Bone breaks easily due to the matrix defect but typically heals promptly and well.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [The bone may break easily but it heals promptly and well.]

category: Define osteogenesis imperfecta and describe its genetic basis and abnormal collagen formation
front: Q: How does the collagen defect in OI result in progressive skeletal deformity?
back: A: Frequent fractures occurring in a weakened matrix lead to cumulative malalignment, which further increases the risk of future fractures.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [In severe forms frequent fractures lead to progressive deformity, which in turn increases fracture risk.]

category: Define osteogenesis imperfecta and describe its genetic basis and abnormal collagen formation
front: Q: Differentiate the primary defect of OI from that of Rickets.
back: A: OI is a defect of the organic matrix (collagen structure), whereas Rickets is a failure of mineralisation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 614 (Book Page)-615: [In rickets, the primary problem is inadequate mineralisation... In OI the defect lies in the organic matrix (collagen)]

category: Define osteogenesis imperfecta and describe its genetic basis and abnormal collagen formation
front: Q: Why is internal fixation with plates often avoided in Osteogenesis Imperfecta surgery?
back: A: The bone is too brittle for local screw fixation; intramedullary techniques are preferred to stabilize the entire length of the bone.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Intramedullary techniques for stabilisation of fractures or osteotomies are preferred to plate fixation.]

category: Define osteogenesis imperfecta and describe its genetic basis and abnormal collagen formation
front: Q: List two dental and ocular signs resulting from the collagen mutation in OI.
back:
A: 1. Poor teeth (dentinogenesis imperfecta)
2. Blue sclerae.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [All structures containing collagen may be affected, accounting for the ligamentous laxity, blue sclerae and poor teeth in some phenotypes.]

category: Define osteogenesis imperfecta and describe its genetic basis and abnormal collagen formation
front: Q: What determines the severity of the Osteogenesis Imperfecta phenotype?
back: A: Whether the genetic mutation results in a reduced amount (quantitative) or structural abnormality (qualitative) of collagen produced.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) represents a spectrum of conditions linked by a qualitative and/or quantitative abnormality of collagen production.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: What is the classic appearance of an acute extradural haematoma on CT scan?
back:
A: 
* Lentiform (lens-shaped or biconvex) hyperdense lesion
* Located between the skull and the brain
* Constrained by dural adherence to skull sutures
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page): [On CT, extradural haematomas appear as a lentiform (lens-shaped or biconvex) hyperdense lesion between the skull and the brain, constrained by the adherence of the dura to the skull.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: Why does a chronic subdural haematoma appear diffuse and hypodense on CT scan?
back:
A: 
* Density decreases as the blood clot degrades and liquefies over days/weeks
* The lesion appears concave and follows the brain surface because the dura is not adherent to the brain.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 388 (Book Page): [Imaging reveals difuse hypodensity overlying the brain surface. Recent bleeding may be isodense or hyperdense, and mixed density can indicate an acute-on -chronic subdural haematoma. ... subdural blood is free to expand across the brain surface, giving a difuse concave appearance.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: Contrast the CT shapes of extradural versus acute subdural haematomas.
back:
A: 
* Extradural: Biconvex (lentiform), limited by skull sutures.
* Subdural: Concave (crescentic), diffuse along the brain surface.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page), 388: [On CT, extradural haematomas appear as a lentiform (lens-shaped or biconvex) hyperdense lesion... since the dura is not as adherent to the brain as it is to the skull, subdural blood is free to expand across the brain surface, giving a difuse concave appearance.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: How is transverse ligament rupture identified in a C1 Jefferson fracture on radiographs?
back:
A: 
* Use the open mouth (odontoid) view
* Combined lateral mass deviation of C1 relative to C2 must exceed 6.9 mm.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 418 (Book Page): [Open mouth view of C1/2 demonstrating C1 lateral mass deviation (arrows). Rupture of the transverse ligament is present when the combined lateral mass deviation exceeds 6.9 mm.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: What are the radiographic hallmarks of rickets in the metaphysis?
back:
A: 
* Widened physes (growth plates)
* Cupped and flared appearances of the adjacent metaphyses.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 636 (Book Page): [radiographs in cases of rickets demonstrate widened physes with cupped, fared metaphyses.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: What is the primary radiographic sign of Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis (SCFE)?
back:
A: 
* A line drawn along the upper margin of the femoral neck (Klein's line) fails to transect the femoral head.
* Displacement is most obvious on frog-leg lateral views.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 622 (Book Page): [A line drawn along the upper margin of the femoral neck should transect the femoral head (right side); if it does not do so (left side) a slip is present. There are many other radiographic features that help to confrm the diagnosis but the changes are often subtle and may be seen frst on the frog lateral view.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: What radiographic findings define instability in a lateral cervical spine injury?
back:
A: 
* Sagittal translation >3.5 mm
* Sagittal angulation >11° compared to the adjacent level.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 414 (Book Page): [Assess for instability: a 3.5 mm of sagittal translation; b sagittal angulation of >11° (compared with the adjacent level).]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: How is a Type C pelvic fracture radiographically distinguished from Type B?
back:
A: 
* Type B: "Open book" widening of pubic symphysis; vertically stable.
* Type C: Disruption of both anterior and entire posterior complexes; vertically and horizontally unstable (vertical shear).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 404 (Book Page), 405: [Type B... pelvis can open and close ‘like a book’... no vertical displacement. Type C... both the anterior pelvis and the entire posterior pelvic complexes are disrupted... free to displace horizontally and vertically.]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: What chest radiographic findings are characteristic of a tension pneumothorax?
back:
A: 
* Mediastinal displacement to the opposite side
* Tracheal deviation away from the affected side
* Complete lung collapse with hyper-lucency.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [The mediastinum is displaced to the opposite side... deviation of the trachea occurs away from the afected side in tension pneumothorax]

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
front: Q: Define 'sequestrum' and 'involucrum' in chronic osteomyelitis radiographic follow-up.
back:
A: 
* Sequestrum: Detached fragment of dead, infected bone.
* Involucrum: New sheath of bone formed around the sequestrum by the periosteum.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 618 (Book Page): [The infected bone reacts to the infection by separating dead fragments of bone (sequestration) and forming sinuses... New bone is laid down around the infection from the periosteum (involucrum)]

category: Define osteogenesis imperfecta and describe its genetic basis and abnormal collagen formation
front: Q: What is the clinical definition of Osteogenesis Imperfecta (OI)?
back: A spectrum of skeletal conditions characterized by qualitative or quantitative abnormalities in collagen production, resulting in extreme bone fragility.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) represents a spectrum of conditions linked by a qualitative and/or quantitative abnormality of collagen production.]

category: Define osteogenesis imperfecta and describe its genetic basis and abnormal collagen formation
front: Q: What is the primary genetic basis of Osteogenesis Imperfecta?
back: Most identified cases involve mutations in the genes responsible for encoding and producing collagen proteins.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Most identified mutations affect the collagen genes.]

category: Define osteogenesis imperfecta and describe its genetic basis and abnormal collagen formation
front: Q: Distinguish between the two types of collagen defects found in OI.
back:
1. Quantitative: A reduced amount of collagen produced.
2. Qualitative: Structural abnormalities in the collagen produced.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [...linked by a qualitative and/or quantitative abnormality of collagen production.]

category: Define osteogenesis imperfecta and describe its genetic basis and abnormal collagen formation
front: Q: Why does OI manifest with non-skeletal features like blue sclerae and poor teeth?
back: The genetic defect affects Type I collagen, which is a key structural component in bone, the sclerae, dentine, and ligaments.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [All structures containing collagen may be affected, accounting for the ligamentous laxity, blue sclerae and poor teeth in some phenotypes.]

category: Define osteogenesis imperfecta and describe its genetic basis and abnormal collagen formation
front: Q: How does cyclical bisphosphonate therapy alter the clinical course of OI?
back: It decreases bone resorption and turnover, which reduces fracture rates and bone pain while strengthening the bone matrix.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Cyclical bisphosphonate treatment decreases bone resorption and turnover. This reduces bone pain and the fracture rate...]

category: Define osteogenesis imperfecta and describe its genetic basis and abnormal collagen formation
front: Q: What are the classic triad of non-skeletal diagnostic features in OI?
back:
1. Blue sclerae
2. Ligamentous laxity
3. Poor dentition (Dentinogenesis imperfecta)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [...accounting for the ligamentous laxity, blue sclerae and poor teeth in some phenotypes.]

category: Define osteogenesis imperfecta and describe its genetic basis and abnormal collagen formation
front: Q: Compare bone fracture healing versus bone strength in OI patients.
back: Bone in OI break easily due to inherent collagen weakness but typically heal promptly and well following the injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [The bone may break easily but it heals promptly and well.]

category: Define osteogenesis imperfecta and describe its genetic basis and abnormal collagen formation
front: Q: How does the pathophysiology of severe OI lead to progressive skeletal deformity?
back: Defective Type I collagen causes frequent fractures; the cumulative effect of recurrent breaks in growing bone results in progressive deformity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [In severe forms frequent fractures lead to progressive deformity, which in turn increases fracture risk.]

category: Define osteogenesis imperfecta and describe its genetic basis and abnormal collagen formation
front: Q: What specific protein abnormality causes generalized ligamentous laxity in OI?
back: The production of defective Type I collagen reduces the structural integrity of ligaments and other connective tissues.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Summary box 44.4: ... There is defective type I collagen production... All structures containing collagen may be affected, accounting for the ligamentous laxity...]

category: Define osteogenesis imperfecta and describe its genetic basis and abnormal collagen formation
front: Q: Which specific collagen type is defective in Osteogenesis Imperfecta?
back: Type I collagen.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Summary box 44.4: In OI: There is defective type I collagen production.]

category: Define osteogenesis imperfecta and describe its genetic basis and abnormal collagen formation
front: Q: Define Osteogenesis Imperfecta (OI) based on its primary skeletal pathology.
back: A spectrum of conditions characterized by brittle bones that break easily but heal promptly and well.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) represents a spectrum of conditions linked by a qualitative and/or quantitative abnormality of collagen production. The bone may break easily but it heals promptly and well.]

category: Define osteogenesis imperfecta and describe its genetic basis and abnormal collagen formation
front: Q: Describe the biochemical abnormality involving collagen in Osteogenesis Imperfecta.
back: It is a qualitative and/or quantitative abnormality of collagen production, specifically affecting the collagen genes.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) represents a spectrum of conditions linked by a qualitative and/or quantitative abnormality of collagen production. Most identifed mutations afect the collagen genes.]

category: Define osteogenesis imperfecta and describe its genetic basis and abnormal collagen formation
front: Q: Distinguish between the two types of collagen defects seen in OI patients.
back:
• Qualitative: Defective structure of collagen.
• Quantitative: Inadequate amount of collagen produced.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) represents a spectrum of conditions linked by a qualitative and/or quantitative abnormality of collagen production.]

category: Define osteogenesis imperfecta and describe its genetic basis and abnormal collagen formation
front: Q: Why does OI present with blue sclerae and dental abnormalities beyond bone fragility?
back: The genetic defect affects all collagen-containing structures, including ligaments, sclerae, and teeth (dentinogenesis imperfecta).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [All structures containing collagen may be afected, accounting for the ligamentous laxity, blue sclerae and poor teeth in some phenotypes.]

category: Define osteogenesis imperfecta and describe its genetic basis and abnormal collagen formation
front: Q: How does cyclical bisphosphonate therapy improve bone quality in OI patients?
back:
• Decreases bone resorption and turnover.
• Reduces bone pain.
• Lowers fracture rates.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Cyclical bisphosphonate treatment decreases bone resorption and turnover. This reduces bone pain and the fracture rate, promoting weight-bearing mobility and bone strength]

category: Define osteogenesis imperfecta and describe its genetic basis and abnormal collagen formation
front: Q: List the three common non-skeletal clinical manifestations of Osteogenesis Imperfecta.
back:
• Blue sclerae.
• Ligamentous laxity.
