category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: State the criteria for diagnosing post-traumatic syringomyelia following spinal cord injury.
back:
* Segmental pain at/above level of injury
* Sensory loss
* Progressive asymmetrical weakness
* Increased spasticity
* Confirmed by MRI showing expanding cavities.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 404 (Book Page): [Clinically, patients present with segmental pain at or above the level of injury, sensory loss, progressive asymmetrical weakness or increased spasticity. This warrants early MRI assessment. Expanding cavities require neurosurgical intervention.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: Describe the clinical presentation and triggers of autonomic dysreflexia in spinal cord injuries.
back: A paroxysmal syndrome of hypertension, bradycardia, and headache. It is triggered by noxious stimuli, most commonly bladder distension or rectal loading (fecal impaction).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 404 (Book Page): [Autonomic dysrefexia: This is a paroxysmal syndrome of hypertension, hyperhidrosis (above the level of injury), bradycardia, fushing and headache... It is most commonly triggered by bladder distension or rectal loading from faecal impaction.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: Contrast the etiology of a Stener lesion versus common ulnar collateral ligament sprains in the thumb.
back: In a Stener lesion, the adductor pollicis aponeurosis becomes interposed between the ruptured ligament and its insertion site, preventing bone-to-ligament healing and necessitating open reduction.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 434 (Book Page): [If the ligament undergoes complete rupture the aponeurosis may become interposed, inhibiting ligament-to-bone healing... Complete ruptures with a Stener lesion (interposed aponeurosis) require open reduction.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: Explain the relationship between Abdominal Compartment Syndrome (ACS) and renal failure.
back: Raised intra-abdominal pressure increases renal vascular resistance. This leads to a reduction in glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and subsequently impaired renal function.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 407 (Book Page): [Table 29.8 Effect of raised intra-abdominal pressure on individual organ function. System: Renal. Effect: Increase in renal vascular resistance leading to a reduction in glomerular fltration rate and impaired renal function.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: What is the pathognomonic radiological feature of a Segond fracture in knee trauma?
back: An avulsion fracture located on the anterolateral tibia. It is pathognomonic for an Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) rupture.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 504 (Book Page): [A Segond fracture located on the anterolateral tibia is pathognomonic for an ACL injury.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What is the defining skeletal feature of Hereditary Multiple Exostoses?
back:
● Sessile or pedunculated bony stalks
● Topped with a cartilaginous cap
● Arises from the metaphysis of long bones
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Exostoses consisting of a cartilaginous cap on a bony stalk may be sessile or pedunculated. They grow as the child grows and may cause cosmetic or functional difculties.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Explain the skeletal pathophysiology of the fragmentation phase in Perthes’ disease.
back:
● Revascularization occurs
● Dead ossific nucleus is resorbed
● Leads to mechanical weakness and collapse of the cartilaginous femoral head
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 619 (Book Page): The avascular bone collapses, this is followed by revascularisation, resorption and fragmentation of the dead ossifc nucleus within the cartilaginous femoral head.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Contrast the skeletal bowing of the tibia in Fibular Hemimelia versus Congenital Pseudarthrosis.
back:
● Fibular Hemimelia: Anteromedial apex bow
● Congenital Pseudarthrosis: Anterolateral apex bow
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 624 (Book Page): Fibular hemimelia... the tibial bow has an anteromedial apex... Congenital pseudarthrosis of the tibia... the tibial bow has an anterolateral apex.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Which specific skeletal findings confirm the diagnosis of Scheuermann’s disease?
back:
● Progressive structural kyphosis
● >5° vertebral wedging at 3+ adjacent levels
● Associated end-plate changes on radiograph
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): Scheuermann’s disease... characterised radiologically by >5° vertebral wedging at three adjacent levels with end-plate changes.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What is the primary skeletal effect of bisphosphonates in Osteogenesis Imperfecta (OI)?
back:
● Decreases bone resorption
● Reduces bone turnover
● Increases bone density and reduces fracture rates
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): Cyclical bisphosphonate treatment decreases bone resorption and turnover. This reduces bone pain and the fracture rate, promoting weight-bearing mobility and bone strength.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What classic radiographic skeletal feature identifies Fibrous Dysplasia?
back:
● Intramedullary "ground-glass" appearance
● Replacement of normal bone by fibrous stroma
● Associated cortical thinning
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 613 (Book Page): Fibrous dysplasia... normal bone is replaced by fbrous stroma... diaphyseal lesions have a ‘ground - glass’ appearance.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Describe the characteristic skeletal appearance of enchondromas in Ollier’s disease.
back:
● Mature hyaline cartilage rests within medullary canals
● Radiolucent lesions in tubular bones
● Vertical lucent streaks in the metaphysis
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 613 (Book Page): Enchondromas arise from chondrocyte rests within the medullary canal of tubular bones... vertical lucent streaks (representing cartilage columns) in the metaphysis.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Distinguish Spondylolysis from Spondylolisthesis based on skeletal findings.
back:
● Spondylolysis: Defect in pars interarticularis
● Spondylolisthesis: Forward slip of a superior vertebra on an inferior one
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 630 (Book Page): Spondylolysis defnes a defect in the pars interarticularis... Spondylolisthesis occurs when the upper vertebra slips forward on the lower.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Describe the structural loop of lesion formation in Osteochondritis Dissecans (OCD).
back:
● Localized ischemic necrosis
● Subchondral bone fragment becomes unstable
● Partial or complete separation of the osteochondral piece
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 623 (Book Page): An osteochondral fragment becomes partially or completely separated from the joint surface... affects the lateral aspect of the medial femoral condyle.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What skeletal structure is specifically damaged following Meningococcal Sepsis?
back:
● The growth plate (physis)
● Damage is caused by endotoxin-induced microvascular injury
● Results in ischemic physeal arrest and limb deformity
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 636 (Book Page): Meningococcal sepsis... late orthopaedic sequelae... secondary to endotoxin-induced microvascular injury and ischaemic physeal damage.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Describe the characteristic skeletal appearance of an Extradural Haematoma on a CT scan.
back: A lentiform (lens-shaped or biconvex) hyperdense lesion located between the skull and the brain, typically constrained by dural adherence.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page): [On CT, extradural haematomas appear as a lentiform (lens-shaped or biconvex) hyperdense lesion between the skull and the brain, constrained by the adherence of the dura to the skull.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: What skeletal failure mechanism defines a pediatric Torus (buckle) fracture?
back: The bone fails on the compression side rather than the tension side, causing the cortex to buckle outward rather than breaking completely.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 422 (Book Page): [torus or buckle fractures. ... the bone has failed on the compression side.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Contrast the skeletal CT density of an acute versus a chronic subdural haematoma.
back:
● Acute: Hyperdense (bright) concave lesion.
● Chronic: Diffuse hypodense (dark) lesion overlying the brain surface.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 387 (Book Page)-388: [Right-sided acute subdural haematoma (hyperdense). ... Chronic subdural haematoma... Imaging reveals diffuse hypodensity overlying the brain surface.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Describe the skeletal and clinical hallmark of a pediatric 'white eye' blowout fracture.
back: Entrapment of the inferior rectus muscle in a trapdoor-style orbital floor fracture with minimal radiographic displacement and no subconjunctival haemorrhage.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): [They are also described as a ‘white eye’ blowout fracture as children often present with no subconjunctival haemorrhage... the orbital floor may appear undisplaced or minimally displaced, which means that a trapdoor defect has opened and then closed again, entrapping the muscle.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: What is the skeletal goal of 'containment' surgery in early Legg–Calvé–Perthes disease?
back: To cover the vulnerable femoral head using femoral or pelvic osteotomy, maintaining sphericity by centering the head within the acetabulum during reossification.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 621 (Book Page): [Early [Timing] ... Femoral osteotomy ... Pelvic osteotomy ... To cover (‘contain’) the vulnerable femoral head.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Identify the skeletal diagnostic feature of a vertebral 'burst' fracture on imaging.
back: Characterized by widening of the interpedicular distance and frequent retropulsion of bone fragments into the spinal canal.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 421 (Book Page): [Burst fractures are comminuted fractures of the vertebral body. They are characterised by widening of the distance between the pedicles and can be associated with retropulsion of bone fragments into the spinal canal.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: How does late-stage prosthetic joint infection manifest on serial radiographic evaluation?
back: Demonstrates progressive bone loss (lysis) and/or early radiographic loosening around a previously stable implant.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 603 (Book Page): [Serial radiographs are helpful to detect progressive bone loss, which may be an indicator of recurrent active infection and can predispose to periprosthetic fracture and implant loosening.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Identify the characteristic metaphyseal skeletal feature of Ollier’s disease (enchondromatosis).
back: Vertical lucent streaks within the metaphysis representing columns of unossified hyaline cartilage.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 613 (Book Page): [Larger lesions may show calcification on radiographs and vertical lucent streaks (representing cartilage columns) in the metaphysis.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: How does Persistent Femoral Neck Anteversion alter the skeletal examination of the hip?
back: It manifests as excessive internal rotation (often >70°) with a corresponding severe limitation or complete absence of external rotation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 610 (Book Page): [Persistent femoral neck anteversion presents clinically with excessive internal rotation at the hip joint... the child has no ability to externally rotate the extended hip.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Identify the specific pelvic skeletal features pathognomonic for Achondroplasia.
back: The presence of a horizontal acetabulum and square-appearing pelvic wings.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 613 (Book Page): [The acetabulum is horizontal and the pelvic wings seem square: classical features of achondroplasia.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What are the characteristic skeletal findings on an anteroposterior pelvic radiograph in achondroplasia?
back: Key features include horizontal acetabula, square-shaped pelvic wings, and disproportionately short limbs with widened metaphyses.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): [The acetabulum is horizontal and the pelvic wings seem square: classical features of achondroplasia.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Describe the characteristic skeletal appearance of the growth plates in a child with active rickets.
back: Radiographs demonstrate widened physes (growth plates) and cupped, flared metaphyses due to inadequate bone mineralisation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 614 (Book Page): [Radiographs in cases of rickets demonstrate widened physes with cupped, flared metaphyses.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: How do skeletal findings contrast in a flexible versus a rigid flat foot during tiptoeing?
back:
• Flexible: Medial longitudinal arch reforms and heel corrects into varus.
• Rigid: Arch remains flat and heel stays in valgus (indicates tarsal coalition).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 611 (Book Page): [Rigid: On tiptoe the arch fails to return and the heel remains in valgus; subtalar joint movements are restricted... Flexible: On tiptoe the arch returns and the heel corrects into varus.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: A neonate presents with a stiff 'rocker-bottom' foot. Which skeletal malposition characterizes this specific condition?
back: Congenital Vertical Talus (CVT). It is defined by dorsal dislocation of the navicular on the talar head with fixed hindfoot equinus.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 627 (Book Page): [Congenital vertical talus (CVT)... presents as a stiff ‘rocker-bottom’ foot with dorsal dislocation of the navicular on the talus.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What pharmacological addition is required for neonatal acute osteomyelitis empiric therapy compared to older children?
back: Gentamicin is added to standard Gram-positive cover (cephalosporins/flucloxacillin) to address Gram-negative organisms in infants under 1 year.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [Empirical intravenous therapy against Gram-positive organisms is given... adding gentamicin to cover Gram-negative organisms in children under 1 year.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What are the skeletal radiographic diagnostic criteria for Scheuermann’s disease?
back: Requirement of at least 5° of anterior vertebral wedging across three or more adjacent levels, accompanied by end-plate irregularities.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [Scheuermann’s disease... characterised radiologically by >5° vertebral wedging at three adjacent levels with end-plate changes.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: At what skeletal measurement threshold is surgical intervention typically recommended for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis?
back: Instrumentation and spinal fusion are typically considered when the lateral curvature reaches a Cobb angle greater than 40 degrees.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): [The Cobb angle is a radiological measurement that defines severity... curves >40° are considered for surgery, which involves instrumenting and fusing the spine.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Identify the skeletal fracture patterns that differentiate non-accidental injury (NAI) from accidental childhood trauma.
back: Posterior rib fractures, metaphyseal corner (bucket-handle) fractures, scapular fractures, and multiple fractures in different healing stages.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 637 (Book Page): [Fracture patterns with a high specificity for non-accidental injury: Posterior rib fractures; Corner or bucket-handle metaphyseal fractures; Scapular fractures.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: List the four progressive physiological phases of the femoral head in Legg–Calvé–Perthes disease.
back:
1. Avascularity/Necrosis
2. Revascularisation and Fragmentation (collapse)
3. Reossification
4. Regeneration/Healing.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 619 (Book Page): [The avascular change... followed by revascularisation, resorption and fragmentation of the dead ossific nucleus... finally by reossification and regeneration (‘healing’) of the bony epiphysis.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Identify the four skeletal components that define the multiplanar deformity of a true structural club foot (CTEV).
back:
• Hindfoot equinus
• Hindfoot varus
• Midfoot adductus
• Forefoot cavus.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 625 (Book Page): [Structural idiopathic club foot has fixed deformity with elements of hindfoot equinus and varus, midfoot adductus and... forefoot cavus.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: What is the classic salvage orthopedic procedure for an irreparable infected hip prosthesis?
back: Girdlestone excision arthroplasty. It involves removing the infected components without re-implantation to palliate symptoms.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 624 (Book Page): [An example is the Girdlestone excision arthroplasty of the hip.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: Pathophysiologically, why is retrobulbar hemorrhage considered an acute maxillofacial surgical emergency?
back: It increases intraorbital pressure, leading to ischemic damage of the optic nerve by reducing retinal artery blood flow.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): [A retrobulbar haemorrhage is an acute surgical emergency as it can lead to blindness secondary to pressureinduced reduced fow on the retinal artery, leading to ischaemic damage to the optic nerve]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: Which four clinical predictors differentiate pediatric septic arthritis from transient hip synovitis?
back: 1. History of fever >38.5°C. 2. Non-weight-bearing. 3. ESR >40 mm/h. 4. White cell count >12 × 10^9/L.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [History of fever >38.5°C; Non-weight-bearing; Erythrocyte sedimentation rate >40 mm/h; White cell count >12 × 10 9 /L]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: A child with a supracondylar humerus fracture cannot perform the 'OK' sign. Identify the complication.
back: Anterior interosseous nerve (median branch) neuropraxia. It results in paralysis of the flexor pollicis longus and flexor digitorum profundus.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 483 (Book Page): [Test for fexor pollicis longus supplied by the anterior interosseous nerve... bring the tips of the thumb and index fnger together (the ‘OK’ sign)]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: What is the primary clinical function of antibiotic-impregnated spacers in two-stage joint revision?
back: 1. Delivers high-dose local antimicrobial therapy. 2. Maintains joint space and soft-tissue tension while infection clears.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 624 (Book Page): [An antibiotic-impregnated spacer may be implanted... This is a temporary measure and cannot withstand full weight-bearing.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: What histopathological finding confirms a prosthetic joint infection according to EBJIS guidelines?
back: The presence of five or more polymorphonuclear neutrophils (PMN) per high-power field (HPF) in at least five tissue samples.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 623 (Book Page): [Infection is confrmed if... Presence of ≥5 neutrophils in ≥5 HPFs]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: How does the BACH classification guide the surgical staging of chronic osteomyelitis?
back: It evaluates bone involvement (B), antimicrobial profile (A), soft-tissue coverage (C), and host health (H) to plan debridement or segmental reconstruction.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 627 (Book Page): [The BACH classifcation divides patients into ‘uncomplicated’, ‘complex’ and ‘limited options available’ based on the four important features of the infection... (B), (A), (C) and (H).]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: A child with an orbital 'white eye' fracture develops bradycardia. Identify the associated reflex.
back: Oculocardiac reflex. It is triggered by the entrapment of the inferior rectus muscle, causing vagal stimulation, nausea, and syncope.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): [Inferior rectus muscle entrapment in children may present as the oculocardiac refex: a triad of bradycardia, nausea and syncope.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: Describe the clinical progression of post-traumatic syringomyelia occurring years after spinal injury.
back: Segmental pain, sensory loss, progressive asymmetrical weakness, or increased spasticity manifest at or above the original injury level.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 404 (Book Page): [Clinically, patients present with segmental pain at or above the level of injury, sensory loss, progressive asymmetrical weakness or increased spasticity.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: What clinical finding defines the 'too many toes' sign in foot examinations?
back: Increased forefoot abduction viewed from behind, typically indicating pes planus (flat foot) or tibialis posterior tendon dysfunction.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 494 (Book Page): [The ‘too many toes’ sign demonstrates increased forefoot abduction (pes planus [fat foot]) and a splayed forefoot.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: What biochemical mechanism is primarily responsible for articular cartilage destruction in septic arthritis?
back: The production of bacterial toxins and proteolytic enzymes (proteases) by leukocytes, which destroy the collagen matrix of articular cartilage.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [Pus in a joint is destructive: the proteases produced by leukocytes destroy both the bacteria and the collagen matrix of the articular cartilage.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: What is the primary pathophysiological mechanism leading to irreversible muscle damage in compartment syndrome?
back: Increased intracompartmental pressure leads to reduced microperfusion, causing tissue ischaemia and cellular anoxia.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 444 (Book Page): [The pathophysiology involves increased tissue pressure, which leads to reduced microperfusion, resulting in tissue ischaemia and irreversible muscle damage from cellular anoxia.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: Distinguish neurogenic shock from hypovolaemic shock based on hemodynamic presentation.
back:
● Neurogenic: Hypotension with bradycardia (normal/low HR) and warm peripheries.
● Hypovolaemic: Hypotension with tachycardia and cold, clammy peripheries.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 424 (Book Page): [Neurogenic shock . This presents with hypotension, a normal heart rate or bradycardia and warm peripheries... Hypovolaemic shock . Hypotension with tachycardia and cold clammy peripheries.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: A patient presents with tense proptosis and reduced visual acuity following midface trauma. What is the immediate complication?
back: Retrobulbar haemorrhage; a surgical emergency requiring immediate lateral canthotomy to prevent ischaemic blindness.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): [A retrobulbar haemorrhage is an acute surgical emergency as it can lead to blindness secondary to pressure-induced reduced fow on the retinal artery... It presents with tense proptosis, increasing pain, reduced visual acuity.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: What histological finding confirms the presence of infection in a prosthetic joint (PJI)?
back: The presence of fve or more polymorphonuclear neutrophils per high-powered feld (HPF) in synovial tissue.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 619 (Book Page): [The presence of fve or more polymorphonuclear neutrophils per high-powered feld is diagnostic in fracture-related joint infections and PJIs.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: Why is avascular necrosis (AVN) a critical risk in displaced talar neck fractures?
back: The displacement interrupts the blood supply to the body of the talus, leading to ischaemic infarction.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 438 (Book Page): [The blood supply to the body of the talus is interrupted in displaced talar neck fractures... to reduce the possibility of avascular necrosis, anatomical reduction and stable fxation of the talar neck should be performed.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: What clinical criterion distinguishes a rigid (pathological) flat foot from a flexible (physiological) flat foot?
back: In a rigid flat foot, the medial arch fails to return and the heel remains in valgus when the patient stands on tiptoe.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 611 (Book Page): [Rigid: On tiptoe the arch fails to return and the heel remains in valgus. Subtalar joint movements are restricted and often painful.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: According to Kocher’s criteria, which four clinical predictors indicate a high probability of pediatric septic arthritis?
back:
1. History of fever (>38.5°C).
2. Non-weight-bearing status.
3. ESR >40 mm/h.
4. White cell count >12,000/μL.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [The clinical predictors of Kocher et al. (2004) for the diagnosis of septic arthritis: History of fever >38.5°C, Non-weight-bearing, Erythrocyte sedimentation rate >40 mm/h, White cell count >12 × 10^9 /L.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: How is an 'unstable' slip of the capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE) defined clinically?
back: A slip is defined as unstable (Loder classification) when the patient is unable to bear weight on the affected limb.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 621 (Book Page): [An unstable slip is defned by Loder as one in which the patient cannot bear weight on the limb.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: What is the most critical mechanical requirement for eradicating infection in an unhealed fracture?
back: Rigid stability. If the implant is unstable, it must be removed and replaced (often with external fixation) to allow healing and infection control.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 603 (Book Page): [Stability is essential for bone healing and eradication of infection. If the implant is not stable, it should be removed and replaced by an external fxator.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: Which specific organism poses a life-threatening complication risk following splenectomy?
back: Streptococcus pneumoniae (Pneumococcus). Patients require inoculation within 2–3 weeks post-surgery to mitigate septic risk.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 402 (Book Page): [Inoculation against Pneumococcus is advisable within 2–3 weeks, by which time the patient’s immune system has recovered.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: What clinical triad characterizes the "coning" stage of brain herniation in TBI?
back:
Cushing’s triad: 
1. Hypertension 
2. Bradycardia 
3. Irregular respiration.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): [tonsillar herniation through the foramen magnum compresses medullary vasomotor and respiratory centres, classically producing Cushing’s triad: hypertension, bradycardia and irregular respiration. The patient is then said to be ‘coning’]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: Contrast the metabolic complications of SIADH versus Diabetes Insipidus in TBI.
back:
SIADH: Water retention leading to hyponatraemia.
Diabetes Insipidus: Compromised ADH secretion resulting in hypernatraemia.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 389 (Book Page): [The syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH) leads to water retention and hyponatraemia... antidiuretic hormone secretion may be compromised... producing diabetes insipidus, resulting in hypernatraemia.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: What life-threatening complication is commonly triggered by bladder distension in spinal cord injury?
back: Autonomic dysreflexia. It presents as paroxysmal hypertension, bradycardia, and headache in response to noxious visceral stimuli.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 404 (Book Page): [Autonomic dysrefexia... paroxysmal syndrome of hypertension... bradycardia... headache in response to noxious visceral and other stimuli. It is most commonly triggered by bladder distension or rectal loading]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: How does Abdominal Compartment Syndrome (ACS) specifically affect renal and cardiovascular function?
back:
Renal: Increased vascular resistance reduces GFR and impairs function.
Cardiovascular: Decreased venous return reduces preload and cardiac output.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 408 (Book Page): [Renal: Increase in renal vascular resistance leading to a reduction in glomerular fltration rate... Cardiovascular: Decrease in venous return resulting in decreased cardiac output]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: Which physiological parameters comprise the cycle of secondary brain injury in TBI?
back:
1. Raised ICP
2. Reduced cerebral perfusion
3. Hypoxia
4. Inflammation and brain swelling.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 390 (Book Page): [Raised ICP can compromise cerebral perfusion, resulting in a cycle of secondary brain injury and swelling... avoidance of hypoxia and hypotension and control of ICP.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: Identify the host factors associated with a better prognosis in Perthes' disease.
back: Younger age at onset and male gender, primarily due to greater remodelling potential before skeletal maturity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 621 (Book Page): [The prognosis is better in younger children (and in boys), who have more remodelling potential before skeletal maturity.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: What is the immediate surgical management for traumatic retrobulbar haemorrhage?
back: Bedside lateral canthotomy and cantholysis under local anaesthesia to relieve pressure and prevent optic nerve ischaemia/blindness.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): [A retrobulbar haemorrhage is an acute surgical emergency... preparation should be made for immediate bedside lateral canthotomy and cantholysis under LA to allow the globe to bulge forwards and relieve the pressure]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: Which Seddon classification of nerve injury implies a functionally poor outcome without surgery?
back: Neurotmesis. It involves complete division of the nerve, sheath, and fibers, preventing guided regeneration.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 421 (Book Page): [Neurotmesis – complete division of the nerve, nerve sheath and nerve fbre. Functionally poor outcome without surgical intervention to restore continuity of the nerve sheath.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: Why is active plantarflexion unreliable for identifying a complete Achilles tendon rupture?
back: Patients may still actively plantarflex using the long toe flexors. Diagnosis requires the Simmonds or Thompson calf-squeeze test.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 439 (Book Page): [Active plantarfexion of the ankle is still possible, although weak, through the use of the toe plantarfexors... squeezing the calf fails to elicit passive plantarfexion of the foot.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Distinguish the skeletal failure mechanism in paediatric Greenstick versus Torus (Buckle) fractures.
back:
- Greenstick: Tension cortex fails (incomplete fracture).
- Torus: Compression cortex buckles or bulges (incomplete fracture).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 422 (Book Page): In children and adolescents the fracture line may be incomplete... These incomplete fractures are called greenstick (Figure 32.8) fractures, where one tension cortex fails. If the compression cortex buckles, they are called torus (Figure 32.9) or buckle fractures.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Explain why acute haematogenous osteomyelitis in children characteristically originates in the long bone metaphyses.
back:
- Presence of slow blood flow through looped vessels.
- Vulnerability to microtrauma.
- These factors facilitate bacterial seeding during bacteraemia.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): Infection starts in the metaphyses of long bones, where the slow fow through the looped vessels combined with microtrauma encourages seeding of infection during a bacteraemia.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Contrast the distinguishing radiographic shapes of extradural versus acute subdural haematomas on CT imaging.
back:
- Extradural: Lentiform (biconvex) hyperdense lesion.
- Subdural: Diffuse concave (crescentic) appearance expanding across the brain surface.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page)-388: On CT, extradural haematomas appear as a lentiform (lens-shaped or biconvex) hyperdense lesion... subdural blood is free to expand across the brain surface, giving a difuse concave appearance.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What specific skeletal mechanism and clinical reflex characterize a paediatric "white eye" orbital blowout fracture?
back:
- Mechanism: Trapdoor defect opening and closing, entrapping the inferior rectus muscle.
- Clinical Sign: Oculocardiac reflex (bradycardia, nausea, syncope).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): the orbital foor may appear undisplaced or minimally displaced, which means that a trapdoor defect has opened and then closed again, entrapping the muscle. They are also described as a ‘white eye’ blowout fracture... Inferior rectus muscle entrapment in children may present as the oculocardiac refex: a triad of bradycardia, nausea and syncope.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Identify the characteristic skeletal radiographic finding in patients with Osteogenesis Imperfecta receiving cyclical bisphosphonates.
back: - Appearance of multiple horizontal growth lines (Zebra lines) in the metaphyses.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): Cyclical bisphosphonate treatment... Figure 44.12 Radiograph of a child with osteogenesis imperfecta who has been treated with cyclical bisphosphonates. Multiple growth lines are visible.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: List three fracture patterns in children that demonstrate high specificity for non-accidental injury (NAI).
back:
- Metaphyseal corner or bucket-handle fractures.
- Posterior rib fractures.
- Scapular fractures.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 637 (Book Page): Fracture patterns with a high specifcity for non-accidental injury: Multiple fractures at different stages of healing/old fractures; Posterior rib fractures; Corner or bucket-handle metaphyseal fractures; Scapular fractures.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Define the four components of the STAR mnemonic used to describe skeletal fracture displacement.
back:
- S: Shortening.
- T: Translation.
- A: Angulation.
- R: Rotation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 421 (Book Page): type and degree of displacement: shortening, translation, angulation, rotation (mnemonic STAR).

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Identify the specific skeletal displacement and angulation that defines a classical Colles' fracture.
back: - Distal radial fracture with dorsal displacement and dorsal angulation (creating the "dinner fork" deformity).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 434 (Book Page): Look for bony deformity (dinner fork deformity, Colles’ fracture)... most dorsally displaced fractures (Colles fracture).

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Identify the skeletal torsional anomalies that constitute the "miserable malalignment syndrome".
back: - Persistent femoral neck anteversion combined with compensatory external tibial torsion.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 610 (Book Page): In others, compensatory external tibial torsion may develop... symptoms of the miserable malalignment syndrome, including knee pain and feelings of instability.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: State the three radiographic skeletal features used to predict avascularity of the humeral head in fractures.
back:
- Fracture through the anatomical neck.
- Loss of the medial hinge.
- Presence of <8 mm of bone along the medial calcar.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 436 (Book Page): Three factors can be used to predict avascularity of the humeral head: 1 fracture through the anatomical neck; 2 loss of the medial hinge; 3 less than 8 mm of bone along the medial calcar.

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: What clinical entities constitute the lethal "triad of death" in severely traumatized patients?
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [P]rolonged procedures result in additional trauma and further immune and physiological derangement; the ‘triad of death’ – a cycle of acidosis, coagulopathy and hypothermia – may develop and result in multiorgan failure and death.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: Describe the pathophysiological mechanism leading to muscle damage in compartment syndrome.
back: Raised pressure within a fascial compartment exceeds capillary perfusion pressure, leading to reduced microperfusion, tissue ischemia, and eventual irreversible cellular anoxia/necrosis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 444 (Book Page): [The pathophysiology involves increased tissue pressure, which leads to reduced microperfusion, resulting in tissue ischaemia and irreversible muscle damage from cellular anoxia.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: List three systemic complications caused by raised intra-abdominal pressure in Abdominal Compartment Syndrome (ACS).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 407 (Book Page): [Table 29.8 Effect of raised intra-abdominal pressure... Renal: Increase in renal vascular resistance... Cardiovascular: Decrease in venous return... Respiratory: Increased ventilation pressures because of splinting of the diaphragm.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: A patient cannot move their shoulder following dislocation. Which specific sensory check identifies axillary nerve injury?
back: Testing sensation in the "regimental badge area," located on the lateral aspect of the upper arm.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 485 (Book Page): [Test sensation in the upper part of the lateral aspect of the arm (‘regimental badge area’) ( Figure 35.22 ). Loss may indicate damage to the axillary nerve (following shoulder dislocation).]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: What vascular anatomical feature predisposes the proximal pole of the scaphoid to avascular necrosis (AVN)?
back: The blood supply enters the scaphoid distally and supplies the bone in a retrograde fashion; a waist fracture interrupts this supply to the proximal pole.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 433 (Book Page): [The blood supply to the scaphoid enters distally and supplies the scaphoid in a retrograde fashion. As such, a displaced waist of scaphoid fracture interrupts the blood supply to the proximal pole, leading to avascular necrosis.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: Identify the clinical hallmark of forefoot abduction seen in tibial posterior tendon dysfunction.
back: The "too many toes" sign, observed from behind the standing patient, indicating an increased splayed/abducted forefoot.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 494 (Book Page): [Look from behind and count the number of toes that can be seen. The ‘too many toes’ sign demonstrates increased forefoot abduction (pes planus [flat foot]) and a splayed forefoot.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: In thumb ulnar collateral ligament (UCL) injuries, what is the clinical significance of a Stener lesion?
back: The adductor pollicis aponeurosis becomes interposed between the ruptured ligament and its insertion, mechanically preventing spontaneous healing.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 434 (Book Page): [If the ligament undergoes complete rupture the aponeurosis may become interposed, inhibiting ligament-to-bone healing. ... A positive test ... suggests the Stener lesion.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: Which specific fracture patterns carry high specificity for non-accidental injury (NAI) in children?
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 637 (Book Page): [Table 44.21 Fracture patterns with a high specifcity for non-accidental injury. ● Posterior rib fractures ● Corner or bucket-handle metaphyseal fractures ● Scapular fractures ● Any fracture in a child below walking age]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: Identify the characteristic radiographic sign of a perilunate dislocation on a lateral wrist view.
back: The capitate is displaced and no longer sits within the concavity (the "cup") of the lunate.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 433 (Book Page): [Review of the radiographs should particularly ensure the anatomical location of the lunate in the radiocarpal fossa and that the capitate in the ‘cup’ of the lunate is maintained.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: What specific orthopedic complications are grouped under the term "plaster disease"?
back: Joint stiffness and muscle wasting, resulting from prolonged immobilization in a cast.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 427 (Book Page): [Table 32.4 ... Disadvantages ● ‘Plaster disease’ – joint stifness and muscle wasting]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: What are the clinical hallmarks of compartment syndrome?
back:
* Pain out of proportion to injury
* Pain on passive stretch
* Paraesthesia (early sign)
* Paralysis, numbness, and pulselessness (late signs)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 444 (Book Page): [Compartment syndrome is a clinical diagnosis characterised by pain out of proportion, increasing pain, and pain on passive stretch, with paraesthesia possible. Paralysis, numbness and pallor are late signs and pulselessness is an extremely late sign.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: When is the 'DAIR' approach indicated for managing prosthetic joint infection (PJI)?
back:
* Indicated only if the prosthesis is well-fixed
* Requires exchange of all modular components
* Requires radical excision of all infected soft tissue and necrotic bone
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 602 (Book Page): [Debridement, antibiotics and implant reten - tion - ‘DAIR’ . This can only be undertaken if the pros - thesis is well fxed. DAIR is not a form of washout as all infected soft tissue and necrotic bone must be fully excised and modular components exchanged.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: Contrast the severity grading of SCFE based on metaphyseal uncovering.
back:
* Mild: <33% uncovering
* Moderate: 33–66% uncovering
* Severe: >66% uncovering
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 621 (Book Page): [Slip severity is assessed on the lateral radiograph in terms of percentage uncovering of the metaphysis (Table 44.8). . . Mild <33; Moderate 33–66; Severe >66]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: A child has a painful hip. Which four clinical predictors differentiate septic arthritis from transient synovitis?
back:
* History of fever >38.5°C
* Non-weight-bearing status
* ESR >40 mm/h
* White cell count >12 × 10^9/L
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [Four clinical predictors can diferentiate between septic arthritis and transient synovitis (Table 44.17). . . History of fever >38.5°C; Non-weight-bearing; Erythrocyte sedimentation rate >40 mm/h; White cell count >12 × 10 9 /L]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: What antibiotic administration strategy did the OVIVA trial validate for orthopedic infections?
back:
* Oral therapy is as effective as intravenous (IV) therapy
* Providing the organism is susceptible
* Providing the patient can tolerate oral antibiotics
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 599 (Book Page): [The recent OVIVA trial has shown that oral therapy is equally efective, providing that the organism(s) is susceptible and the patient can tolerate the chosen antibiotic.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: What are the diagnostic criteria for an 'unstable' ankle fracture?
back:
* Involvement of two or more anatomical columns (medial, lateral, posterior)
* Radiographic evidence of talar shift
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 438 (Book Page): [It is useful to think of the ankle mortise as having three columns: medial, lateral and posterior. . . If both or all three columns are involved or there is evidence of talar shift, it is an unstable injury.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: Describe the management of a 'pink pulseless hand' in pediatric supracondylar fractures.
back:
* Perform urgent fracture reduction and stabilization
* Use expectant observation if distal perfusion is adequate and neurology is intact
* Pulse typically returns within 24–48 hours
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 441 (Book Page): [The pink pulseless hand is more controversial. . . If there is satisfactory perfusion of the limb, no suggestion of compartment syndrome and no neurological injury, then reduction and stabilisation of the fracture is warranted and a more expectant approach to the vascular injury can be taken. Often the pulse will return within 24–48 hours.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: Contrast the clinical presentation of 'white eye' blowout fractures in children.
back:
* Absence of subconjunctival hemorrhage
* Entrapment of the inferior rectus muscle
* Oculocardiac reflex triad: Bradycardia, nausea, and syncope
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): [Inferior rectus muscle entrapment in children may present as the oculocardiac refex: a triad of bradycardia, nausea and syncope. . . also described as a ‘white eye’ blowout fracture as children often present with no subconjunctival haemorrhage]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: How does biofilm formation contribute to antibiotic resistance in bone infections?
back:
* Bacteria adhere to dead bone or implants in a polysaccharide matrix
* Bacteria enter an altered metabolic state
* Matrix protects bacteria from host immune systems and systemic antibiotics
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 596 (Book Page): [Bacteria can adhere to dead bone or implant surfaces, forming a complex community enveloped in a polysaccharide matrix, known as a bioflm. These bacteria alter their metabolic state, making them more resistant both to the host immune system and to antibiotics.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: What does the 'too many toes' sign signify during clinical inspection from behind?
back:
* Increased forefoot abduction
* Indicates pes planus (flat foot) or tibialis posterior tendon dysfunction
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 494 (Book Page): [The ‘too many toes’ sign demonstrates increased forefoot abduction (pes planus [fat foot]). . . Page 499 (Book Page): Pathology of the tibialis posterior typically presents with. . . the ‘too many toes’ sign.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: What are the three primary long-term complications associated with depressed skull fractures?
back:
• Intracranial infection
• Permanent neurological deficit
• Late-onset epilepsy
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page): [Depressed skull fractures] are usually compound (open) fractures, and are associated with a high incidence of infection, neurological defcit and late-onset epilepsy.

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: Why must a sucking chest wound not be fully closed until a chest drain is inserted?
back: To prevent converting a stable open pneumothorax into a life-threatening, unstable tension pneumothorax.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 394 (Book Page): No attempt should be made to close a sucking chest wound until controlled drainage has been achieved, in case a stable patient with an open pneumothorax is converted into an unstable patient with a tension pneumothorax.

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: Contrast the metabolic/electrolyte complications of SIADH versus Diabetes Insipidus in traumatic brain injury.
back:
• SIADH: Pituitary damage causing water retention and hyponatraemia.
• Diabetes Insipidus: Compromised ADH secretion causing hypernatraemia.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 390 (Book Page): The syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH) leads to water retention and hyponatraemia... Conversely antidiuretic hormone secretion may be compromised in the context of trauma, producing diabetes insipidus, resulting in hypernatraemia.

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: What is the primary clinical complication of performing mechanical 'springing' of the pelvis in trauma?
back: It disrupts established blood clots formed around the pelvic fracture, potentially causing catastrophic, uncontrollable hemorrhage.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): Mechanical testing of the pelvis in the emergency room (‘springing the pelvis’) adds no useful clinical examination and will disrupt any blood clot that has formed around a pelvic fracture. It should never be performed.

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: Which specific infectious complication must be mitigated with inoculation after a trauma-related splenectomy?
back: Overwhelming post-splenectomy sepsis, specifically requiring inoculation against Pneumococcus within 2–3 weeks post-surgery.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 381 (Book Page): Inoculation against Pneumococcus is advisable within 2–3 weeks, by which time the patient’s immune system has recovered.

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: What orthopedic deformity is indicated by the 'too many toes' sign when viewed from behind?
back: Pes planus (flat foot) characterized by increased forefoot abduction and a splayed forefoot.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 494 (Book Page): The ‘too many toes’ sign demonstrates increased forefoot abduction (pes planus [fat foot]) and a splayed forefoot.

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: What is the most severe delayed complication of an unrepaired traumatic breach of the diaphragm?
back: Delayed herniation of abdominal contents into the thorax, resulting in organ strangulation and high mortality.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 397 (Book Page): A complication of a breach of the diaphragm is herniation of abdominal contents into the chest. This may present much later, and strangulation of any of the contents can then occur, with a high mortality rate.

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: What clinical features distinguish the complications of a rigid flat foot caused by tarsal coalition?
back:
• Hindfoot pain
• Recurrent ankle sprains
• Rigid heel valgus (fails to correct to varus on tiptoe)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 497 (Book Page)/627: In tarsal coalition there is failure of segmentation of adjacent tarsal bones. School-aged children present with hindfoot pain and recurrent ankle sprains... The symptomatic, rigid fat foot is due to infammation or a tarsal coalition.

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: Describe the acute respiratory complications resulting from Abdominal Compartment Syndrome (ACS).
back:
• Increased airway/ventilation pressures
• Decreased lung compliance
• Splinting of the diaphragm
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 407 (Book Page): Respiratory: Increased ventilation pressures because of splinting of the diaphragm, decreased lung compliance and increased airway pressures.

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: What is a potentially fatal iatrogenic complication of using Kirschner (K-) wires around the shoulder girdle?
back: Wire migration into the thoracic cavity or the heart.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 428 (Book Page): It is not advisable to use non-threaded K-wires around the shoulder girdle and clavicle as migration into the thoracic cavity and heart has been reported.

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: Identify the three clinical components of Cushing’s triad in traumatic brain injury.
back:
1. Hypertension
2. Bradycardia
3. Irregular respiration

*Indicates life-threatening brainstem compression/herniation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): [Cerebellar tonsillar herniation through the foramen magnum compresses medullary vasomotor and respiratory centres, classically producing Cushing’s triad: hypertension, bradycardia and irregular respiration.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: Which three physiological derangements constitute the 'triad of death' in polytrauma patients?
back:
1. Acidosis
2. Coagulopathy
3. Hypothermia

*This cycle leads to multiorgan failure if not managed with Damage Control Surgery.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [the ‘triad of death’ – a cycle of acidosis, coagulopathy and hypothermia – may develop and result in multiorgan failure and death.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: Identify the four Kocher’s clinical predictors used to diagnose pediatric septic arthritis.
back:
1. History of fever >38.5°C
2. Inability to weight-bear
3. ESR >40 mm/h
4. WCC >12 × 10⁹/L
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [Four clinical predictors can diferentiate between septic arthritis and transient synovitis... History of fever >38.5°C, Non-weight-bearing, Erythrocyte sedimentation rate >40 mm/h, White cell count >12 × 10⁹/L]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: A patient with an orbital fracture presents with proptosis and vision loss. Identify the complication.
back:
Retrobulbar Haemorrhage.

*Emergency Management: Lateral canthotomy and cantholysis to prevent optic nerve ischaemia and permanent blindness.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): [A retrobulbar haemorrhage is an acute surgical emergency as it can lead to blindness secondary to pressure-induced reduced fow on the retinal artery... It presents with tense proptosis, increasing pain, reduced visual acuity and loss of the pupillary response.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: Define the 'DAIR' strategy for managing Prosthetic Joint Infection (PJI).
back:
Debridement, Antibiotics, and Implant Retention.

*Criteria: Only indicated if the prosthesis is well-fixed and soft-tissue cover is adequate.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 602 (Book Page): [Debridement, antibiotics and implant retention - ‘DAIR’. This can only be undertaken if the prosthesis is well fxed. DAIR is not a form of washout as all infected soft tissue and necrotic bone must be fully excised and modular components exchanged.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: Identify the clinical hallmark of Autonomic Dysreflexia in spinal cord injury patients.
back:
Paroxysmal hypertension and bradycardia with hyperhidrosis above the lesion level.

*Common Triggers: Bladder distension or rectal loading/fecal impaction.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 404 (Book Page): [Autonomic dysrefexia... paroxysmal syndrome of hypertension, hyperhidrosis (above the level of injury), bradycardia, fushing and headache in response to noxious visceral and other stimuli. It is most commonly triggered by bladder distension or rectal loading from faecal impaction.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: Which specific triad suggests inferior rectus muscle entrapment in pediatric 'white eye' orbital fractures?
back:
The Oculocardiac Reflex:
1. Bradycardia
2. Nausea
3. Syncope

*This requires urgent surgery to prevent irreversible muscle necrosis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): [Inferior rectus muscle entrapment in children may present as the oculocardiac refex: a triad of bradycardia, nausea and syncope. This needs to be treated as an emergency because irreversible damage related to muscle necrosis can occur within hours.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: Differentiate between the definitions of 'delayed union' and 'non-union' in fracture complications.
back:
Delayed Union: Slow healing beyond expected time frame.
Non-union: No clinical/radiographic improvement over 3 months or failed union by 6 months.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 424 (Book Page): [Delayed union... slow to heal and that has not healed in the expected time frame. Non-union... fails to demonstrate clinical or radiological improvement over 3 months. In general, you do not describe a fracture as ‘non-union’ until 6 months after the injury.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: Identify the accepted intracompartmental pressure thresholds diagnostic for Compartment Syndrome.
back:
1. Absolute Pressure: $\geq$ 30 mmHg
2. Delta Pressure (Diastolic - Compartment): $\leq$ 30 mmHg
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 444 (Book Page): [Generally accepted pressure thresholds include an absolute pressure greater than or equal to 30 mmHg or pressure diference (diastolic pressure – compartment pressure) less than or equal to 30 mmHg.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: Identify the primary mechanisms of late orthopaedic sequelae in Meningococcal Sepsis.
back:
1. Ischaemic physeal (growth plate) damage
2. Endotoxin-induced microvascular injury
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 636 (Book Page): [The often debilitating, late orthopaedic sequelae of meningococcal septicaemia are secondary to endotoxin-induced microvascular injury and ischaemic physeal damage.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: What clinical triad constitutes the "triad of death" in severely traumatized patients?
back:
The lethal cycle consists of:
- Acidosis
- Coagulopathy
- Hypothermia
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [the ‘triad of death’ – a cycle of acidosis, coagulopathy and hypothermia – may develop and result in multiorgan failure and death.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: Which specific signs make up Cushing’s triad in the context of raised intracranial pressure?
back:
1. Hypertension
2. Bradycardia
3. Irregular respiration (indicates impending coning)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): [Cushing’s triad: hypertension, bradycardia and irregular respiration. The patient is then said to be ‘coning’]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: Differentiate the circulatory status in hypovolaemic vs. neurogenic shock during spinal trauma.
back:
- Hypovolaemic: Hypotension, tachycardia, cold/clammy peripheries.
- Neurogenic: Hypotension, normal/bradycardia, warm peripheries.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 402 (Book Page): [Hypovolaemic shock. Hypotension with tachycardia and cold clammy peripheries... Neurogenic shock. This presents with hypotension, a normal heart rate or bradycardia and warm peripheries.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: A patient with a midface fracture presents with proptosis and loss of red colour perception. Diagnosis?
back:
Retrobulbar haemorrhage.
- Urgent intervention: Bedside lateral canthotomy and cantholysis to prevent permanent blindness.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): [A retrobulbar haemorrhage is an acute surgical emergency as it can lead to blindness... It presents with tense proptosis, increasing pain, reduced visual acuity and loss of the pupillary response. One of the early signs may be altered perception of red colour]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: What is the specific IV dosing regimen for Tranexamic Acid in suspected trauma haemorrhage?
back: 1 gram IV given over 10 minutes, followed by a maintenance dose of 1 gram over the next 8 hours.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [One gram is given intravenously over 10 minutes, followed by a further 1-g dose over 8 hours. Tranexamic acid should be given to all trauma patients suspected to have signifcant haemorrhage]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: List the four Kocher clinical predictors used to diagnose paediatric septic arthritis.
back:
1. History of fever >38.5°C
2. Non-weight-bearing status
3. ESR >40 mm/h
4. White cell count >12 × 10^9/L
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [The clinical predictors of Kocher et al. (2004) for the diagnosis of septic arthritis: History of fever >38.5°C; Non-weight-bearing; Erythrocyte sedimentation rate >40 mm/h; White cell count >12 × 10 9 /L]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: What is the primary clinical indicator differentiating compartment syndrome from standard fracture pain?
back: Pain that is out of proportion to the injury and significant pain elicited by passive stretching of the affected muscle.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 444 (Book Page): [Compartment syndrome is a clinical diagnosis characterised by pain out of proportion, increasing pain, and pain on passive stretch]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: A child with a supracondylar humeral fracture develops severe forearm swelling and a 'pink pulseless hand'. Complication risk?
back: Volkmann’s ischaemic contracture secondary to missed forearm compartment syndrome.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 441 (Book Page): [A very rare but feared complication of paediatric supracondylar fractures is Volkmann’s ischaemic contracture. This is due to excessive swelling and missed compartment syndrome in the forearm.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: How does Abdominal Compartment Syndrome (ACS) impact cardiovascular and renal physiology?
back:
- Cardiovascular: Decreased venous return and decreased cardiac output (preload reduction).
- Renal: Increased renal vascular resistance causing reduced GFR.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page): [Renal: Increase in renal vascular resistance leading to a reduction in glomerular fltration rate... Cardiovascular: Decrease in venous return resulting in decreased cardiac output]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: In thumb metacarpophalangeal ulnar collateral ligament injuries, what is a Stener lesion?
back: Complete ligament rupture where the adductor pollicis aponeurosis becomes interposed between the ligament and bone, preventing healing.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 434 (Book Page): [if the ligament undergoes complete rupture the aponeurosis may become interposed, inhibiting ligament-to-bone healing... the Stener lesion.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: Which specific prophylactic intervention is mandatory within 2–3 weeks following a post-traumatic splenectomy?
back: Inoculation against Pneumococcus is required once the immune system recovers.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 402 (Book Page): [Inoculation against Pneumococcus is advisable within 2–3 weeks, by which time the patient’s immune system has recovered.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: Describe the common physiological triggers for autonomic dysreflexia in patients with high-level spinal cord injuries.
back:
It is most commonly triggered by:
- Bladder distension
- Rectal loading (faecal impaction)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 424 (Book Page): [It is most commonly triggered by bladder distension or rectal loading from faecal impaction.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: List the four clinical predictors used to differentiate paediatric septic arthritis from transient synovitis.
back:
- History of fever >38.5°C
- Inability to weight-bear
- ESR >40 mm/h
- White cell count >12 × 10⁹/L
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [The clinical predictors of Kocher et al. (2004) for the diagnosis of septic arthritis: History of fever >38.5°C, Non-weight-bearing, Erythrocyte sedimentation rate >40 mm/h, White cell count >12 × 10⁹/L]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: A patient with midface trauma presents with tense proptosis and loss of red colour perception. Identify the emergency complication.
back: Retrobulbar haemorrhage (requires immediate lateral canthotomy).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 434 (Book Page): [A retrobulbar haemorrhage is an acute surgical emergency... presents with tense proptosis... One of the early signs may be altered perception of red colour in the afected eye.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: What is the required administration window for Tranexamic Acid (TXA) in trauma patients suspected of major bleeding?
back: Ideally within the first hour; the first dose must not be administered more than 3 hours from injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [It needs to be administered as early as possible and ideally within the frst hour from injury; the frst dose should not be administered more than 3 hours from injury.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: Identify the three clinical components of Cushing’s triad in the context of traumatic brainstem compromise.
back:
1. Hypertension
2. Bradycardia
3. Irregular respiration
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): [tonsillar herniation through the foramen magnum compresses medullary vasomotor and respiratory centres, classically producing Cushing’s triad: hypertension, bradycardia and irregular respiration.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: Why is a 'Stener lesion' a significant complication of thumb ulnar collateral ligament ruptures?
back: The adductor pollicis aponeurosis becomes interposed between the ligament and bone, preventing non-operative healing.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 454 (Book Page): [if the ligament undergoes complete rupture the aponeurosis may become interposed, inhibiting ligament-to-bone healing... The presence of a Stener lesion (interposed aponeurosis) ... requires open reduction]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: In a child with an orbital floor fracture, identify the clinical significance of bradycardia associated with nausea.
back: Oculocardiac reflex caused by entrapment of the inferior rectus muscle.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 434 (Book Page): [Inferior rectus muscle entrapment in children may present as the oculocardiac refex: a triad of bradycardia, nausea and syncope.]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: Explain the physiological mechanism of renal impairment in Abdominal Compartment Syndrome (ACS).
back: Raised intra-abdominal pressure increases renal vascular resistance, reducing glomerular filtration rate and function.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 407 (Book Page): [Renal: Increase in renal vascular resistance leading to a reduction in glomerular fltration rate and impaired renal function]

category: Identify orthopedic complications
front: Q: Where is the characteristic 'C-sign' pain located in patients suffering from intra-articular hip derangements?
back: Anterolateral groin.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 524 (Book Page): [Intra-articular hip derangements most commonly manifest as anterolateral groin pain in a characteristic distribution, referred to as a ‘C-sign’]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: Define Marfan syndrome clinical presentation.
back:
● An autosomal dominant multisystemic connective tissue disorder.
● Characterized by defective extracellular matrix integrity.
● Primarily affects the ocular, skeletal, and cardiovascular systems.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 611 (Book Page): [Summary box 44.10 Causes of pes planus: Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: What is the molecular genetic basis of Marfan syndrome?
back:
● Mutations in the FBN1 gene.
● Encodes the glycoprotein Fibrillin-1.
● Results in impaired microfibril formation in connective tissues.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 611 (Book Page): [Summary box 44.10 Causes of pes planus: Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: On which chromosome is the primary mutation for Marfan syndrome located?
back:
● Chromosome 15.
● Specifically localized to 15q21.1.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 611 (Book Page): [Summary box 44.10 Causes of pes planus: Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: What is the inheritance pattern of Marfan syndrome?
back:
● Autosomal dominant.
● Displays high penetrance and significant variable expressivity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 611 (Book Page): [Summary box 44.10 Causes of pes planus: Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: How does Fibrillin-1 deficiency affect cell signaling in Marfan syndrome?
back:
● Causes dysregulation and excessive activation of TGF-β (Transforming Growth Factor-beta).
● Excessive TGF-β activity leads to tissue degradation and abnormal growth.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 611 (Book Page): [Summary box 44.10 Causes of pes planus: Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: Identify the most common orthopaedic foot deformity associated with Marfan syndrome.
back:
● Pes planus (flat feet).
● Caused by underlying generalized joint hyperlaxity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 611 (Book Page): [Summary box 44.10 Causes of pes planus: Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: List the classic skeletal hallmarks of Marfan syndrome.
back:
● Tall stature and arachnodactyly.
● Increased arm span-to-height ratio (>1.05).
● Pectus excavatum or carinatum.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 611 (Book Page): [Summary box 44.10 Causes of pes planus: Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: What ocular pathology is pathognomonic for Marfan syndrome genetics?
back:
● Ectopia lentis (dislocation of the lens).
● Typically occurs in an upward and outward direction.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 611 (Book Page): [Summary box 44.10 Causes of pes planus: Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: A tall patient with joint hyperlaxity presents with sudden chest pain. What is the suspected diagnosis?
back:
● Marfan syndrome with acute aortic dissection.
● Genetic defect in fibrillin-1 weakens the aortic media.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 611 (Book Page): [Summary box 44.10 Causes of pes planus: Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: Which criteria are used for the clinical diagnosis of Marfan syndrome?
back:
● Ghent criteria.
● Relies on systemic score, family history, and presence of ectopia lentis or aortic root dilation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 611 (Book Page): [Summary box 44.10 Causes of pes planus: Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: How is Marfan syndrome clinically defined within the context of skeletal hyperlaxity?
back: Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder. It is clinically defined as a multi-systemic hyperlaxity syndrome resulting in excessive joint flexibility and elongated bone growth.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 633 (Book Page): [Summary box 44.10: Causes of pes planus... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan's syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: What is the primary genetic basis of Marfan syndrome?
back: The condition is caused by a mutation in the FBN1 gene. This gene provides instructions for producing fibrillin-1, a protein essential for the structural integrity of the extracellular matrix.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 633 (Book Page): [Summary box 44.10: Causes of pes planus... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan's syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: How does the skeletal presentation of Marfan syndrome contrast with normal physiological growth?
back: Unlike normal development, Marfan syndrome involves excessive longitudinal bone growth and extreme ligamentous laxity. This contrast often results in arachnodactyly and distinctive deformities like pectus excavatum.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 633 (Book Page): [Summary box 44.10: Causes of pes planus... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan's syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: A tall athlete presenting with hyperlaxity and pes planus likely has which syndrome?
back: Marfan syndrome. The textbook identifies it as a classic hyperlaxity syndrome frequently associated with musculoskeletal findings such as pes planus (flat foot).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 633 (Book Page): [Summary box 44.10: Causes of pes planus... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan's syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: What protein defect results from the genetic mutation in Marfan syndrome?
