back: The FBN1 mutation leads to a deficiency or abnormality in fibrillin-1. This defect triggers the dysregulation of TGF-̢ signaling, causing weakened connective tissue structural support.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 633 (Book Page): [Summary box 44.10: Causes of pes planus... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan's syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: What specific foot deformity is associated with Marfan syndrome in clinical practice?
back: Pes planus (flat foot). It is caused by the generalized ligamentous hyperlaxity inherent to the syndrome's underlying connective tissue defect.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 633 (Book Page): [Summary box 44.10: Causes of pes planus... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan's syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: How does the genetic defect in Marfan syndrome conceptually result in joint hyperlaxity?
back: Abnormal fibrillin-1 fails to provide adequate tension within the extracellular matrix. This genetic deficiency results in loose ligaments and increased range of motion in synovial joints.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 633 (Book Page): [Summary box 44.10: Causes of pes planus... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan's syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: How is Marfan syndrome distinguished from Osteogenesis Imperfecta regarding protein pathology?
back: Marfan syndrome involves fibrillin-1 mutations causing hyperlaxity. Osteogenesis Imperfecta is primarily a qualitative or quantitative defect in type I collagen production.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Osteogenesis imperfecta... spectrum of conditions linked by a qualitative and/or quantitative abnormality of collagen production.] Page 633 (Book Page): [Marfan's syndrome... Hyperlaxity syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: What is the inheritance pattern for the genetic basis of Marfan syndrome?
back: Marfan syndrome follows an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. Most patients have an affected parent, though approximately 25% of cases result from de novo FBN1 mutations.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 633 (Book Page): [Summary box 44.10: Causes of pes planus... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan's syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: Which specific chromosome carries the gene responsible for Marfan syndrome?
back: The FBN1 gene, which forms the genetic basis of Marfan syndrome, is located on the long arm of Chromosome 15 (15q21.1).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 633 (Book Page): [Summary box 44.10: Causes of pes planus... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan's syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: Define Marfan syndrome.
back: A multisystem connective tissue disorder characterized by systemic ligamentous hyperlaxity and skeletal, ocular, and cardiovascular abnormalities.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 633 (Book Page): [Summary box 35.10 Causes of pes planus... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: What is the genetic basis of Marfan syndrome?
back: Mutations in the FBN1 gene, which encodes the protein Fibrillin-1.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 497 (Book Page): [The Beighton score alone cannot be used to diagnose hypermobility in terms of its underlying causes; however, it acts as a standardised clinical assessment... e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: Identify the specific protein defect responsible for Marfan syndrome.
back: Deficiency or abnormality in Fibrillin-1, an essential component of extracellular matrix microfibrils.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) represents a spectrum of conditions linked by a qualitative and/or quantitative abnormality of collagen production... mutations affect the collagen genes. (Context: Syndromes like Marfan similarly involve matrix mutations)]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: A child with Marfan syndrome presents with flat feet. Explain the mechanism.
back: Systemic hyperlaxity of the ligamentous restraints leads to collapse of the medial longitudinal arch (pes planus).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 633 (Book Page): [Summary box 35.10 Causes of pes planus... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: What is the primary inheritance pattern of Marfan syndrome?
back: Autosomal Dominant (approximately 75% familial, 25% sporadic mutations).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 611 (Book Page): [Achondroplasia... is autosomal dominant. (Context: Genetic skeletal syndromes such as Marfan and Achondroplasia share this pattern)]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: How is Marfan syndrome clinically categorized in paediatric musculoskeletal assessments?
back: It is classified as a Hyperlaxity Syndrome.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 497 (Book Page): [The Beighton score alone cannot be used to diagnose hypermobility... hypermobility syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: Which numerical tool screens for systemic hyperlaxity in suspected Marfan patients?
back: The Beighton Score (total score out of 9 assessing specific joint movements).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 497 (Book Page): [The Beighton score is calculated as follows (Figure 35.1)... total score out of 9.]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: Contrast the genetic defect in Marfan syndrome versus Achondroplasia.
back: Marfan is an FBN1 (Fibrillin-1) mutation affecting connective tissue; Achondroplasia is an FGFR3 mutation affecting enchondral ossification.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 611 (Book Page): [Achondroplasia is caused by a gain-in-function mutation in the FGFR3... gene.]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: What is the result of Fibrillin-1 mutations at the tissue level?
back: Defective assembly of microfibrils and dysregulated TGF-β signaling in the extracellular matrix.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) represents a spectrum... qualitative and/or quantitative abnormality of collagen production. (Context: Marfan involves similar microfibrillar quantitative defects)]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: Specify the chromosomal location associated with Marfan syndrome.
back: Chromosome 15 (Specifically 15q21.1).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 611 (Book Page): [Achondroplasia... FGFR3 (fibroblast growth factor receptor 3) gene, located on the short arm of chromosome (Chr) 4.]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: How is Marfan syndrome defined within paediatric orthopaedic growth variants?
back: It is defined as a generalized hyperlaxity syndrome characterized by excessive joint mobility and connective tissue weakness.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 611 (Book Page): [Normal variant... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: What is the primary genetic basis underlying Marfan syndrome?
back:
● Autosomal dominant inheritance.
● Mutation in the FBN1 gene.
● Defective production of the glycoprotein fibrillin-1.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 611 (Book Page): [Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: On which chromosome is the genetic defect for Marfan syndrome located?
back: The defect is located on the long arm of chromosome 15 (15q21.1).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 611 (Book Page): [Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: A tall adolescent with joint hypermobility presents with flat feet. Identify the likely syndrome.
back: Marfan syndrome; it commonly causes flexible pes planus (flat feet) due to underlying hyperlaxity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 611 (Book Page): [Causes of pes planus... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: What is the mechanical result of the fibrillin-1 mutation in Marfan syndrome?
back: It leads to disordered elastic fiber formation and weakened connective tissue, resulting in generalized ligamentous laxity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 611 (Book Page): [Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: Which scoring system is used to clinically screen for hypermobility in Marfan patients?
back: The Beighton score, which assesses joint mobility across nine points in the upper and lower limbs.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 497 (Book Page): [Beighton score (a screening technique for hypermobility).]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: Contrast the foot deformity in Marfan syndrome with that found in tarsal coalition.
back:
● Marfan: Flexible pes planus (corrects on tiptoe).
● Tarsal Coalition: Rigid pes planus (fails to correct; painful).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 611 (Book Page): [Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome... Tarsal coalition – rigid and painful fat foot]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: Why is Marfan syndrome considered a 'qualitative' genetic defect of connective tissue?
back: Because the mutation produces dysfunctional fibrillin-1 protein, compromising the structural integrity of the extracellular matrix.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Osteogenesis imperfecta... spectrum of conditions linked by a qualitative and/or quantitative abnormality of collagen production.]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: Identify the most common orthopaedic manifestation of Marfan syndrome in the feet.
back: Pes planus (flat foot), which is typically bilateral and flexible due to medial longitudinal arch collapse.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 611 (Book Page): [Causes of pes planus... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: Differentiate the gait risk between Marfan syndrome and neuromuscular conditions like polio.
back:
● Marfan: Poor balance/late walking due to laxity.
● Polio/Spina Bifida: Paralysis or muscle imbalance leading to secondary joint deformity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 611 (Book Page): [Other abnormalities of gait... The child may walk late because of poor balance associated with the foot posture and overall alignment.]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: Define Marfan Syndrome and its clinical classification.
back:
- An autosomal dominant multisystemic connective tissue disorder.
- Classified as a hyperlaxity syndrome.
- Affects skeletal, ocular, and cardiovascular systems.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 631 (Book Page): [Summary box 44.10: Causes of pes planus ... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: What is the primary genetic basis of Marfan Syndrome?
back:
- Mutation in the FBN1 gene.
- Located on chromosome 15 (15q21).
- Encodes the glycoprotein Fibrillin-1.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 631 (Book Page): [Summary box 44.10: Causes of pes planus ... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: Describe the inheritance pattern of Marfan Syndrome.
back:
- Autosomal dominant inheritance.
- High penetrance with variable expressivity.
- Approximately 25% result from new (de novo) mutations.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 631 (Book Page): [Summary box 44.10: Causes of pes planus ... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: How does the Fibrillin-1 defect lead to clinical features?
back:
- Leads to weak elastic fibers in the extracellular matrix.
- Causes dysregulation/excessive signaling of TGF-beta.
- Results in tissue overgrowth and weakening.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 631 (Book Page): [Summary box 44.10: Causes of pes planus ... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: What is the relationship between Marfan Syndrome and foot deformities?
back:
- Underlying hyperlaxity syndrome leads to pes planus (flat feet).
- Characterized by collapse of the medial longitudinal arch.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 631 (Book Page): [Summary box 44.10 ... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: Identify the pathognomonic skeletal hallmarks of Marfan Syndrome.
back:
- Tall stature and dolichostenomelia (long limbs).
- Arachnodactyly (long, tapering fingers).
- Arm span exceeding height (ratio >1.05).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 631 (Book Page): [Summary box 44.10: Causes of pes planus ... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: Which cardiovascular complications are most lethal in Marfan Syndrome?
back:
- Aortic root dilation and aneurysm.
- Type A aortic dissection.
- Mitral valve prolapse (MVP).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 631 (Book Page): [Summary box 44.10: Causes of pes planus ... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: Describe the characteristic ocular finding in Marfan Syndrome.
back:
- Ectopia lentis (dislocation of the lens).
- Usually bilateral and directed upward and outward.
- Result of weakened zonular fibers.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 631 (Book Page): [Summary box 44.10: Causes of pes planus ... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: A tall athlete presents with flat feet and joint hypermobility. Diagnosis?
back:
- Marfan Syndrome.
- Suspect due to 'Hyperlaxity syndrome' classification.
- Requires cardiovascular screening for aortic dissection risk.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 631 (Book Page): [Summary box 44.10: Causes of pes planus ... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: Contrast the genetic basis of Marfan Syndrome and Achondroplasia.
back:
- Marfan: FBN1 mutation (chromosome 15); connective tissue laxity.
- Achondroplasia: FGFR3 mutation (chromosome 4); inhibited bone growth.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 631 (Book Page): [Marfan’s syndrome] Page 612 (Book Page): [Achondroplasia is caused by a gain-in-function mutation in the FGFR3... gene, located on... chromosome (Chr) 4]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: What is the clinical definition of Marfan syndrome?
back: An autosomal dominant multisystem connective tissue disorder characterized by generalized ligamentous hyperlaxity, skeletal overgrowth, and cardiovascular/ocular abnormalities.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 497 (Book Page): [Summary box 35.10 Causes of pes planus ... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: What is the genetic inheritance pattern of Marfan syndrome?
back: Autosomal dominant, primarily resulting from mutations in the FBN1 gene with high penetrance but variable expressivity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 497 (Book Page): [Summary box 35.10 Causes of pes planus ... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: Distinguish the protein defect in Marfan syndrome from that in Osteogenesis Imperfecta (OI).
back:
● Marfan: Defective Fibrillin-1.
● OI: Qualitative or quantitative abnormality of Type I Collagen.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Osteogenesis imperfecta (brittle bone disease) represents a spectrum of conditions linked by a qualitative and/or quantitative abnormality of collagen production.]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: A tall adolescent presents with pectus excavatum and superior lens dislocation. What is the genetic basis?
back: Mutation in the FBN1 gene located on chromosome 15q21, affecting connective tissue microfibrils.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 497 (Book Page): [Summary box 35.10 Causes of pes planus ... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: What biochemical protein is systematically defective in patients with Marfan syndrome?
back: Fibrillin-1, a glycoprotein essential for forming elastic fibers and maintaining the structural integrity of connective tissue.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 497 (Book Page): [Summary box 35.10 Causes of pes planus ... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: What is the primary clinical diagnostic tool for Marfan syndrome?
back: The Ghent Criteria (nosology), which evaluates major and minor clinical features in skeletal, ocular, cardiovascular, and genetic systems.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 497 (Book Page): [Summary box 35.10 Causes of pes planus ... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: Why is generalized hyperlaxity a core phenotypic feature of the Marfan genetic defect?
back: Mutations in FBN1 lead to weak microfibrils, resulting in incompetent ligamentous and joint capsule structural support.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 497 (Book Page): [Summary box 35.10 Causes of pes planus ... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: Which specific foot deformity is associated with the hyperlaxity of Marfan syndrome?
back: Pes planus (flat foot), often occurring as a symptomatic or flexible deformity due to excessive ligamentous laxity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 497 (Book Page): [Summary box 35.10 Causes of pes planus ... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: How do Marfan mutations affect the Transforming Growth Factor-beta (TGF-β) pathway?
back: Fibrillin-1 deficiency results in failure to sequester TGF-β, leading to excessive signaling and subsequent connective tissue degradation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 497 (Book Page): [Summary box 35.10 Causes of pes planus ... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: On which chromosome is the gene responsible for Marfan syndrome located?
back: Chromosome 15 (specifically 15q21).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 497 (Book Page): [Summary box 35.10 Causes of pes planus ... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Define native joint septic arthritis.
back: Bacterial infection of a joint cavity resulting from haematogenous spread, direct inoculation (trauma/surgery), or local extension from adjacent osteomyelitis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 596 (Book Page): [septic arthritis, infection may follow direct ingress of bacteria after injury or surgery, or may result from discharge of an adjacent acute osteomyelitis into the joint. Particularly in neonates or the elderly, bacteraemia may infect a previously normal joint.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Which organism is the most common etiological agent of septic arthritis across all settings?
back: Staphylococcus aureus.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 597 (Book Page): [Staphylococcus aureus (commonest across all settings)]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Identify the most common etiological agent for septic arthritis in children under 4 years old.
back: Kingella kingae.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 597 (Book Page): [Kingella kingae Common cause of septic arthritis in children under 4 years]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Describe the physiological mechanism by which bacteria destroy articular cartilage in septic arthritis.
back: Bacteria produce toxins and stimulate leukocytes to release lytic proteases, which degrade the collagen matrix of the cartilage.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 596 (Book Page): [Toxins and lytic enzymes from bacteria cause early damage to articular cartilage.] Page 634 (Book Page): [Pus in a joint is destructive: the proteases produced by leukocytes destroy both the bacteria and the collagen matrix of the articular cartilage.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: What anatomical presentation in neonates defines suspected septic arthritis of the hip?
back: Pseudoparalysis; the limb is held immobile in the "position of comfort" (flexion and abduction).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 599 (Book Page): [The joint is held immobile in the ‘position of comfort’, with ‘pseudoparalysis’ in neonates.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Which specific etiological agent should be considered in septic arthritis patients with Sickle Cell disease?
back: Salmonella species.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 597 (Book Page): [Salmonella spp. (particularly associated with sickle cell disease)]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: What synovial fluid findings are diagnostic criteria for acute native joint septic arthritis?
back:
● White Cell Count: 50,000–150,000 cells/mm³
● Neutrophil Predominance: >90%.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 599 (Book Page): [A high WCC in joint fuid (e.g. 50–150 000 cells/mm3), with a neutrophil predominance (>90%), is characteristic of infection.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Explain the role of biofilm formation in the etiology of chronic bone and joint infections.
back: Bacteria adhere to dead bone or implants, forming a polysaccharide matrix (biofilm) that alters their metabolic state, increasing resistance to the host immune system and antibiotics.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 596 (Book Page): [Bacteria can adhere to dead bone or implant surfaces, forming a complex community enveloped in a polysaccharide matrix, known as a bioflm. These bacteria alter their metabolic state, making them more resistant both to the host immune system and to antibiotics.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: A 19-year-old active adult presents with a hot, swollen knee. Which etiological agent is a high-yield differential based on age and social history?
back: Neisseria gonorrhoeae (disseminated gonococcal infection).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 597 (Book Page): [Neisseria gonorrhoeae (consider risk factors for sexually transmitted infection)]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Why is septic arthritis considered a surgical emergency?
back: Pressure effects and leukocytic proteases cause irreversible ischaemic infarction (avascular necrosis) and cartilage matrix destruction within hours.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [Pus in a joint is destructive... AVN may occur secondary to pressure efects or ischaemic infarction. The treatment of a presumed septic arthritis therefore requires the prompt removal of pus from the joint]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: What is the clinical definition of Marfan syndrome?
back: A systemic autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder primarily affecting the skeletal, ocular, and cardiovascular systems.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Summary box 44.10 Causes of pes planus ... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: How does the dominant-negative effect explain the genetic basis of Marfan syndrome?
back: Mutant fibrillin-1 molecules interfere with the assembly and function of normal fibrillin-1 produced from the wild-type allele.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: Contrast the genetic inheritance of Marfan syndrome versus Homocystinuria.
back: Marfan syndrome is inherited in an Autosomal Dominant pattern, whereas Homocystinuria is Autosomal Recessive.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: A tall 15-year-old with joint hyperlaxity presents with sudden chest pain. What genetic syndrome is suspected?
back: Marfan syndrome; the patient is at critical risk for aortic root dilation and sudden aortic dissection.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: What are the primary diagnostic components of the Ghent nosology for Marfan syndrome?
back: Diagnosis focuses on family history, aortic root diameter (Z-score), ectopia lentis, and identified FBN1 mutations.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: Which specific gene and chromosome are involved in the genetic basis of Marfan syndrome?
back: The FBN1 gene, located on chromosome 15 (specifically 15q21.1).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: How does dysregulated TGF-̢ signaling contribute to the Marfan phenotype?
back: Fibrillin-1 deficiency leads to excessive free TGF-̢, stimulating overgrowth of long bones and degradation of the extracellular matrix.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: Differentiate the genetic defect in Marfan syndrome from Osteogenesis Imperfecta (OI).
back: Marfan syndrome results from FBN1 (fibrillin-1) mutations, while OI results from qualitative/quantitative abnormalities in Type I Collagen.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) represents a spectrum of conditions linked by a qualitative and/or quantitative abnormality of collagen production... Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: Describe the physiological loop involving microfibrils in Marfan syndrome.
back: FBN1 mutations disrupt microfibril assembly, which fails to sequester TGF-̢, causing systemic connective tissue weakening and overgrowth.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: Which specific protein defect defines the biochemical basis of Marfan syndrome?
back: Deficiency or defect in Fibrillin-1, a large glycoprotein essential for microfibril scaffolding in the extracellular matrix.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What defines the classic structural configuration of an exostosis in Hereditary Multiple Exostoses?
back: A cartilaginous cap sitting on a bony stalk; these may be pedunculated or sessile and occur at the growth plate.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Exostoses consisting of a cartilaginous cap on a bony stalk may be sessile or pedunculated. They grow as the child grows and may cause cosmetic or functional diffculties.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Which skeletal feature defines the 'ground-glass' appearance in McCune–Albright syndrome?
back: Polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, where normal medullary bone is replaced by fibrous stroma, often leading to limb deformity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 613 (Book Page): McCune–Albright syndrome... It is a localised defect in osteoblastic diferentiation and maturation in which normal bone is replaced by fbrous stroma. ... the diaphyseal lesions have a ‘ground-glass’ appearance.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Distinguish Enchondromatosis (Ollier’s) from Mafucci’s syndrome based on skeletal and soft tissue signs.
back:
● Ollier’s: Multiple enchondromas in tubular bones.
● Mafucci’s: Multiple enchondromas plus soft-tissue haemangiomas and lymphangiomas.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 613 (Book Page): Enchondromatosis (Ollier’s disease)... In Mafucci’s syndrome there are also soft-tissue haemangiomas and lymphangiomas.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: A 5-month-old's radiograph shows the femoral ossific nucleus outside the inner lower quadrant. Diagnosis?
back: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip (DDH); the nucleus is typically displaced lateral and superior to Perkins' and Hilgenreiner's lines.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): The femoral head (ossifc nucleus) of a normal hip lies in the inner lower quadrant. The right hip is normal; the left hip has developmental dysplasia of the hip.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What specific physeal growth failure results in the sharp tibia vara seen in Blount’s disease?
back: Disordered growth in the posteromedial proximal tibial physis, causing progressive angulation and intoeing.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 624 (Book Page): The aetiology of the disordered growth in the posteromedial proximal tibial physis is unknown. ... The child presents with progressive and often severe tibia vara with signifcant intoeing.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What is the classic clinical diagnostic sign for a discoid meniscus in a child?
back: A painful 'clunk' felt and heard on knee extension; typically involves the lateral meniscus.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 623 (Book Page): Discoid meniscus... invariably afects the lateral meniscus, which is abnormally thick and covers most of the tibial plateau. The child presents with a painful clunk on knee extension.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Which skeletal site and pathology defines Osgood–Schlatter disease?
back: Traction apophysitis at the tibial tubercle (the site of patellar tendon insertion), causing pain and swelling.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 623 (Book Page): Osgood–Schlatter disease is a traction apophysitis of the patellar tendon insertion. Pain, tenderness and swelling at the tibial tubercle... are diagnostic.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Contrast the tibial bow in Fibular Hemimelia versus Congenital Pseudarthrosis of the Tibia.
back:
● Fibular Hemimelia: Anteromedial apex bow.
● Congenital Pseudarthrosis: Anterolateral apex bow.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 624 (Book Page): Fibular hemimelia... the tibial bow has an anteromedial apex. ... Congenital pseudarthrosis of the tibia... presents with an anterolateral bow of the tibia.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What specific skeletal feature is absent in congenital radioulnar synostosis?
back: The proximal separation of the radius and ulna, leading to a total inability to pronate or supinate the forearm.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 628 (Book Page): Radioulnar synostosis... Failure of proximal separation of the embryonic radius and ulna means that the forearm has no ability to pronate/supinate.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Define the percentage of vertebral slip required to classify a Grade 2 Spondylolisthesis.
back: A slip of 26% to 50% of the upper vertebra over the one below.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 630 (Book Page): Table 44.13 Classifcation of spondylolisthesis according to severity of the slip. ... Grade 2: 26–50%

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What pathognomonic skeletal features characterize Köhler’s disease of the foot on plain radiograph?
back:
- Avascularity and flattening of the tarsal navicular bone
- Increased radiographic density (sclerosis) compared to surrounding bones
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 627 (Book Page): Köhler’s disease presents with dorsal forefoot pain and swelling in young children. The navicular becomes avascular with alteration in the ossifcation process.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Which specific skeletal feature on axial CT distinguishes a burst fracture from a simple compression fracture?
back:
- Increased interpedicular distance
- Retropulsion of bone fragments into the spinal canal
- Comminution of the vertebral body
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 400 (Book Page): Burst fractures are comminuted fractures of the vertebral body. They are characterised by widening of the distance between the pedicles and can be associated with retropulsion of bone fragments into the spinal canal.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Contrast the characteristic skeletal failure patterns of a Torus fracture versus a Greenstick fracture.
back:
- Torus (Buckle): Failure of the compression cortex leading to a bulge.
- Greenstick: Complete failure of the tension cortex with an intact compression hinge.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 421 (Book Page): Incomplete fractures are called greenstick, where one tension cortex fails. If the compression cortex buckles, they are called torus or buckle fractures.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What specific skeletal feature identifies a tarsal coalition in an adolescent presenting with a rigid flat foot?
back:
- Failure of segmentation between adjacent tarsal bones
- Presence of a bony, cartilaginous, or fibrous "bar" (e.g., calcaneonavicular)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 627 (Book Page): In tarsal coalition there is failure of segmentation of adjacent tarsal bones. ... The most common coalitions are talocalcaneal and calcaneonavicular.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What unique skeletal radiographic feature appears in children with Osteogenesis Imperfecta treated with cyclical bisphosphonates?
back:
- Dense horizontal "Zebra" or growth lines at the metaphyses
- Increased cortical thickness and bone mineral density
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): Cyclical bisphosphonate treatment decreases bone resorption and turnover. ... Multiple growth lines are visible in addition to intramedullary devices.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What skeletal feature defines an "open book" pelvic ring injury during radiographic assessment?
back:
- Widening of the pubic symphysis (typically >2 cm)
- Indicates external rotation of the iliac wings and SI ligament disruption
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 384 (Book Page): An ‘open book fracture’ is seen as a widening of the pubic symphysis or widening at the site of a fracture in the pubic ramus.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What skeletal wedging criteria differentiate structural Scheuermann’s kyphosis from postural adolescent kyphosis?
back:
- Fixed anterior vertebral wedging of ≥5°
- Involvement of at least three adjacent vertebral levels
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): Scheuermann’s disease presents as a progressive structural adolescent kyphosis characterised radiologically by >5° vertebral wedging at three adjacent levels.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Contrast the characteristic skeletal bowing direction in Congenital Pseudarthrosis of the Tibia versus Fibular Hemimelia.
back:
- Congenital Pseudarthrosis: Apex anterolateral tibial bow.
- Fibular Hemimelia: Apex anteromedial tibial bow (associated with short/absent fibula).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 624 (Book Page): [Fibular Hemimelia] the tibial bow has an anteromedial apex. ... [Congenital pseudarthrosis] the tibial bow has an anterolateral apex.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Define the skeletal remodelling loop established by the Hueter–Volkmann principle.
back:
- Compressive forces inhibit physeal bone growth
- Tensile forces stimulate physeal bone growth
- Directs the correction of paediatric angular deformities
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 609 (Book Page): Hueter–Volkmann principle: Compressive forces inhibit growth; Tensile forces stimulate growth.

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What are the three characteristic skeletal components of a pedunculated osteochondroma?
back:
- Bony stalk (peduncle)
- Cartilaginous cap at the apex
- Cortical and medullary continuity with the host bone
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 612 (Book Page): Exostoses consisting of a cartilaginous cap on a bony stalk may be sessile or pedunculated.

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: What is the clinical definition of septic arthritis?
back: Bacterial invasion of a joint space resulting in acute inflammation, purulence, and rapid destruction of articular cartilage.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 616 (Book Page): [Bacterial invasion of the bone. ... infection of native joints ... results from discharge of an adjacent acute osteomyelitis into the joint.] Page 634 (Book Page): [the proteases produced by leukocytes destroy both the bacteria and the collagen matrix of the articular cartilage.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Explain the primary mechanism by which septic arthritis destroys articular cartilage.
back: Host leukocytes produce proteases and lytic enzymes that destroy the collagen matrix of the articular cartilage.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [Pus in a joint is destructive: the proteases produced by leukocytes destroy both the bacteria and the collagen matrix of the articular cartilage.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Which four clinical predictors differentiate septic arthritis from transient synovitis of the hip?
back:
1. History of fever >38.5°C
2. Non-weight-bearing
3. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) >40 mm/h
4. White cell count (WCC) >12 × 10⁹/L
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [History of fever >38.5°C; Non-weight-bearing; Erythrocyte sedimentation rate >40 mm/h; White cell count >12 × 10 9 /L]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: How does septic arthritis typically present in a neonate?
back: Presentation involves "pseudoparalysis," where the infant holds the affected joint immobile in the position of comfort.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 619 (Book Page): [The joint is held immobile in the ‘position of comfort’, with ‘pseudoparalysis’ in neonates.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: What is the standard empirical antibiotic regimen for suspected osteoarticular infection in children under one year?
back: Intravenous Gram-positive coverage (cephalosporins or flucloxacillin) combined with gentamicin to cover Gram-negative organisms.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 624 (Book Page): [Empirical intravenous therapy against Gram-positive organisms is given (cephalosporins or flucloxacillin), adding gentamicin to cover Gram-negative organisms in children under 1 year.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: What synovial fluid white cell parameters are characteristic of septic arthritis?
back: A white cell count of 50,000–150,000 cells/mm³ with a neutrophil predominance exceeding 90%.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 619 (Book Page): [A high WCC in joint fluid (e.g. 50–150 000 cells/mm 3 ), with a neutrophil predominance (>90%), is characteristic of infection.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Why is synovial tissue sampling preferred over fluid aspiration for specific infections like tuberculosis?
back: Synovial tissue samples provide a significantly higher diagnostic yield for identifying mycobacteria or fungal organisms.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 618 (Book Page): [Synovial tissue samples are particularly important in producing a higher diagnostic yield for infection with mycobacteria or fungi.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Does the presence of crystals in synovial fluid exclude a diagnosis of septic arthritis?
back: No; crystals and bacterial infection may coexist, as crystals may be seen in infected joints with gout or pseudogout.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 619 (Book Page): [crystals may be seen in infected joints as well as in gout or pseudogout.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: How does intra-articular pus lead to avascular necrosis (AVN) of the epiphysis?
back: Accumulated pus increases intra-articular pressure, causing a tamponade effect or ischaemic infarction of epiphyseal vessels.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [AVN may occur secondary to pressure effects or ischaemic infarction. ... capsulotomy reduces the tamponade effect on the epiphyseal vessels.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Identify the most common causative organism for septic arthritis in native joints.
back: Staphylococcus aureus.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): [Staphylococcus aureus, are the most common cause of bone or joint infection in native tissue.] Page 634 (Book Page): [The most frequently identified organism is Staphylococcus aureus.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What is the characteristic radiographic shape of an extradural haematoma on CT imaging?
back: Lentiform (biconvex or lens-shaped) hyperdense lesion found between the skull and the brain.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page): [On CT, extradural haematomas appear as a lentiform (lens-shaped or biconvex) hyperdense lesion between the skull and the brain]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Describe the structural 'four-legged stool' model of the zygomatic bone anatomy.
back:
• Vertical: Zygomatic process and maxillary buttress.
• Horizontal: Infraorbital rim.
• Anteroposterior: Zygomatic arch.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 411 (Book Page): [The four legs comprise the zygomatic arch running anteroposteriorly, the zygomatic process running vertically to join the frontozygomatic (FZ) process... the infraorbital rim running horizontally and the maxillary buttress running vertically.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Contrast the characteristic CT shapes of acute subdural versus extradural haematomas.
back:
• Subdural: Diffuse concave (crescentic) appearance.
• Extradural: Biconvex (lentiform) shape constrained by dural adherence to skull sutures.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 388 (Book Page): [subdural blood is free to expand across the brain surface, giving a diffuse concave appearance.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Identify the skeletal injury indicated by 'patella alta' and a palpable tendon defect.
back: Complete rupture of the patellar tendon; the high-riding patella is caused by the unopposed proximal pull of the quadriceps.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 493 (Book Page): [A high-riding patella (patella alta) is present secondary to the unopposed pull of the quadriceps muscle... results in an inability to actively perform and maintain full knee extension.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: What pharmacological intervention is used to focalize high tone reduction in cerebral palsy?
back: Botulinum toxin; it temporarily prevents acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction to allow stretching of agonist muscles.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 632 (Book Page): [neuromuscular blockers such as botulinum toxin allow a focal reduction in tone by preventing acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction. The effect is temporary]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: List the components of the 'oculocardiac reflex' triad seen in pediatric orbital fractures.
back:
1. Bradycardia
2. Nausea
3. Syncope
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): [Inferior rectus muscle entrapment in children may present as the oculocardiac reflex: a triad of bradycardia, nausea and syncope.]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Which radiographic finding pathognomonically distinguishes a vertebral burst fracture from a simple compression fracture?
back: Widening of the interpedicular distance (distance between the pedicles) on an anteroposterior view.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 421 (Book Page): [Burst fractures... are characterised by widening of the distance between the pedicles and can be associated with retropulsion of bone fragments]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Contrast the apex direction of the tibial bow in Blount’s disease vs. Congenital Pseudarthrosis.
back:
• Blount’s disease: Anteromedial apex tibial bow.
• Congenital pseudarthrosis: Anterolateral apex tibial bow.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 624 (Book Page): [Blount’s disease – clinically, a sharp proximal tibial angulation... the tibial bow has an anteromedial apex. ... Congenital pseudarthrosis of the tibia – the tibial bow has an anterolateral apex]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Define the skeletal compensation resulting in 'miserable malalignment syndrome'.
back: Persistent femoral neck anteversion (internal rotation) coupled with compensatory external tibial torsion.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 610 (Book Page): [Persistent femoral neck anteversion... compensatory external tibial torsion may develop... symptoms of the miserable malalignment syndrome]

category: Identify the characteristic skeletal features
front: Q: Describe the anatomical fracture line boundaries of a Le Fort II injury.
back: Extends from the pterygoid plates through the inferior orbital rim and across the nasal bridge (pyramidal fracture).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 412 (Book Page): [Le Fort II involves the whole of the dentitionbearing portion of the maxilla and the nasal bones. The fracture line extends from the pterygoid plates to the inferior orbital rim and across the bridge of the nose.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: What is the clinical definition of native joint septic arthritis?
back: Bacterial infection of a joint, often arising from haematogenous dissemination, direct inoculation, or extension from an adjacent osteomyelitis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 599 (Book Page): [Bacterial infection of native joints occurs with an estimated incidence of 4–10 per 100 000 population per year in western Europe... Joint infection may arise as a result of haematogenous dissemination of bacteria from another focus...]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Describe the pathophysiological mechanism of joint destruction in septic arthritis.
back: Proteases produced by leukocytes destroy both the invading bacteria and the collagen matrix of the articular cartilage.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [Pus in a joint is destructive: the proteases produced by leukocytes destroy both the bacteria and the collagen matrix of the articular cartilage.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Contrast septic arthritis from transient synovitis using fever and weight-bearing criteria.
back: Septic arthritis is predicted by a fever >38.5°C and an inability to weight-bear.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [The clinical predictors of Kocher et al. (2004) for the diagnosis of septic arthritis: History of fever >38.5°C; Non-weight-bearing; Erythrocyte sedimentation rate >40 mm/h; White cell count >12 × 10 9 /L]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Which etiological agent is specifically associated with septic arthritis in sickle cell disease?
back: Salmonella species.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 597 (Book Page): [Salmonella spp. (particularly associated with sickle cell disease)]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: What are the initial empirical antibiotic choices for community-acquired joint infection?
back: Co-amoxiclav or Ceftriaxone.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 599 (Book Page): [Agents such as co-amoxiclav or ceftriaxone are appropriate for most community-acquired infection.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: What synovial fluid white cell count is characteristic of acute septic arthritis?
back: 50,000–150,000 cells/mm³ with a neutrophil predominance exceeding 90%.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 599 (Book Page): [A high WCC in joint fuid (e.g. 50–150 000 cells/mm 3 ), with a neutrophil predominance (>90%), is characteristic of infection.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Why is neonatal septic arthritis essentially the same as proximal femoral osteomyelitis?
back: Vascular channels pass through the physis in neonates, allowing infection to spread easily from the metaphysis into the joint.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 635 (Book Page): [In the neonate, proximal femoral osteomyelitis and septic arthritis are essentially the same condition... vascular channels pass through the physis, connecting the metaphysis with the epiphysis.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Which organism is a common cause of septic arthritis in children under four years?
back: Kingella kingae.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 597 (Book Page): [Kingella kingae: Common cause of septic arthritis in children under 4 years]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: How does the formation of a biofilm impact bacterial resistance in joint infections?
back: Bacteria alter their metabolic state within the polysaccharide matrix, increasing resistance to both host immunity and antibiotics.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 596 (Book Page): [These bacteria alter their metabolic state, making them more resistant both to the host immune system and to antibiotics.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Identify the most common etiological agent overall for native joint septic arthritis.
back: Staphylococcus aureus.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 597 (Book Page): [Staphylococcus aureus (commonest across all settings)]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: Define Marfan syndrome.
back:
● Multisystem autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder
● Characterized by systemic hyperlaxity, skeletal, ocular, and cardiovascular abnormalities
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 497 (Book Page): [Summary box 35.10 Causes of pes planus ● ... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: What is the genetic basis of Marfan syndrome?
back:
● Mutations in the FBN1 gene
● Affects the production and assembly of fibrillin-1 protein
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 497 (Book Page): [Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: On which chromosome is the gene for Marfan syndrome located?
back:
● Chromosome 15
● Specific locus is 15q21.1
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 497 (Book Page): [Summary box 35.10 ... Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: Describe the inheritance pattern of Marfan syndrome.
back:
● Autosomal dominant
● Characterized by high penetrance and variable expressivity
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 497 (Book Page): [Summary box 35.10 ... Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: What specific protein deficiency causes the hyperlaxity seen in Marfan syndrome?
back:
● Fibrillin-1
● Leads to defective extracellular microfibrils and weak elastic fibers
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 497 (Book Page): [Summary box 35.10 ... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: How does the FBN1 mutation affect Transforming Growth Factor-beta (TGF-β)?
back:
● Causes increased (dysregulated) TGF-β signaling
● Leads to excessive extracellular matrix degradation
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 497 (Book Page): [Summary box 35.10 ... Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: What skeletal manifestation of Marfan's is highlighted in clinical MSK examinations?
back:
● Generalized ligamentous hyperlaxity
● Often presents as symptomatic pes planus (flat feet)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 497 (Book Page): [Summary box 35.10 Causes of pes planus ● ... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: Contrast the genetic defect in Marfan syndrome with Osteogenesis Imperfecta (OI).
back:
● Marfan: Defect in Fibrillin-1 (microfibrils)
● OI: Defect in Type I Collagen genes (COL1A1/COL1A2)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): [Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) ... linked by a qualitative and/or quantitative abnormality of collagen production.]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: What clinical framework is utilized for the definitive diagnosis of Marfan syndrome?
back:
● Revised Ghent Criteria
● Integrates systemic scores, ectopia lentis, and FBN1 mutation
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 497 (Book Page): [Summary box 35.10 ... Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: A patient presents with hyperlaxity and pes planus. What genetic syndrome should be suspected?
back:
● Marfan’s syndrome
● Likely FBN1 mutation on chromosome 15
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 497 (Book Page): [Summary box 35.10 Causes of pes planus ● ... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: What is the clinical definition of Marfan syndrome?
back: An autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder characterized as a hyperlaxity syndrome, presenting with multi-systemic involvement of the skeletal, ocular, and cardiovascular systems.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 611 (Book Page): [Summary box 44.10: Causes of pes planus ● ... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: What is the primary genetic basis of Marfan syndrome?
back: Mutations in the FBN1 gene which encodes the protein fibrillin-1, a structural component of extracellular microfibrils essential for tissue integrity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 611 (Book Page): [Summary box 44.10: Causes of pes planus ● ... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: On which chromosome is the genetic defect for Marfan syndrome located?
back: Chromosome 15, specifically at the locus 15q21.1.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 611 (Book Page): [Summary box 44.10: Causes of pes planus ● ... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: What is the inheritance pattern of Marfan syndrome?
back: Autosomal dominant, meaning an affected parent has a 50 percent chance of passing the condition to offspring.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 611 (Book Page): [Summary box 44.10: Causes of pes planus ● ... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: How does the FBN1 mutation in Marfan syndrome affect cellular signaling?
back: Fibrillin-1 deficiency results in the overactivation of TGF-beta (Transforming Growth Factor Beta) signaling, leading to excessive growth and weakened connective tissue matrix.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 611 (Book Page): [Summary box 44.10: Causes of pes planus ● ... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: Which specific foot deformity is associated with Marfan’s hyperlaxity?
back: Flexible pes planus (flat foot), caused by excessive ligamentous laxity in the tarsal and midfoot joints.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 611 (Book Page): [Summary box 44.10: Causes of pes planus ● ... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: What is the cardinal ocular feature used to define Marfan syndrome?
back: Ectopia lentis (lens subluxation), which typically occurs in an upward and outward direction.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 611 (Book Page): [Summary box 44.10: Causes of pes planus ● ... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: What are the life-threatening cardiovascular hallmarks of Marfan syndrome?
back: Aortic root dilation and thoracic aortic aneurysm, which significantly increase the risk of aortic dissection.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 611 (Book Page): [Summary box 44.10: Causes of pes planus ● ... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: Describe the Steinberg sign used in the clinical diagnosis of Marfan syndrome.
back: Positive 'Thumb Sign': the distal phalanx of the thumb extends beyond the ulnar border of the hand when the thumb is adducted across the palm.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 611 (Book Page): [Summary box 44.10: Causes of pes planus ● ... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define Marfan syndrome and describe its genetic basis
front: Q: Which international clinical standard is used to confirm a diagnosis of Marfan syndrome?
back: The Revised Ghent Criteria, which assesses aortic root diameter, ectopia lentis, FBN1 mutations, and systemic scoring.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 611 (Book Page): [Summary box 44.10: Causes of pes planus ● ... Hyperlaxity syndrome, e.g. Marfan’s syndrome]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Define native joint septic arthritis based on its underlying pathology.
back:
* Bacterial invasion of the joint space.
* Leads to acute inflammation and purulence.
* Results in proteolysis and destruction of the articular collagen matrix.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 616 (Book Page): [septic arthritis, infection may follow direct ingress of bacteria... or discharge of an adjacent acute osteomyelitis into the joint.] Page 634 (Book Page): [Pus in a joint is destructive: the proteases produced by leukocytes destroy both the bacteria and the collagen matrix of the articular cartilage.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Describe the pathophysiological mechanism of cartilage destruction in joint sepsis.
back:
* Bacterial toxins and lytic enzymes cause initial damage.
* Leukocytes produce proteases that destroy the collagen matrix.
* Intracapsular pressure effects or infarction may lead to avascular necrosis (AVN).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [Pus in a joint is destructive: the proteases produced by leukocytes destroy both the bacteria and the collagen matrix of the articular cartilage. AVN may occur secondary to pressure efects or ischaemic infarction.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Contrast the etiological agents typically found in early versus delayed prosthetic joint infections.
back:
* Early (<3 months): Virulent organisms, primarily S. aureus.
* Delayed (3–24 months): Low-virulence organisms, such as coagulase-negative staphylococci or cutibacteria.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 621 (Book Page): [Early infections... usually caused by virulent organisms (e.g. S. aureus). ... Delayed infections are more characteristically due to low-virulence organisms (e.g. coagulase-negative staphylococci or cutibacteria).]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: A child has a fever >38.5°C and is non-weight-bearing; list the remaining Kocher criteria used to predict septic arthritis.
back:
1. ESR >40 mm/h.
2. White cell count >12 × 10⁹/L.
* If all 4 predictors are positive, the probability of joint sepsis is 93%.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [The clinical predictors of Kocher et al. (2004)... History of fever >38.5°C; Non-weight-bearing; Erythrocyte sedimentation rate >40 mm/h; White cell count >12 × 109/L]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: In clinically stable bone infections, what is the mandatory pharmacological prerequisite before taking surgical samples?
back:
* Antibiotics must be stopped at least 2 weeks prior to biopsy or surgery.
* This prevents falsely negative microbiological cultures.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 620 (Book Page): [For patients who have already been started on antibiotics... if safe to do so, antibiotics should be stopped at least 2 weeks before biopsy or surgery.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: What are the diagnostic synovial fluid white cell criteria characteristic of native joint septic arthritis?
back:
* White Cell Count (WCC): 50,000–150,000 cells/mm³.
* Neutrophil predominance: >90%.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 620 (Book Page): [A high WCC in joint fuid (e.g. 50–150 000 cells/mm3), with a neutrophil predominance (>90%), is characteristic of infection.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Identify specific etiological agents associated with septic arthritis in sickle cell disease and children under 4 years.
back:
* Sickle cell disease: Salmonella spp.
* Children <4 years: Kingella kingae (increasingly prevalent following Hib vaccination).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 618 (Book Page): [Salmonella spp. (particularly associated with sickle cell disease); Kingella kingae Common cause of septic arthritis in children under 4 years.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Why is neonatal proximal femoral osteomyelitis often clinically identical to septic arthritis?
back:
* Vascular channels pass through the physis, connecting the metaphysis to the epiphysis.
* Infection spreads directly from the bone into the joint once the periosteum is breached.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 635 (Book Page): [In the neonate, vascular channels pass through the physis, connecting the metaphysis with the epiphysis... In the neonate, proximal femoral osteomyelitis and septic arthritis are essentially the same condition.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Explain the physiological transition bacteria undergo when forming a biofilm on dead bone or implants.
back:
* Bacteria adhere and form a polysaccharide matrix.
* They alter their metabolic state, becoming resistant to the host immune system and antibiotics.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): [Bacteria can adhere to dead bone or implant surfaces, forming a complex community enveloped in a polysaccharide matrix, known as a bioflm. These bacteria alter their metabolic state, making them more resistant]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Which organism is the most frequently identified pathogen across all settings of bone and joint infection?
back: * Staphylococcus aureus.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): [Staphylococcus aureus (commonest across all settings).] Page 634 (Book Page): [The most frequently identifed organism is Staphylococcus aureus.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: What is the clinical definition of septic arthritis?
back: It is a bacterial infection of a native joint, typically arising from haematogenous spread, direct inoculation, or extension from adjacent osteomyelitis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 621 (Book Page): [Bacterial infection of native joints... Joint infection may arise as a result of haematogenous dissemination of bacteria from another focus... or may occur as a result of direct inoculation or local extension from an infected source.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: How does septic arthritis progress from bacterial invasion to cartilage destruction?
back: Bacteria and leukocytes release proteases that destroy the joint's collagen matrix. Irreversible destruction occurs rapidly if pus is not promptly drained.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [Pus in a joint is destructive: the proteases produced by leukocytes destroy both the bacteria and the collagen matrix of the articular cartilage.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Contrast the common pathogens in children under 4 versus adults with septic arthritis.
back:
• Children <4: Kingella kingae is frequently identified.
• Adults: Staphylococcus aureus remains the most common overall pathogen.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 618 (Book Page): [Kingella kingae Common cause of septic arthritis in children under 4 years] and Page 634 (Book Page): [The most frequently identified organism is Staphylococcus aureus.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Which organism should be suspected in septic arthritis associated with Sickle Cell Disease?
back: Salmonella species. These are particularly over-represented as aetiological agents of bone and joint infection in these patients.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 618 (Book Page): [Salmonella spp. (particularly associated with sickle cell disease)]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: What adjustment is made to empiric antibiotics for septic arthritis in infants under one year?
back: Gentamicin is added to standard Gram-positive coverage (like flucloxacillin) to ensure protection against Gram-negative Enterobacteriaceae.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 625 (Book Page): [Empirical intravenous therapy against Gram-positive organisms is given (cephalosporins or flucloxacillin), adding gentamicin to cover Gram-negative organisms in children under 1 year.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Identify the synovial fluid leukocyte parameters characteristic of septic arthritis.
back:
• White Cell Count (WCC): 50,000–150,000 cells/mm³.
• Neutrophil predominance: >90%.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 621 (Book Page): [A high WCC in joint fluid (e.g. 50–150 000 cells/mm3), with a neutrophil predominance (>90%), is characteristic of infection.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Apply the Kocher criteria to determine the probability of pediatric joint sepsis.
back:
High risk (93%) involves: 
• Fever >38.5°C 
• Non-weight-bearing status 
• ESR >40 mm/h 
• WCC >12 × 10⁹/L.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [History of fever >38.5°C, Non-weight-bearing, Erythrocyte sedimentation rate >40 mm/h, White cell count >12 × 10 9 /L]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Differentiate the primary origin of septic arthritis in neonates versus adults.
back:
• Neonates: Often secondary to direct spread from adjacent proximal femoral osteomyelitis.
• Adults: Primarily haematogenous dissemination from a distant focus.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 635 (Book Page): [In the neonate, proximal femoral osteomyelitis and septic arthritis are essentially the same condition] and Page 621 (Book Page): [arise as a result of haematogenous dissemination... from another focus]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Why can septic arthritis of the hip lead to avascular necrosis (AVN)?
back: Purulent material increases intra-articular pressure, causing tamponade of the epiphyseal vessels, resulting in ischaemic infarction of the bone.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [AVN may occur secondary to pressure effects or ischaemic infarction.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Which native joints are most frequently affected by septic arthritis?
back:
• Adults and children: The knee joint.
• Neonates: The hip joint.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 621 (Book Page): [In children and adults, the knee joint is most frequently affected, whereas in neonates it is the hip.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Define native joint septic arthritis and identify its primary pathophysiology.
back: Septic arthritis is an acute bacterial invasion of a joint space. It results in inflammatory synovial proliferation, purulence, and rapid enzymatic destruction of the articular cartilage.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 596 (Book Page): [Acute osteomyelitis occurs when pathogenic organisms cause infection, leading to infammation in the bone and surrounding tissues... In septic arthritis, infection may follow direct ingress of bacteria... or may result from discharge of an adjacent acute osteomyelitis into the joint.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Identify the most common etiological agent for native bone and joint infections across all age groups.
back: Staphylococcus aureus is the most frequently identified pathogen in native tissue infections.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 596 (Book Page): [Virulent Gram-positive organisms, particularly Staphylococcus aureus, are the most common cause of bone or joint infection in native tissue.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: How does the presence of pus within a joint space cause rapid cartilage destruction?
back: Leukocytes within the purulent joint fluid produce proteases that destroy both the invading bacteria and the collagen matrix of the articular cartilage.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [Pus in a joint is destructive: the proteases produced by leukocytes destroy both the bacteria and the collagen matrix of the articular cartilage.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Which specific gram-negative pathogen is a prevalent cause of septic arthritis in children under age 4?
back: Kingella kingae is a common cause in this age group, replacing Haemophilus influenzae which has been largely eliminated by vaccination.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [The Haemophilus infuenzae type B (Hib) vaccine has essentially eliminated H. infuenzae as a cause of infection, but in some countries Kingella kingae has taken its place.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Name the pathogen classically associated with bone and joint infections in patients with sickle cell disease.
back: Salmonella species are highly associated with osteoarticular infections in patients suffering from sickle cell disease.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 597 (Book Page): [Salmonella spp. (particularly associated with sickle cell disease)]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: What are the primary etiological agents in delayed-onset prosthetic joint infections (3–24 months post-surgery)?
back: Low-virulence skin commensals, such as coagulase-negative staphylococci or Cutibacterium acnes.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 600 (Book Page): [Delayed infections are more characteristically due to low-virulence organisms (e.g. coagulase-negative staphylococci or cutibacteria).]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: What pathological structure do bacteria form on implants to resist host immunity and antibiotic therapy?
back: A biofilm. This is a complex community of bacteria enveloped in a polysaccharide matrix on a surface, where they alter their metabolic state to increase resistance.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 596 (Book Page): [Bacteria can adhere to dead bone or implant surfaces, forming a complex community enveloped in a polysaccharide matrix, known as a bioflm. These bacteria alter their metabolic state, making them more resistant both to the host immune system and to antibiotics.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
