front: Q: What is the most common route of bacterial spread leading to native joint septic arthritis?
back: Haematogenous dissemination (blood-borne spread) from a distant site of infection, such as endocarditis or respiratory tract infections.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 599 (Book Page): [Joint infection may arise as a result of haematogenous dissemination of bacteria from another focus (e.g. endocarditis)]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Besides S. aureus, which organism group is a common cause of joint sepsis in neonates?
back: Streptococcal infections (specifically Beta-haemolytic streptococci like Streptococcus agalactiae).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [The most frequently identifed organism is Staphylococcus aureus. Streptococcal infection is also common and other organisms are more prevalent in certain age groups, e.g. the neonate]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Which gram-negative diplococcus causes septic arthritis specifically in young, sexually active adults?
back: Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 597 (Book Page): [Neisseria gonorrhoeae (consider risk factors for sexually transmitted infection)]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Define septic arthritis and identify its most common etiological agent across all age groups.
back:
- Definition: Bacterial invasion of a native or prosthetic joint space causing acute inflammation. 
- Most common pathogen: Staphylococcus aureus.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 596 (Book Page): [virulent Gram-positive organisms, particularly Staphylococcus aureus, are the most common cause of bone or joint infection in native tissue.] Page 634 (Book Page): [The most frequently identifed organism is Staphylococcus aureus.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: By what mechanism do bacteria and inflammatory cells cause irreversible cartilage destruction in septic arthritis?
back:
- Leukocyte-released proteases and bacterial toxins degrade the articular collagen matrix. 
- High intra-articular pressure causes ischaemic infarction and avascular necrosis (AVN).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [Pus in a joint is destructive: the proteases produced by leukocytes destroy both the bacteria and the collagen matrix of the articular cartilage. AVN may occur secondary to pressure efects or ischaemic infarction.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Identify the specific etiological agent characteristically associated with septic arthritis in patients with Sickle Cell Disease.
back:
- Salmonella species (highly characteristic association). 
- Staphylococcus aureus (remains the most frequent overall even in these patients).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 597 (Book Page): [Table 43.1 Salmonella spp. (particularly associated with sickle cell disease)] Page 634 (Book Page): [The most frequently identifed organism is Staphylococcus aureus. ... children with sickle cell disease are at increased risk.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Define septic arthritis and its primary mode of bacterial acquisition.
back: A bacterial infection of a joint typically occurring via haematogenous spread, direct inoculation (trauma/surgery), or extension from an adjacent bone infection.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 599 (Book Page): [Joint infection may arise as a result of haematogenous dissemination of bacteria from another focus... or may occur as a result of direct inoculation or local extension from an infected source]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: How does purulence within a joint cause rapid destruction of articular cartilage?
back: Leukocytes within the pus produce proteases that destroy both the invading bacteria and the collagen matrix of the articular cartilage.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [Pus in a joint is destructive: the proteases produced by leukocytes destroy both the bacteria and the collagen matrix of the articular cartilage.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Identify the most common etiological agent of native joint septic arthritis.
back: Staphylococcus aureus is the most frequently identified pathogen across all age groups in native joint infections.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [The most frequently identifed organism is Staphylococcus aureus.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: A neonate presents with pseudoparalysis of the hip. Identify the likely etiological link.
back: Septic arthritis arising from proximal femoral osteomyelitis; in neonates, vascular channels connect the metaphysis and epiphysis, allowing direct spread.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 635 (Book Page): [In the neonate, proximal femoral osteomyelitis and septic arthritis are essentially the same condition]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Which antibiotic is added to covers Gram-negative organisms in infants under one year?
back: Gentamicin is added to cephalosporins or flucloxacillin to provide necessary coverage for Gram-negative bacilli in this age group.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 603 (Book Page): [Empirical intravenous therapy against Gram-positive organisms is given (cephalosporins or fucloxacillin), adding gentamicin to cover Gram-negative organisms in children under 1 year.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Which organism has increasingly replaced Haemophilus influenzae as a cause of joint infection?
back: Kingella kingae is now a common cause of septic arthritis in children, particularly following the implementation of Hib vaccines.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [The Haemophilus infuenzae type B (Hib) vaccine has essentially eliminated H. infuenzae... but in some countries Kingella kingae has taken its place.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: How does joint sepsis lead to avascular necrosis (AVN) of intra-articular epiphyses?
back: AVN occurs secondary to increased intra-articular pressure effects or direct ischaemic infarction of the epiphyseal vessels.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [AVN may occur secondary to pressure efects or ischaemic infarction.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: A patient presents with insidious onset 'boggy' joint swelling. Identify the causative agent.
back: Mycobacterium tuberculosis; it typically presents with malaise, weight loss, boggy joint swelling, and muscle wasting.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 636 (Book Page): [The clinical presentation is often insidious, with malaise and weight loss combined with a boggy joint swelling, muscle wasting and joint contractures.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Which specific patient population is at significantly increased risk for Salmonella septic arthritis?
back: Patients with sickle cell disease have a markedly increased susceptibility to joint infections caused by Salmonella species.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 597 (Book Page): [Salmonella spp. (particularly associated with sickle cell disease)]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Why is septic arthritis common during osteomyelitis of the proximal femur or shoulder?
back: Because their metaphyses are intracapsular, permitting infection to spread directly into the joint once the bone periosteum is breached.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 635 (Book Page): [The metaphysis of a long bone may be intracapsular and infection may spread easily into the joint once the periosteum is breached.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: What is the clinical definition of native joint septic arthritis?
back:
Bacterial invasion of a joint space resulting in:
- Acute inflammatory destruction of articular cartilage.
- Accumulation of purulent material (pus).
- Severe pain on active/passive motion.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 596 (Book Page): [In septic arthritis, infection may follow direct ingress of bacteria after injury or surgery, or may result from discharge of an adjacent acute osteomyelitis into the joint.] Page 634 (Book Page): [Pus in a joint is destructive: the proteases produced by leu - kocytes destroy both the bacteria and the collagen matrix of the articular cartilage.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Which specific organism is the most common etiological agent of septic arthritis across all age groups?
back:
Staphylococcus aureus.
- Highly virulent Gram-positive cocci.
- Most frequent pathogen in both native tissue and implant-associated infections.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 599 (Book Page): [The most common organism is Staphylococcus aureus.] Page 634 (Book Page): [The most frequently identifed organism is Staphylococcus aureus.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: What is the most common etiological agent for septic arthritis in children under 4 years old?
back:
Kingella kingae.
- It has emerged as a leading cause in this age group, replacing Haemophilus influenzae following the Hib vaccine.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 597 (Book Page): [Kingella kingae Common cause of septic arthritis in children under 4 years.] Page 634 (Book Page): [The Haemophilus infuenzae type B (Hib) vaccine has essentially eliminated H. infuenzae as a cause of infection, but in some countries Kingella kingae has taken its place.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Identify the three primary routes of bacterial entry into a joint space.
back:
1. Hematogenous dissemination (e.g., from endocarditis).
2. Direct inoculation (e.g., trauma, surgery, or injection).
3. Contiguous spread (e.g., from adjacent osteomyelitis).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 599 (Book Page): [Joint infection may arise as a result of haematogenous dissemination of bacteria from another focus... or may occur as a result of direct inoculation or local extension from an infected source (e.g. traumatic wound or adjacent osteomyelitis).]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: What synovial fluid white cell count (WCC) and differential are characteristic of acute septic arthritis?
back:
- WCC: 50,000–150,000 cells/mm³.
- Differential: Neutrophil predominance (>90%).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 599 (Book Page): [A high WCC in joint fuid (e.g. 50–150 000 cells/mm 3 ), with a neutrophil predominance (>90%), is characteristic of infection.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: In patients with sickle cell disease, which specific Gram-negative organism is a frequent cause of bone/joint infection?
back:
Salmonella species.
- These patients are at a specifically increased risk for osteoarticular infections involving this pathogen.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 597 (Book Page): [Salmonella spp. (particularly associated with sickle cell disease)] Page 634 (Book Page): [Neonates, children with immunocompromise and those with sickle cell disease are at increased risk.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: What mechanism is responsible for the rapid destruction of the articular collagen matrix in septic arthritis?
back:
- Release of bacterial toxins.
- Proteases produced by host leukocytes (white blood cells).
- Ischaemic infarction/necrosis due to high intra-articular pressure.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [Pus in a joint is destructive: the proteases produced by leu - kocytes destroy both the bacteria and the collagen matrix of the articular cartilage. AVN may occur secondary to pressure efects or ischaemic infarction.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Which etiological agent is most commonly associated with septic arthritis in neonates?
back:
Group B Streptococcus (Streptococcus agalactiae).
- Often associated with neonatal bacteraemia and direct spread into intracapsular metaphyses.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 597 (Book Page): [β -haemolytic streptococci (e.g. Streptococcus pyogenes, Streptococcus agalactiae)] Page 634 (Book Page): [Streptococcal infection is also common and other organisms are more prevalent in certain age groups, e.g. the neonate.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Describe the classic clinical hallmark of acute septic arthritis during physical examination.
back:
- Reluctance to weight-bear or move the joint.
- Extreme pain upon any attempt at active or passive movement.
- Joint held in a characteristic "position of comfort."
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 599 (Book Page): [The joint is held immobile in the ‘position of comfort’... There is severe pain if any attempt is made to move the afected joint actively or passively.]

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
front: Q: Why are synovial tissue samples sometimes preferred over fluid aspiration for microbiological diagnosis?
back:
Tissue samples provide a higher diagnostic yield for specific or fastidious organisms, including:
- Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
- Fungal species (e.g., Candida).
- Slow-growing anaerobes like C. acnes.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 597 (Book Page): [Synovial tissue samples are particularly important in producing a higher diagnostic yield for infection with mycobacteria or fungi.]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: What is the primary mechanism of cartilage destruction in acute septic arthritis?
back:
- Bacterial toxins/lytic enzymes cause initial damage
- Leukocyte-produced proteases destroy the collagen matrix
- Synovial inflammation accelerates cartilage loss
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): [Toxins and lytic enzymes from bacteria cause early damage to articular cartilage.] ... Page 620 (Book Page): [the proteases produced by leu - kocytes destroy both the bacteria and the collagen matrix of the articular cartilage.]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: Describe the sequence of bacterial invasion in a native joint.
back:
- Haematogenous seeding from distant focus (commonest)
- Direct inoculation (trauma/surgery)
- Local extension from adjacent acute osteomyelitis
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 620 (Book Page): [Joint infection may arise as a result of haematogenous dis - semination of bacteria from another focus (e.g. endocarditis) or may occur as a result of direct inoculation or local exten - sion from an infected source (e.g. traumatic wound or adjacent osteomyelitis).]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: Differentiate synovial fluid in septic arthritis vs. other inflammatory conditions.
back:
- WCC: 50,000–150,000 cells/mm³
- Neutrophil predominance: >90%
- Presence of crystals does NOT exclude infection
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 620 (Book Page): [A high WCC in joint fuid (e.g. 50–150 000 cells/mm 3 ), with a neutrophil predominance (>90%), is characteristic of infection. However, other infam - matory conditions can also cause a raised cell count, and crystals may be seen in infected joints as well as in gout or pseudogout.]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: What defines the 'pseudoparalysis' presentation in neonatal septic arthritis?
back:
- Joint held immobile in the position of comfort
- Severe pain upon active or passive movement
- Often involves the hip joint
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 620 (Book Page): [The joint is held immobile in the ‘position of comfort’, with ‘pseudoparalysis’ in neonates. There is severe pain if any attempt is made to move the afected joint actively or passively. ... in neonates it is the hip.]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: What is the mandatory immediate procedural step for confirmed purulence in a joint?
back:
- Formal surgical washout (irrigation)
- Maintenance of free drainage (capsulotomy or aspiration)
- Initiation of empirical antibiotics AFTER sampling
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [The treatment of a presumed septic arthritis therefore requires the prompt removal of pus from the joint and appropriate adequate antibiotic therapy. ... if pus is confrmed, a formal washout is mandatory; standard teaching states that the joint must be opened, irrigated and free drainage encouraged via the capsulotomy.]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: List the Kocher clinical predictors for pediatric septic arthritis diagnosis.
back:
1. History of fever >38.5°C
2. Inability to weight-bear
3. ESR >40 mm/h
4. WCC >12 × 10⁹/L
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [The clinical predictors of Kocher et al. (2004) for the diagnosis of septic arthritis: History of fever >38.5°C, Non-weight-bearing, Erythrocyte sedimentation rate >40 mm/h, White cell count >12 × 10 9 /L]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: How does septic arthritis lead to Avascular Necrosis (AVN) of epiphyses?
back:
- Intra-articular pus increases joint pressure
- Causes tamponade effect on epiphyseal vessels
- Leads to secondary ischaemic infarction
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [AVN may occur secondary to pressure efects or ischaemic infarction. ... the joint must be opened, irrigated and free drainage encouraged... Joint instability, particularly in the hip joint, may require the reduced joint to be splinted]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: Why might a joint effusion occur without identifiable bacteria in acute osteomyelitis?
back:
- Termed a 'sympathetic effusion'
- Result of reactive inflammation from adjacent metaphyseal infection
- Requires differentiation from direct intracapsular spread
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [The diferentiation between the two may be difcult and a sympathetic joint efusion may occur with metaphyseal osteomyelitis. Thus, if there are no organ - isms seen on microscopy of a joint aspirate, the possibility of a coexisting osteomyelitis must be considered.]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: Explain the role of biofilms in pathogenesis on prosthetic materials.
back:
- Bacteria adhere to dead bone/implants
- Form community in a polysaccharide matrix
- Altered metabolic state increases antibiotic and immune resistance
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): [Bacteria can adhere to dead bone or implant surfaces, forming a complex community enveloped in a polysaccharide matrix, known as a bioflm. These bacteria alter their metabolic state, making them more resistant both to the host immune system and to antibiotics.]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: Which organism is most commonly cultured in native joint septic arthritis?
back:
- Staphylococcus aureus (most frequent across all ages)
- Kingella kingae (emerging in children under 4)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [The most frequently identifed organism is Staphylococcus aureus. ... H. infuenzae type B (Hib) vaccine has essentially eliminated H. infuenzae... in some countries Kingella kingae has taken its place.]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: What are the three primary routes of bacterial entry in native joint septic arthritis?
back:
- Haematogenous dissemination (most common)
- Direct inoculation (trauma or surgery)
- Local extension (e.g., from adjacent osteomyelitis)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 599 (Book Page): [Joint infection may arise as a result of haematogenous dissemination of bacteria from another focus... or may occur as a result of direct inoculation or local extension from an infected source (e.g. traumatic wound or adjacent osteomyelitis).]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: Which host components are primarily responsible for destroying articular cartilage during septic arthritis?
back:
- Proteases produced by host leukocytes
- Bacterial toxins and lytic enzymes
- These degrade the collagen matrix of the cartilage
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [Pus in a joint is destructive: the proteases produced by leukocytes destroy both the bacteria and the collagen matrix of the articular cartilage. Toxins and lytic enzymes from bacteria cause early damage to articular cartilage.]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: How does acute osteomyelitis lead to the formation of dead bone (sequestrum)?
back:
- Medullary abscess increases pressure
- Pus tracks through cortex, elevating the periosteum
- Periosteal elevation devascularizes cortical bone, causing death
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 596 (Book Page): [The medullary bone may form abscesses and pus may track through the cortex to form periosteal elevation and soft-tissue extension. This process will devascularise the cortical bone, causing bone death – the characteristic feature of chronic osteomyelitis.]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: Why are neonates uniquely prone to concurrent osteomyelitis and septic arthritis in the hip?
back:
- Vascular channels cross the physis
- Metaphysis of the proximal femur is intracapsular
- Breached periosteum allows easy spread into the joint
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 635 (Book Page): [The metaphysis of a long bone may be intracapsular and infection may spread easily into the joint once the periosteum is breached. In the neonate, proximal femoral osteomyelitis and septic arthritis are essentially the same condition]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: What two mechanisms lead to avascular necrosis (AVN) in a septic joint?
back:
- Direct pressure effects from intra-articular pus
- Ischaemic infarction of epiphyseal vessels
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [AVN may occur secondary to pressure effects or ischaemic infarction. The treatment of a presumed septic arthritis therefore requires the prompt removal of pus from the joint]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: Define the 'biofilm' community found on infected dead bone or implants.
back:
- Bacteria in a polysaccharide matrix
- Altered metabolic state
- High resistance to host immune cells and antibiotics
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 596 (Book Page): [Bacteria can adhere to dead bone or implant surfaces, forming a complex community enveloped in a polysaccharide matrix, known as a biofilm. These bacteria alter their metabolic state, making them more resistant both to the host immune system and to antibiotics.]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: What is an 'involucrum' and what stimulates its formation?
back:
- Layer of new bone laid down around infected bone
- Stimulated by periosteal elevation from pus or trauma
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 635 (Book Page): [periosteal elevation is a potent stimulus for new bone formation. In cases of untreated or chronic infection this new bone or involucrum may surround the dead bone]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: A patient presents with a chronically discharging sinus and fragments of bone. What is this fragment termed?
back: - Sequestrum (dead fragment of bone separated from living tissue by infection)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 596 (Book Page): [The infected bone reacts to the infection by separating dead fragments of bone (sequestration) and forming sinuses to drain pus and discharge small bone fragments.]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: Describe the positive feedback loop between infection and bone death in chronic osteomyelitis.
back:
- Bacteria survive in avascular sequestra (biofilm)
- Host cannot deliver immune cells/antibiotics due to lack of blood supply
- Persistent infection promotes further periosteal elevation and bone death
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 596 (Book Page): [This process will devascularise the cortical bone, causing bone death... bacteria alter their metabolic state, making them more resistant both to the host immune system and to antibiotics.]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: What is the most frequently identified pathogen in pediatric native joint septic arthritis?
back: - Staphylococcus aureus
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [The most frequently identified organism is Staphylococcus aureus. Streptococcal infection is also common]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: What is the primary biochemical cause of initial articular cartilage damage in joint infections?
back: Bacterial toxins and lytic enzymes released directly into the joint space.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): Toxins and lytic enzymes from bacteria cause early damage to articular cartilage.

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: Explain the role of host leukocytes in the pathogenesis of cartilage destruction.
back: Leukocytes release proteases that degrade both the infecting bacteria and the essential collagen matrix of the articular cartilage.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): Pus in a joint is destructive: the proteases produced by leukocytes destroy both the bacteria and the collagen matrix of the articular cartilage.

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: Why are neonates uniquely prone to septic arthritis spreading from proximal femoral osteomyelitis?
back: The proximal femoral metaphysis is intracapsular in neonates, allowing pus to track through the cortex directly into the joint space.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 635 (Book Page): In the neonate, proximal femoral osteomyelitis and septic arthritis are essentially the same condition (Figure 44.41c).

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: How does the intra-articular pressure of septic arthritis lead to epiphyseal avascular necrosis?
back: High-pressure pus causes tamponade of epiphyseal vessels or direct ischaemic infarction of the bone.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): AVN may occur secondary to pressure effects or ischaemic infarction.

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: Describe the metabolic state of bacteria within an orthopaedic bioflm.
back: Bacteria alter their metabolic state within a polysaccharide matrix, becoming highly resistant to host immunity and antibiotics.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): These bacteria alter their metabolic state, making them more resistant both to the host immune system and to antibiotics.

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: Define 'Sequestrum' as seen in the progression of chronic osteomyelitis.
back: A fragment of dead cortical bone that has separated from living bone due to devascularisation by the infection.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): The infected bone reacts to the infection by separating dead fragments of bone (sequestration).

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: What is the mechanism of cortical bone death in acute osteomyelitis?
back: Pus tracks through the cortex and elevates the periosteum, stripping the blood supply and rendering the underlying bone avascular.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): Pus may track through the cortex to form periosteal elevation... This process will devascularise the cortical bone, causing bone death.

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: Why does haematogenous osteomyelitis typically begin in the metaphysis of long bones?
back: The slow, turbulent blood flow through looped sinusoidal vessels in the metaphysis encourages bacterial seeding during bacteraemia.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): Infection starts in the metaphyses of long bones, where the slow fow through the looped vessels combined with microtrauma encourages seeding of infection.

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: Pathologically, how does an 'Involucrum' form in response to bone infection?
back: Elevated periosteum (due to pus/inflammation) acts as a stimulus to lay down a new layer of reactive bone around the infected site.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): New bone is laid down around the infection from the periosteum (involucrum).

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: What is the hallmark of chronic bone infection following acute infammation?
back: Bone death (necrosis) resulting from impaired vascularity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): This process will devascularise the cortical bone, causing bone death – the characteristic feature of chronic osteomyelitis.

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: What are the three primary routes of bacterial entry into a native joint?
back:
1. Haematogenous dissemination (from another focus).
2. Direct inoculation (trauma or surgery).
3. Local extension from an adjacent focus (e.g., osteomyelitis).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 619 (Book Page): [Joint infection may arise as a result of haematogenous dissemination of bacteria from another focus (e.g. endocarditis) or may occur as a result of direct inoculation or local extension from an infected source (e.g. traumatic wound or adjacent osteomyelitis).]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: What two types of bacterial products cause early damage to articular cartilage?
back: Bacterial toxins and lytic enzymes cause the initial damage to articular cartilage during joint infection.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): [Toxins and lytic enzymes from bacteria cause early damage to articular cartilage.]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: How does a bacterial biofilm contribute to the pathogenesis of chronic joint infection?
back: Bacteria adhere to dead bone or implants, forming a polysaccharide matrix (biofilm) that protects them from host immunity and antibiotics.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): [Bacteria can adhere to dead bone or implant surfaces, forming a complex community enveloped in a polysaccharide matrix, known as a bioflm. These bacteria alter their metabolic state, making them more resistant both to the host immune system and to antibiotics.]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: In the pathogenesis of septic arthritis, what cellular products destroy the collagen matrix?
back: Proteases produced by leukocytes destroy both the bacteria and the structural collagen matrix of the articular cartilage.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [Pus in a joint is destructive: the proteases produced by leu - kocytes destroy both the bacteria and the collagen matrix of the articular cartilage.]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: What mechanism causes ischaemic infarction and avascular necrosis within a septic joint?
back: High intra-articular pressure from pus accumulation causes pressure effects and ischaemic infarction of the epiphyses.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [AVN may occur secondary to pressure efects or ischaemic infarction.]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: Why is the long bone metaphysis highly susceptible to bacterial seeding during bacteraemia?
back: The region features slow blood flow through looped vessels and a high vulnerability to microtrauma.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [Infection starts in the metaphyses of long bones, where the slow fow through the looped vessels combined with microtrauma encourages seeding of infection during a bacteraemia]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: How does acute osteomyelitis lead to the pathogenesis of ischaemic bone death?
back: Pus tracks through the cortex and elevates the periosteum, which devascularises the cortical bone and forms a sequestrum.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): [The medullary bone may form abscesses and pus may track through the cortex to form periosteal elevation and soft-tissue extension. This process will devascularise the cortical bone, causing bone death]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: Define the pathological terms 'sequestrum' and 'involucrum' in chronic bone infection.
back:
1. Sequestrum: Fragments of dead bone separated from living bone.
2. Involucrum: A sheath of new bone laid down by the periosteum around the infection.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): [The infected bone reacts to the infection by separating dead fragments of bone (sequestration)... New bone is laid down around the infection from the periosteum (involucrum)]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: How do bacteria within a biofilm evade the host's metabolic targeting by antibiotics?
back: Bacteria alter their metabolic state to a dormant or less active phase, increasing phenotypic resistance to antimicrobial agents.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): [These bacteria alter their metabolic state, making them more resistant both to the host immune system and to antibiotics.]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: Which organism is the most common pathogen in native bone and joint infection?
back: Staphylococcus aureus.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): [Virulent Gram-positive organisms, particularly Staphylococcus aureus, are the most common cause of bone or joint infection in native tissue.]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: What is the primary pathological event marking the transition to chronic osteomyelitis?
back: Devascularization of the cortical bone, resulting in the formation of dead bone (sequestrum).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): This process will devascularise the cortical bone, causing bone death – the characteristic feature of chronic osteomyelitis.

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: How does biofilm formation contribute to the persistence of orthopaedic infections?
back: Bacteria create a polysaccharide matrix and alter their metabolism, becoming resistant to antibiotics and the host immune system.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): Bacteria can adhere to dead bone or implant surfaces, forming a complex community enveloped in a polysaccharide matrix, known as a bioflm. These bacteria alter their metabolic state, making them more resistant both to the host immune system and to antibiotics.

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: Contrast the bone reactive processes of sequestration and involucrum formation.
back:
• Sequestrum: Separation of dead fragments of bone.
• Involucrum: Deposition of new bone around the infection by the periosteum.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): The infected bone reacts to the infection by separating dead fragments of bone (sequestration) and forming sinuses to drain pus and discharge small bone fragments. New bone is laid down around the infection from the periosteum (involucrum).

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: Why is neonatal proximal femoral osteomyelitis often accompanied by septic arthritis?
back: The proximal femoral metaphysis is intracapsular; once the periosteum is breached, infection spreads directly into the joint cavity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 635 (Book Page): The metaphysis of a long bone may be intracapsular and infection may spread easily into the joint once the periosteum is breached. In the neonate, proximal femoral osteomyelitis and septic arthritis are essentially the same condition.

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: Which specific agents are responsible for rapid cartilage destruction in septic arthritis?
back:
• Bacterial toxins.
• Lytic enzymes from bacteria.
• Host leukocyte proteases.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): Toxins and lytic enzymes from bacteria cause early damage to articular cartilage. Page 634 (Book Page): Pus in a joint is destructive: the proteases produced by leukocytes destroy both the bacteria and the collagen matrix of the articular cartilage.

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: What is the most common pathogen for native joint and bone infections across all ages?
back: Staphylococcus aureus.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): Virulent Gram-positive organisms, particularly Staphylococcus aureus, are the most common cause of bone or joint infection in native tissue.

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: How does pus accumulation leads to avascular necrosis (AVN) of intra-articular epiphyses?
back: Increased intra-articular pressure leads to mechanical tamponade or ischemic infarction of the epiphyses.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): AVN may occur secondary to pressure efects or ischaemic infarction. The treatment of a presumed septic arthritis therefore requires the prompt removal of pus from the joint.

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: Differentiate primary septic arthritis from a sympathetic joint effusion in pediatric cases.
back:
• Septic Arthritis: Direct bacterial infection/pus in joint.
• Sympathetic Effusion: Reactive fluid secondary to adjacent metaphyseal osteomyelitis without joint organisms.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 635 (Book Page): The diferentiation between the two may be difcult and a sympathetic joint efusion may occur with metaphyseal osteomyelitis. Thus, if there are no organisms seen on microscopy of a joint aspirate, the possibility of a coexisting osteomyelitis must be considered.

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: Why are long bone metaphyses the most common site for haematogenous infection seeding?
back: Slow blood flow through looped vessels combined with localized microtrauma encourages bacterial seeding during bacteraemia.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): Infection starts in the metaphyses of long bones, where the slow fow through the looped vessels combined with microtrauma encourages seeding of infection during a bacteraemia.

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: What is the primary role of leukocyte proteases in an infected joint?
back: They destroy the collagen matrix of the articular cartilage.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): the proteases produced by leukocytes destroy both the bacteria and the collagen matrix of the articular cartilage.

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: What are the three primary routes for bacterial entry into a joint?
back:
1. Haematogenous spread (via blood).
2. Direct inoculation (trauma or surgery).
3. Contiguous extension (spread from adjacent osteomyelitis).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 599 (Book Page): [Joint infection may arise as a result of haematogenous dissemination of bacteria from another focus... or may occur as a result of direct inoculation or local extension from an infected source (e.g. traumatic wound or adjacent osteomyelitis).]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: Describe the pathophysiological role of a biofilm in joint infections.
back: Bacteria adhere to dead bone or implants and form a polysaccharide matrix (biofilm). This envelopes bacterial communities, altering their metabolic state to resist both host immunity and antibiotic therapy.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 596 (Book Page): [Bacteria can adhere to dead bone or implant surfaces, forming a complex community enveloped in a polysaccharide matrix, known as a biofilm. These bacteria alter their metabolic state, making them more resistant both to the host immune system and to antibiotics.]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: Contrast the common pathogens involved in native versus prosthetic joint infections.
back: Native joints are primarily infected by virulent Gram-positive organisms (Staphylococcus aureus). Prosthetic infections often involve low-virulence skin commensals (coagulase-negative staphylococci, Cutibacterium acnes).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 596 (Book Page): [Virulent Gram-positive organisms, particularly Staphylococcus aureus, are the most common cause of bone or joint infection in native tissue. However, once prosthetic material is implanted... This includes organisms with low virulence that are usually considered skin commensals, such as coagulase-negative staphylococci... and Cutibacterium acnes.]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: A child has pus under pressure in a septic hip. Explain the fate of the cartilage.
back: Pus is destructive; proteases produced by leukocytes destroy the collagen matrix of the articular cartilage. Additionally, bacterial toxins and lytic enzymes cause early cartilage damage.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [Pus in a joint is destructive: the proteases produced by leukocytes destroy both the bacteria and the collagen matrix of the articular cartilage... Toxins and lytic enzymes from bacteria cause early damage to articular cartilage.]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: How does the biofilm metabolic state specifically impede pharmacological treatment?
back: Bacteria in the biofilm enter a sessile, altered metabolic state. This, combined with the physical barrier of the polysaccharide matrix, significantly reduces antibiotic efficacy compared to planktonic (free-floating) cells.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 596 (Book Page): [These bacteria alter their metabolic state, making them more resistant both to the host immune system and to antibiotics.]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: What specific histological threshold confirms the presence of periprosthetic infection?
back: The presence of 5 or more polymorphonuclear neutrophils (PMNs) per high-powered field (HPF) in at least five separate fields.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 599 (Book Page): [The presence of fve or more polymorphonuclear neutrophils per high-powered feld is diagnostic in fracture-related joint infections and PJIs.]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: Differentiate between a sequestrum and an involucrum in chronic osteomyelitis.
back: A sequestrum is a fragment of dead, avascular bone separated from living tissue. An involucrum is a layer of new bone laid down around the site of infection by the periosteum.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 596 (Book Page): [The infected bone reacts to the infection by separating dead fragments of bone (sequestration) and forming sinuses to drain pus... New bone is laid down around the infection from the periosteum (involucrum).]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: Why is hip osteomyelitis frequently indistinguishable from septic arthritis in neonates?
back: In neonates, vascular channels pass directly through the physis, connecting the metaphysis and epiphysis. This allows metaphyseal infection to spread easily into the joint space once the periosteum is breached.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 635 (Book Page): [In the neonate, proximal femoral osteomyelitis and septic arthritis are essentially the same condition... vascular channels pass through the physis, connecting the metaphysis with the epiphysis.]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: Explain the physiological mechanism by which a septic joint causes secondary avascular necrosis.
back: The accumulation of purulent material increases intra-articular pressure, creating a tamponade effect on epiphyseal vessels. Direct ischemic infarction follows, leading to head destruction.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [AVN may occur secondary to pressure efects or ischaemic infarction. The treatment of a presumed septic arthritis therefore requires the prompt removal of pus from the joint...]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: What is the primary biochemical target of leukocyte-produced proteases in the joint?
back: The collagen matrix of the articular cartilage.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [Pus in a joint is destructive: the proteases produced by leukocytes destroy both the bacteria and the collagen matrix of the articular cartilage.]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: What are the three primary routes through which bacteria reach and infect native joints?
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 599 (Book Page): [Joint infection may arise as a result of haematogenous dissemination of bacteria from another focus (e.g. endocarditis) or may occur as a result of direct inoculation or local extension from an infected source (e.g. traumatic wound or adjacent osteomyelitis).]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: Describe the structural formation and biological significance of a bacterial biofilm in orthopaedic infection.
back: Bacteria adhere to dead bone or implants, creating a complex community in a polysaccharide matrix. This alters bacterial metabolism, increasing resistance to host immunity and antibiotics.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 596 (Book Page): [Bacteria can adhere to dead bone or implant surfaces, forming a complex community enveloped in a polysaccharide matrix, known as a biofilm. These bacteria alter their metabolic state, making them more resistant both to the host immune system and to antibiotics.]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: Which specific substances are primarily responsible for the rapid destruction of articular cartilage in septic joints?
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 596 (Book Page): [Toxins and lytic enzymes from bacteria cause early damage to articular cartilage.] Page 634 (Book Page): [Pus in a joint is destructive: the proteases produced by leukocytes destroy both the bacteria and the collagen matrix of the articular cartilage.]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: Explain the mechanism by which joint sepsis leads to Avascular Necrosis (AVN) of the femoral head.
back: Pus accumulation creates excessive intra-articular pressure and ischaemic infarction. This causes secondary pressure effects or vascular obstruction, leading to epiphyseal death.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [AVN may occur secondary to pressure effects or ischaemic infarction. The treatment of a presumed septic arthritis therefore requires the prompt removal of pus from the joint...]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: What are the characteristic synovial fluid leukocyte findings diagnostic of native joint septic arthritis?
back:
1. White Cell Count (WCC) between 50,000–150,000 cells/mm³;
2. Neutrophil predominance greater than 90%.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 599 (Book Page): [A high WCC in joint fluid (e.g. 50–150 000 cells/mm3), with a neutrophil predominance (>90%), is characteristic of infection.]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: List the four clinical predictors used to differentiate pediatric septic arthritis from transient synovitis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [Four clinical predictors can differentiate between septic arthritis and transient synovitis... History of fever >38.5°C; Non-weight-bearing; Erythrocyte sedimentation rate >40 mm/h; White cell count >12 × 10 9 /L]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: Why are neonatal joints uniquely susceptible to septic arthritis secondary to adjacent osteomyelitis?
back: In neonates, vascular channels pass through the physis. This connects the metaphysis to the epiphysis, allowing medullary infection to spread easily into the joint cavity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 636 (Book Page): [In the neonate, vascular channels pass through the physis, connecting the metaphysis with the epiphysis, and a poorer outcome may ensue... In the neonate, proximal femoral osteomyelitis and septic arthritis are essentially the same condition]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: What is the primary histological indicator of confirmed infection around an orthopaedic implant?
back: The presence of five or more polymorphonuclear neutrophils per high-powered field (HPF).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 598 (Book Page): [The presence of five or more polymorphonuclear neutrophils per high-powered field is diagnostic in fracture-related joint infections and PJIs.]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: Describe the Gächter stages that necessitate open synovectomy rather than simple arthroscopic washout.
back: Gächter stages 3 and 4, characterized by major synovial thickening, aggressive synovitis, or subchondral erosions visible on radiology.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 600 (Book Page): [A synovectomy is recommended if there is major synovial thickening, aggressive synovitis or subchondral erosions seen on radiology (Gächter stages 3 and 4).]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: What is the most common pathogen responsible for native joint septic arthritis across all age groups?
back: Staphylococcus aureus.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 597 (Book Page): [Virulent Gram-positive organisms, particularly Staphylococcus aureus, are the most common cause of bone or joint infection in native tissue.]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: What is the primary pathological trigger for acute osteomyelitis?
back: Pathogenic bacterial invasion causing inflammation and the formation of medullary bone abscesses.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): [Acute osteomyelitis occurs when pathogenic organisms cause infection, leading to infammation in the bone and surrounding tissues. The medullary bone may form abscesses...]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: How do leukocyte proteases contribute to subsequent cartilage destruction in septic arthritis?
back: While destroying bacteria, these proteases simultaneously degrade the collagen matrix of the articular cartilage.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [Pus in a joint is destructive: the proteases produced by leukocytes destroy both the bacteria and the collagen matrix of the articular cartilage.]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: Define the structural composition of a bacterial biofilm in bone infection.
back: A complex community of bacteria enveloped within a polysaccharide matrix adhered to dead bone or implants.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): [Bacteria can adhere to dead bone or implant surfaces, forming a complex community enveloped in a polysaccharide matrix, known as a bioflm.]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: How does pus tracking through the cortex lead to bone death (necrosis)?
back: Pus causes periosteal elevation, which devascularizes the cortical bone, resulting in sequestration of dead fragments.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): [...pus may track through the cortex to form periosteal elevation and soft-tissue extension. This process will devascularise the cortical bone, causing bone death – the characteristic feature of chronic osteomyelitis.]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: How does the metabolic state of bacteria change within a biofilm to resist antibiotics?
back: Bacteria alter their metabolic state within the polysaccharide matrix, rendering them highly resistant to host immunity and antimicrobial agents.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): [These bacteria alter their metabolic state, making them more resistant both to the host immune system and to antibiotics.]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: Contrast the definitions of sequestrum and involucrum in chronic bone infection.
back:
• Sequestrum: Fragments of dead bone separated from living tissue.
• Involucrum: New bone laid down by the periosteum surrounding the infection.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): [The infected bone reacts to the infection by separating dead fragments of bone (sequestration)... New bone is laid down around the infection from the periosteum (involucrum)]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: By what two physical mechanisms does septic arthritis cause avascular necrosis (AVN)?
back: AVN occurs secondary to direct pressure effects from accumulated pus or resulting ischaemic infarction.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [AVN may occur secondary to pressure efects or ischaemic infarction.]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: Which specific bacterial products cause early damage to articular cartilage during infection?
back: Bacterial toxins and lytic enzymes are primarily responsible for initial cartilage injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): [Toxins and lytic enzymes from bacteria cause early damage to articular cartilage.]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: Describe the physiological loop leading to the 'bone-within-a-bone' appearance in chronic osteomyelitis.
back: Periosteal elevation stimulates new bone (involucrum) formation that completely envelops necrotic bone (sequestrum).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 635 (Book Page): [In cases of untreated or chronic infection this new bone or involucrum may surround the dead bone, the sequestrum, leading to a ‘bone-within-a-bone’ appearance]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: Why does haematogenous osteomyelitis characteristically initiate in the metaphysis?
back: The slow blood flow through looped vessels in the metaphysis, combined with microtrauma, facilitates bacterial seeding.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [Infection starts in the metaphyses of long bones, where the slow fow through the looped vessels combined with microtrauma encourages seeding of infection during a bacteraemia]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: What is the primary enzymatic mechanism for cartilage destruction in septic arthritis?
back:
• Proteases produced by host leukocytes (neutrophils).
• Bacterial toxins and lytic enzymes.
• These agents degrade the collagen matrix of the articular cartilage.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [Pus in a joint is destructive: the proteases produced by leukocytes destroy both the bacteria and the collagen matrix of the articular cartilage.]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: How does purulent joint effusion lead to avascular necrosis (AVN) of the intra-articular epiphysis?
back:
• High intra-articular pressure from pus accumulation.
• Pressure produces a tamponade effect causing ischaemic infarction.
• Interruption of blood flow leads to bone death in the epiphysis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [AVN may occur secondary to pressure effects or ischaemic infarction.]

category: Explain the pathogenesis of joint infection and subsequent cartilage destruction
front: Q: What specific neonatal anatomical feature facilitates the spread of infection from bone to joint?
back:
• Persistent vascular channels traverse the physis.
• These connect the metaphysis with the epiphysis, allowing direct bacterial migration.
• Many neonatal long bone metaphyses are also located intracapsularly.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 635 (Book Page): [In the neonate, vascular channels pass through the physis, connecting the metaphysis with the epiphysis... The metaphysis of a long bone may be intracapsular and infection may spread easily into the joint once the periosteum is breached.]

category: Identify the clinical features of acute septic arthritis in children and adults
front: Q: What is the hallmark clinical triad of acute septic arthritis?
back:
- Acute onset hot joint
- Joint swelling and inflammation
- Severe pain on active/passive movement with systemic upset (e.g., fever).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 599 (Book Page): [Most patients present after an acute or subacute history with a single hot, swollen, painful joint... There is severe pain if any attempt is made to move the affected joint actively or passively. Fever and other systemic signs are usually present.]

category: Identify the clinical features of acute septic arthritis in children and adults
front: Q: Describe the characteristic clinical feature of 'pseudoparalysis' in neonatal septic arthritis.
back: The neonate avoids all movement of the affected limb to minimize pain, mimicking paralysis despite normal nerve function.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 599 (Book Page): [In children and adults, the knee joint is most frequently affected, whereas in neonates it is the hip... The joint is held immobile in the 'position of comfort', with 'pseudoparalysis' in neonates.]

category: Identify the clinical features of acute septic arthritis in children and adults
front: Q: How do the most common sites for septic arthritis differ between neonates and adults?
back:
- Neonates: Hip joint
- Children/Adults: Knee joint.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 599 (Book Page): [In children and adults, the knee joint is most frequently affected, whereas in neonates it is the hip.]

category: Identify the clinical features of acute septic arthritis in children and adults
front: Q: What is the clinical significance of a patient refusing to move a joint in the 'position of comfort'?
back: It indicates a distended capsule with pus; moving the joint from this mid-flexion position increases intra-articular pressure and pain.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 599 (Book Page): [The joint is held immobile in the 'position of comfort'... There is severe pain if any attempt is made to move the affected joint actively or passively.]

category: Identify the clinical features of acute septic arthritis in children and adults
front: Q: What are the diagnostic synovial fluid leukocyte findings for septic arthritis?
back:
- White Cell Count (WCC): 50,000–150,000 cells/mm³
- Neutrophil predominance: >90%.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 599 (Book Page): [A high WCC in joint fluid (e.g. 50–150 000 cells/mm3), with a neutrophil predominance (>90%), is characteristic of infection.]

category: Identify the clinical features of acute septic arthritis in children and adults
front: Q: Why is septic arthritis considered a surgical emergency regarding cartilage integrity?
back: Proteases produced by invading leukocytes rapidly destroy both bacteria and the collagen matrix of the articular cartilage.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [Pus in a joint is destructive: the proteases produced by leukocytes destroy both the bacteria and the collagen matrix of the articular cartilage.]

category: Identify the clinical features of acute septic arthritis in children and adults
front: Q: Does the absence of fever rule out septic arthritis in adults?
back: No. Fever is absent in approximately one-third of adult cases; the diagnosis must be based on local clinical findings.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 599 (Book Page): [Fever and other systemic signs are usually present, but their absence does not rule out the diagnosis. Fever is absent in about one-third of cases.]

category: Identify the clinical features of acute septic arthritis in children and adults
front: Q: Which specific pediatric population is at significantly increased risk for haematogenous septic arthritis?
back:
- Neonates
- Immunocompromised children
- Children with Sickle Cell Disease.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [Neonates, children with immunocompromise and those with sickle cell disease are at increased risk.]

category: Identify the clinical features of acute septic arthritis in children and adults
front: Q: Why can neonatal proximal femoral osteomyelitis often present as septic arthritis?
back: In neonates, vascular channels cross the physis, allowing infection to spread directly from the metaphysis into the joint space.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 635 (Book Page): [In the neonate, proximal femoral osteomyelitis and septic arthritis are essentially the same condition... vascular channels pass through the physis, connecting the metaphysis with the epiphysis.]

category: Identify the clinical features of acute septic arthritis in children and adults
front: Q: What is the most common pathogen causing native joint septic arthritis in both children and adults?
back: Staphylococcus aureus.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 600 (Book Page): [The most frequently identified organism is Staphylococcus aureus.]

category: Identify the clinical features of acute septic arthritis in children and adults
coreConcept: Physical Hallmarks of Native Joint Sepsis
front: Identify the cardinal physical examination hallmarks of acute native joint septic arthritis in adults and children.
back:
• Single hot, swollen, painful joint.
• Joint held immobile in a 'position of comfort'.
• Severe pain elicited by both active and passive range of motion.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 599 (Book Page): [Most patients present after an acute or subacute history with a single hot, swollen, painful joint... The joint is held immobile in the ‘position of comfort’... There is severe pain if any attempt is made to move the afected joint actively or passively.]

category: Identify the clinical features of acute septic arthritis in children and adults
front: What specific clinical features characterize acute septic arthritis presentations in neonates and young children?
back:
• Neonates: 'Pseudoparalysis' of the affected limb.
• Children: Sudden onset of high fever, systemic toxaemia, and refusal to weight-bear.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [Classically, the child presents with pain, fever and a reluctance to move the joint; in the lower limb, this implies a reluctance to weight bear. ... ‘pseudoparalysis’ in neonates.]

category: Identify the clinical features of acute septic arthritis in children and adults
coreConcept: Systemic Variation in Adult Joint Sepsis
front: Why is the absence of systemic fever a significant diagnostic pitfall in adult acute septic arthritis?
back:
• Fever and systemic signs are absent in approximately one-third of adult cases.
• Clinical diagnosis must rely on localized joint pain, swelling, and inflammatory signs.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 599 (Book Page): [Fever and other systemic signs are usually present, but their absence does not rule out the diagnosis. Fever is absent in about one-third of cases.]

category: Identify the clinical features of acute septic arthritis in children and adults
front: Q: What are the cardinal clinical local signs of acute native joint septic arthritis?
back:
• Single hot, swollen, painful joint
• Reluctance to move the joint (active/passive)
• Lower limb: reluctance to weight-bear
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 599 (Book Page): [Most patients present after an acute or subacute history with a single hot, swollen, painful joint... there is severe pain if any attempt is made to move the affected joint actively or passively.]

category: Identify the clinical features of acute septic arthritis in children and adults
front: Q: How do host leukocytes physiologically contribute to articular destruction in septic arthritis?
back:
• Production of proteases
• Direct destruction of the collagen matrix
• Simultaneous destruction of infecting bacteria
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [Pus in a joint is destructive: the proteases produced by leukocytes destroy both the bacteria and the collagen matrix of the articular cartilage.]

category: Identify the clinical features of acute septic arthritis in children and adults
front: Q: Which four clinical predictors differentiate pediatric septic arthritis from transient synovitis?
back:
• Fever >38.5°C
• Non-weight-bearing status
• ESR >40 mm/h
• White cell count >12 × 10⁹/L
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [Four clinical predictors can differentiate between septic arthritis and transient synovitis... History of fever >38.5°C, Non-weight-bearing, Erythrocyte sedimentation rate >40 mm/h, White cell count >12 × 10 9 /L]

category: Identify the clinical features of acute septic arthritis in children and adults
front: Q: Describe the clinical manifestation of acute joint infection specifically in a neonate.
back:
• Pseudoparalysis (limb held immobile)
• Joint held in "position of comfort"
• Systemic toxaemia or overwhelming sepsis
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 599 (Book Page): [The joint is held immobile in the ‘position of comfort’, with ‘pseudoparalysis’ in neonates.]

category: Identify the clinical features of acute septic arthritis in children and adults
front: Q: What is the recommended antibiotic strategy and duration for native joint sepsis?
back:
• Total duration: 3–6 weeks
• Initial route: High-dose intravenous
• Longer courses for S. aureus or bacteremia
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 600 (Book Page): [Antibiotics are usually given for 3–6 weeks (beginning with intravenous therapy). Longer courses should be considered... if the infection is caused by S. aureus.]

category: Identify the clinical features of acute septic arthritis in children and adults
front: Q: What synovial fluid white cell count findings are characteristic of acute infection?
back:
• WCC: 50,000–150,000 cells/mm³
• Neutrophil predominance: >90%
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 599 (Book Page): [A high WCC in joint fluid (e.g. 50–150 000 cells/mm3), with a neutrophil predominance (>90%), is characteristic of infection.]

category: Identify the clinical features of acute septic arthritis in children and adults
front: Q: Identify the most common causative pathogen of septic arthritis across all age groups.
back:
• Staphylococcus aureus
• Streptococcal species (also common)
• Kingella kingae (specifically children <4 years)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 597 (Book Page): [Staphylococcus aureus (commonest across all settings)... Kingella kingae Common cause of septic arthritis in children under 4 years]

category: Identify the clinical features of acute septic arthritis in children and adults
front: Q: Contrast the clinical presentation of systemic fever in adult versus pediatric septic arthritis.
back:
• Children: Often toxic and febrile
• Adults: Fever absent in approximately one-third of cases
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 599 (Book Page): [Fever and other systemic signs are usually present, but their absence does not rule out the diagnosis. Fever is absent in about one-third of cases.]

category: Identify the clinical features of acute septic arthritis in children and adults
front: Q: How does hip joint instability manifest pathologically following neonatal septic arthritis?
back:
• Joint subluxation/dislocation
• Distension of joint capsule by effusion
• Avascular necrosis (AVN) from pressure effects
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [AVN may occur secondary to pressure effects or ischaemic infarction... Joint instability, particularly in the hip joint (Figure 44.40), may require the reduced joint to be splinted]

category: Identify the clinical features of acute septic arthritis in children and adults
front: Q: Describe the physical attitude of a limb in an adult with acute hip sepsis.
back:
• Limb held immobile
• Position of Comfort (slight flexion, abduction, external rotation)
• Severe pain on any attempted motion
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 599 (Book Page): [The joint is held immobile in the ‘position of comfort’... There is severe pain if any attempt is made to move the affected joint actively or passively.]

category: Identify the clinical features of acute septic arthritis in children and adults
front: Q: What is the classic clinical triad of symptoms for acute septic arthritis in children?
back:
- Joint pain
- High fever
- Reluctance to move the joint or weight-bear
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): "Classically, the child presents with pain, fever and a reluctance to move the joint; in the lower limb, this implies a reluctance to weight bear."

category: Identify the clinical features of acute septic arthritis in children and adults
front: Q: What physiological mechanism causes rapid joint destruction in acute septic arthritis?
back:
- Bacterial toxins destroy cartilage
- Leukocytes release proteases
- These enzymes digest the collagen matrix of the articular cartilage
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): "Pus in a joint is destructive: the proteases produced by leukocytes destroy both the bacteria and the collagen matrix of the articular cartilage."

category: Identify the clinical features of acute septic arthritis in children and adults
front: Q: Define 'pseudoparalysis' as it relates to neonatal septic arthritis.
back:
- The infant holds the affected joint completely immobile
- Positioned in the 'position of comfort' to minimize pain
- Mimics true paralysis due to severe pain on movement
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 599 (Book Page): "The joint is held immobile in the ‘position of comfort’, with ‘pseudoparalysis’ in neonates."

category: Identify the clinical features of acute septic arthritis in children and adults
front: Q: Why is a single hot, swollen joint in an adult with Rheumatoid Arthritis considered a surgical emergency?
back:
- Pre-existing arthropathy is a major risk factor for septic arthritis
- Infection can be masked by baseline inflammation or steroid use
- Delay causes rapid, irreversible joint destruction
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 599 (Book Page): "The condition most characteristically affects patients at extremes of age, usually with pre-existing arthropathy or immunocompromise (Table 43.2)."

category: Identify the clinical features of acute septic arthritis in children and adults
front: Q: Which organism has largely replaced Haemophilus influenzae as a cause of septic arthritis in immunized children?
back: - Kingella kingae
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): "The Haemophilus infuenzae type B (Hib) vaccine has essentially eliminated H. infuenzae as a cause of infection, but in some countries Kingella kingae has taken its place."

category: Identify the clinical features of acute septic arthritis in children and adults
front: Q: What synovial fluid white cell count (WCC) and neutrophil percentage typically identifies septic arthritis?
back:
- WCC: 50,000–150,000 cells/mm³
- Neutrophils: >90%
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 599 (Book Page): "A high WCC in joint fuid (e.g. 50–150 000 cells/mm3), with a neutrophil predominance (>90%), is characteristic of infection."

category: Identify the clinical features of acute septic arthritis in children and adults
front: Q: What is the mechanical significance of a patient holding a septic joint in the 'position of comfort'?
back:
- Posture that allows for maximum intracapsular volume
- Minimizes pain by reducing intra-articular pressure from pus
